questions.question: The newborn eye is usually ______.
questions.explanation:
A newborn is usually hypermetropic by +2D to +3D.

The anteroposterior (AP) diameter of the eyeball at birth is about 16.5 mm, which is about 70% of the adult size. This reduced axial length causes light to converge behind the retina, leading to hypermetropia.

Additionally, the corneal diameter at birth is 10 mm. The adult size (11.7 mm) is attained by 2 years of age. The orbit is more divergent (50°) as compared to adult (45°).

Note: The lacrimal glands are underdeveloped in a newborn and, hence, do not secrete tears.

questions.question: At what age would a child attain full visual acuity?
questions.explanation:
Full visual acuity is attained by the age of 6 years.

Important milestones in visual development are:

• At birth, there is no central fixation, and the eyes move randomly.

• By the first month of life, the fixation reflex starts developing and becomes established by 6 months.

• By 3 months, binocular vision is established.

• By 6 months, macular stereopsis and accommodation reflex are fully developed.

• By 6 years of age, full visual acuity (6/6) is attained.

questions.question: A 45-year-old lady presents with the abnormality as shown below. She is diagnosed with uveal melanoma. What is the embryological origin of the cells involved?
questions.explanation: Uveal melanomas arise from uveal melanocytes. Uveal and conjunctival melanocytes are derived from the neural crest cells.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the development of the eye?
options: The macula is fully developed at birth.
The cornea attains normal diameter by 2 years.
Full visual acuity is attained by 6 years of age.
questions.answer: A. The macula is fully developed at birth.
questions.explanation:
The macula is fully developed by 4–6 months of age. Apart from the macula, the rest of the retina is fully developed at birth.

Postnatal Development of Eye:

• 3 Months - Binocular single vision develops.

• 4-6 Months - Macula fully develops. Fusional reflexes, stereopsis, and accommodation become well developed

• 6 Months - Fixation, which had started developing in the first month is now complete

• 2 Years - Cornea develops to the normal adult diameter

• 6 Years - Visual acuity fully develops and reaches 6/6

• The lens, however, continues to grow throughout the life

questions.question: By how many weeks of embryonic development does the optic groove appear?
questions.explanation: The optic groove appears by 3 weeks. By approximately day 22, 2 small grooves appear on either side of the developing forebrain in the neural folds, these are called optic grooves. As the neural tube closes, these grooves develop outpouchings called optic vesicles. These optic vesicles extend from the forebrain to the surface ectoderm.

questions.question: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from _______.
questions.explanation: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from the neural crest.

questions.question: After conception, the canal of Schlemm appears by __________________ .
questions.explanation: The canal of Schlemm appears by the 4th month after conception.

questions.question: What is the anteroposterior diameter of the adult eyeball?
questions.explanation:
The anteroposterior (AP) diameter of the adult eye is 24 mm/2.4 cm.

At birth, the average axial length of the eyeball is 16.5 mm. By 3 years, it grows rapidly to approximately 23 mm. From 3 to 14 years of age, the axial length gradually increases by a further 1 mm, bringing it to the adult size of 24 mm. This overall adjustment in the eye size, including the refractive power, is called emmetropization.

questions.question: A 34-year-old lady comes to the clinic complaining of problems in her vision. On perimetry, a visual field defect as shown below is obtained. Which of the following vessels does not supply the anatomical location of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
The image shows bitemporal hemianopia, a defect caused by optic chiasmal lesions. The middle cerebral artery does not supply the optic chiasma.

Blood supply of optic chiasma:

• Anterior cerebral artery - dorsal chiasma

• Anterior communicating artery - ventral chiasma

• Internal carotid artery - ventral chiasma

• Superior hypophyseal artery - ventral (branch of internal carotid artery).

questions.question: A college student comes to the OPD for refractive error testing. Her eyes are dilated using tropicamide. Which of the following statements is false about the structure this drug acts on?
options: It is triangular in cross section.
There are around 30-40 processes in pars plana and pars plicata
Its epithelium is derived from the anterior edge of the optic cup.
The pars plana is approximately 4.5 mm from the limbus.
questions.answer: B. There are around 30-40 processes in pars plana and pars plicata
questions.explanation:
Tropicamide is a cycloplegic drug that acts on the ciliary body to cause mydriasis for refractory error testing. The ciliary body is a triangular structure that contains 60-70 ciliary processes in each eye, present on the pars plicata.

The pars plana is 4.5mm from the limbus while the distance between the equator and the limbus is 14mm.

The ciliary epithelium is derived from the optic cup (neuroectoderm) by the continued growth of the outer lip's anterior edge.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl you examined in an outreach camp is found to have this abnormality. What is the most common site where the condition is seen?
questions.explanation:
The condition depicted in the image is a coloboma of the iris, and the most common site of coloboma is the inferonasal quadrant.

A coloboma is a congenital malformation in one of the structures in the eye, such as the iris, retina, choroid, or optic disc, due to the failure of embryonic fissure closure. Coloboma of the uveal tract may be typical (seen in the inferonasal quadrant) or atypical (occasionally found in other positions). Typical coloboma is of two types:

• Complete: Extends from pupil to optic nerve, causing a corresponding lens indentation.

• Incomplete: May involve iris alone, or iris and ciliary body (more common), or iris, ciliary body and a part of choroid.

Other embryonic remnants in the eye:

• Mittendorf's dot - Remnant of the anterior end of the hyaloid artery

• Bergmeister papilla - Remnant of the posterior end of the hyaloid artery

• Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) - Failure of fetal vasculature to regress

The image below shows a fundoscopy view of persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.

questions.question: A child was brought with complaints of decreased vision. Fundus examination shows a developmental anomaly as shown below. What is the cause of this anomaly?
options: Incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure
Faulty migration of neural crest cells
questions.answer: A. Incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure
questions.explanation:
The image shows a coloboma of the optic disc, accompanied by a large chorioretinal coloboma located below the optic disc, which is caused by incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure.

This developmental anomaly may involve the optic nerve, choroid, retina, and iris. Coloboma of the optic disc can present in two forms: a minor effect often associated with refractive errors like hypermetropia and astigmatism and a fully developed coloboma that appears as a large inferonasal whitish excavation resembling the optic disc.

Defective vision and superior visual field defects are typically associated with fully developed coloboma. Additionally, this condition may be associated with chorioretinal coloboma, a congenital anomaly where the developing optic cup fails to fuse completely, leading to abnormal choroidal and retinal development.

Note: Faulty migration of neural crest cells results in anterior segment dysgenesis.

questions.question: What is the embryological origin of the structure marked in the image?
questions.explanation: The lacrimal gland arises from the surface ectoderm.

questions.question: The optic foramen is situated between the:
options: Lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid
Lesser wing and body of the sphenoid
Greater wing and body of the sphenoid
Two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid
questions.answer: D. Two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid
questions.explanation:
The optic foramen is situated between the two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid.

The optic foramen leads into the optic canal, which is formed medially by the body and laterally by the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, connecting the orbit's apex to the middle cranial fossa.

The optic canal transmits the optic nerve with its meningeal coverings; the ophthalmic artery, which is below the nerve, is embedded in its dural sheath, and a few twigs from the sympathetic plexus accompanying the artery.

questions.question: During a game, a 26-year-old baseball player is hit in the head by a baseball, which fractures the optic canal. Which of the following pairs of structures is most likely to be damaged?
questions.answer: C. Ophthalmic artery and optic nerve
questions.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario, a fracture of the optic canal is most likely to damage the ophthalmic artery and optic nerve, as these are the primary structures passing through it.

The optic foramen leads into the optic canal, which is a short cylindrical structure bounded medially by the body and laterally by the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, connecting the orbit's apex to the middle cranial fossa, serving as a pathway for the aforementioned structures along with its sympathetic plexus.

Optic canal fractures, often associated with basilar skull fractures, can lead to optic neuropathy. The intracanalicular and intracranial portion of the optic nerve is most commonly affected in head trauma.

Note: The greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bound the superior orbital fissure.

questions.question: The anterior segment of the eye includes all except ______.
questions.explanation:
The anterior segment of the eye does not include vitreous humor as it is a constituent of the posterior segment of the eye.

Anterior Segment
Posterior Segment

questions.question: The posterior chamber in the eyeball is filled with _______.
questions.explanation:
The posterior chamber of the eyeball is filled with aqueous humor.

The eyeball is divided into anterior and posterior segments. The anterior segment includes the lens and the structures anterior to it, such as the cornea, iris and two aqueous humor-filled spaces:

• Anterior chamber: Located between cornea and iris, contains aqueous humor and communicates with the posterior chamber through the pupil.

• Posterior chamber: Triangular-shaped space, also contains aqueous humor, bounded anteriorly by the posterior surface of the iris, laterally by the ciliary body, and posteriorly by the lens.

The posterior segment includes all structures located posterior to the lens, comprising of the vitreous humor, retina, choroid and optic disc.

questions.question: Which of the following structures is attached to Whitnall’s tubercle?
options: Check ligament of the medial rectus
Check ligament of the lateral rectus
questions.answer: C. Check ligament of the lateral rectus
questions.explanation:
Check ligament of the lateral rectus is attached to Whitnall’s tubercle.

Lateral orbital tubercle or Whitnall's tubercle is a small elevation on the orbital surface of the zygomatic bone, just within the lateral orbital margin. It is about 11 mm below the fronto-zygomatic suture.

Four structures are attached to it:

1. Check ligament of the lateral rectus

2. Lockwood’s ligament (Suspensory ligament of the eyeball)

3. Lateral palpebral ligament

4. Lateral horn of the levator aponeurosis

The Whitnall's ligament or the superior transverse ligament of the eye, is attached to the superior tarsal plate and the orbital bone.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the tarsal plates?
options: They give structural support to the eyelid.
LPS aponeurosis is attached to the superior border of the upper tarsal plate.
Their medial and lateral ends form the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments, respectively.
questions.answer: A. Tarsal plates are cartilaginous structures.
questions.explanation:
The tarsal plates are not cartilaginous structures but firm, dense connective tissue (fibrous tissue) plates.

The tarsal plates serve as the structural support of the eyelids. The height of the upper tarsal plate is about 10 mm, and that of the lower tarsal plate is 4 mm. Both plates have a thickness of about 1 mm. The ends form the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments (medial and lateral canthal tendons). The levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) aponeurosis is attached to the superior border of the upper tarsal plate.

The meibomian glands are located within the tarsus. These are holocrine-secreting sebaceous glands that are not associated with lash follicles.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man is being evaluated for herpes zoster ophthalmicus. On eliciting corneal reflex, there is no response. Which of the following nerves forms the afferent limb of this reflex?
questions.explanation:
The sensory supply of the cornea comes from the long ciliary nerve (branch of the nasociliary nerve). It forms the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.

The sensory nerve supply of the eye is by the ophthalmic nerve.

• Lacrimal nerve- lacrimal gland, conjunctiva, lateral eyelid

• Frontal nerve- conjunctiva, eyelid, part of the forehead

• Nasociliary nerve

• Long ciliary nerve- cornea, ciliary body, iris

• Infra-trochlear nerve- conjunctiva, lacrimal sac, caruncle, medial part of the eyelids

Corneal sensation is reduced in leprosy and diabetes mellitus (neuropathy).

questions.question: Which intrinsic ocular muscle has a parasympathetic innervation?
questions.explanation:
The intrinsic ocular muscle supplied by parasympathetic innervation is the sphincter pupillae.

1. Parasympathetic innervation:

• Sphincter pupillae: Short ciliary nerve–Ciliary ganglion

• Ciliary muscle–Accessory ganglion

2. Sympathetic innervation: Dilator pupillae and Muller’s muscle

3. Motor Supply:

• 3rd nerve: All extraocular muscles (except the 2 given below)

• 6th nerve: Lateral rectus (LR6)

• 4th nerve: Superior oblique (SO4)

• 7th nerve: Orbicularis oculi

questions.question: What is the thinnest part of the retina?
questions.explanation:
The retina is the thinnest (0.080 mm) at the ora serrata, and thickest, at the foveal rim (0.23, 0.320 mm).

The ora serrata is the serrated junction between the retina and ciliary body.

questions.question: In the anatomy dissection hall, you are shown the dissected orbit with the markers as shown below. You are asked to choose the muscles causing depression of the eyeball. Which will you choose?
questions.explanation:
The muscles responsible for the depression of the eyeball are the inferior rectus (E) and superior oblique (A).

Image markings:

• A- Superior oblique

• B- Levator palpebrae superiors

• C- Superior rectus

• D- Inferior oblique

• E- Inferior rectus

Nerve supply of extra-ocular muscles:

• Oculomotor nerve (III)- Superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris

• Abducens nerve (VI)- Lateral rectus

• Trochlear nerve (IV)- Superior oblique

questions.explanation: Image 4, which is formed on the posterior surface of the lens, is inverted.

questions.question: The visual axis is the line joining the _________.
options: Centre of the cornea to the retina
Centre of the lens to the cornea
questions.explanation: The visual axis is the line joining the fixation point (object), nodal point (centre of the lens), and the fovea.

questions.question: What is the angle formed between the optic axis and visual axis at the nodal point?
questions.explanation:
Angle alpha (α) is the angle between the optical axis and visual axis at the nodal point.

Angle lambda (λ) is the angle between the pupillary axis and the line of sight. It is the global tilt offset of the eye when it fixates on a specific target and is a response to the eccentric displaced position of the fovea from the geometrical center of the retina. (Option B)

Angle kappa (κ) is the angle between the visual axis and the pupillary line at the cornea. It is the only angle that can be measured and is of clinical significance. (Option C)

• Positive κ is seen in pseudoexotropia

• Negative κ is seen in pseudoesotropia

Angle gamma (γ) is the angle between the optical axis and the fixation axis at the center of eyeball rotation. (Option D)

questions.question: A 28-year-old man comes to get his power checked. The optometrist finds the focal length of his lens to be 0.75m; what will be its refractive power?
questions.explanation:
Refractive power (dioptre) = 1/Focal length in metres

So, for the given question, refractive power (D) = 1/0.75 = 1.33 D

What is the distance between point A and B shown below?

DD - Disc Diameter
questions.explanation:
In the image, point A is the optic disc and point B is the fovea. The fovea is situated about 2 disc diameters (3–4 mm) away from the temporal margin of the optic disc.

The optic disc is an area of about 1.5 mm. There is a blind spot / physiological scotoma, corresponding to the optic disc.

questions.question: A 6-year-old child complains that she cannot see anything on the whiteboard clearly. On ophthalmological examination, she is found to have a 2 mm shortening of the axial length of the eyeball. How much eye power will this lead to?
questions.explanation:
Shortening of 2mm of the axial length of the eyeball will lead to 6D of hypermetropia.

In axial hypermetropia, 1mm shortening of the anteroposterior diameter of the eye results in 3 dioptres of hypermetropia. Therefore, 2-mm shortening will lead to 6D of hypermetropia.

In curvature hypermetropia, a 1mm increase in radius of curvature results in 6 dioptres of hypermetropia.

questions.question: You are studying the optics of a patient with regular astigmatism. Identify the point at which the clearest image is formed?
questions.explanation:
The given figure is a Sturm's conoid. It represents a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic surface. The image is clearest or least confusing as point D, the circle of least confusion.

When light passes through a regularly astigmatic surface(surface with toric curvature), vertical and horizontal rays converge at different points.

The distance between the points of convergence (focus) of the vertical and horizontal rays is called the focal interval of strum. (distance between points B and F). The circle of least confusion/ circle of diffusion lies at the mid-point of this interval.

For the given Sturm's conoid,

• At point A, a horizontal oval is formed because vertical rays converge more rapidly than horizontal rays.

• At point B, vertical rays come to a focus, while horizontal rays are still converging; so, it will be a horizontal straight line.

• At points C, D, and E, the vertical rays are diverging and horizontal rays are still converging.

• At point D, the vertical rays have diverged as much as the horizontal rays have converged; so, we get a perfect circle called the circle of least confusion.

• At point E, a vertical oval is formed.

• At point F, a vertical straight line is formed

• At point G and beyond, both rays are diverging, and we always get a vertical oval/prolate ellipse.

questions.question: What is the Stiles-Crawford effect?
options: Cutting off of the peripheral rays by the iris
High refractive index of the core of nucleus of the lens than that of the peripheral cortex
Low sensitivity of the peripheral retina
More sensitivity of the retina to perpendicular rays than the oblique rays
questions.answer: D. More sensitivity of the retina to perpendicular rays than the oblique rays
questions.explanation:
The Stiles–Crawford effect refers to the greater sensitivity of the retina to perpendicular rays than the oblique rays. It is one of the natural mechanisms that decrease aberration in the eye. The rays of light that enter through the center of the pupil have higher sensitivity as compared to those entering from the periphery of the pupil.

Natural mechanisms that decrease aberrations in the human eye:

• Cutting-off of the peripheral rays by the iris

• The high refractive index of the core of the nucleus of the lens than that of the peripheral cortex

• Low sensitivity of the peripheral retina

• Stiles–Crawford effect

options: Rods and cones release Ach at their synapses.
Bipolar cells show either depolarization or hyperpolarization.
questions.answer: A. Rods and cones release Ach at their synapses.
questions.explanation:
Rods and cones release glutamate (not acetylcholine) at their synapses.

Photoreceptors get hyperpolarized in response to stimulus, and hence, phototransduction is associated with hyperpolarization.

Amacrine cells secrete at least eight types of neurotransmitters, including GABA, glycine, dopamine, acetylcholine, and indolamine, all of which function as inhibitory neurotransmitters.

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for inducing phototransduction?
questions.explanation:
Metarhodopsin II is responsible for phototransduction.

It activates transducin member of G proteins. This leads to the closure of Na+ channels and hyperpolarization, thereby inducing phototransduction (signal transduction in the retina).

questions.question: During the dark phase of the visual cycle, which form of vitamin A combines with opsin to form rhodopsin?
questions.explanation:
Opsin combines with 11-cis-retinal to produce rhodopsin.

Only the retinal form of vitamin A is involved in the formation of the photopigment.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the physiology of photoreceptors?
options: Phototransduction results in closure of c-GMP-gated cation channels.
Chromophore regeneration occurs in the outer segment of photoreceptors.
Photon absorption induces photo-isomerisation of 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal.
11-cis-Retinal is bound to opsins by covalent bonds.
questions.answer: B. Chromophore regeneration occurs in the outer segment of photoreceptors.
questions.explanation:
Chromophore regeneration occurs in the retinal pigment epithelial cells.

Phototransduction:

• Rhodopsin is a G-protein-coupled receptor found in the outer segments of rod photoreceptors.

• 11-cis-retinal (a chromophore) is covalently bound to opsins via a lysine residue on one of the transmembrane domains.

• The receptor is activated by photo-isomerization of prebound 11-cis-retinal to ALL-TRANS-retinal.

• Activation of the receptor causes binding and activation of the G protein, transducin, with signal transduction via cGMP phosphodiesterase, resulting in a decrease in the intracellular cGMP levels and closure of the cGMP-gated Na channels.

• This causes hyperpolarization of the photoreceptor cell, which modulates neurotransmitter release at the synapse with bipolar cells.

• This entire process triggered by the activation of rhodopsin is phototransduction, which occurs in the outer segment of photoreceptors and converts light energy into an electrical signal.

Chromophore regeneration:

• All-trans retinAL is converted to all-trans-retinOL.

• All-trans-retinOL gets transported by interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP) to the retinal pigment epithelial cells, where it is reconstituted into the 11-cis retinal isoform.

The koniocellular pathway is ventral to each parvocellular and magnocellular layer of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). K cells are neurochemically and anatomically distinct from M and P cells. questions.question: What is the visible range of the electromagnetic spectrum of the human eye?
questions.explanation:
The visible range of the electromagnetic spectrum for the human eye is 400–700 nm.

Theories of color vision:

• Trichromatic theory (Young–Helmholtz theory) assumes that there are three types of color receptors. Each receptor is assumed to respond to all wavelengths, however, each has different spectral sensitivities.

• Opponent process theory, also known as the Hering theory, assumes three sets of receptor systems—red-green, blue-yellow, and black-white. Each one of these functions as an antagonistic pair (e.g., red light stimulates the red receptors and, at the same time, inhibits the green).

• Edwin Land's theory has three separate color systems (retinexes). Each is an analog to a black-and-white picture.

questions.question: What is the characteristic visual defect in deuteranomaly?
questions.answer: C. Green color perception is defective.
questions.explanation:
In deuteranomaly, the perception of green color is defective. It is the most common disorder of color vision.

Monochromacy: Only one of the three primary colors (red, blue, or green) can be appreciated.

Dichromacy: Two primary colors are appreciated. (anopia = absent).

• Protanopia: Red color is not perceived.

• Deuteranopia: Green color is not perceived.

• Tritanopia: Blue color is not perceived.

Trichromacy: All the three primary colors are appreciated, but one of them can be defective (anomaly = defective).

• Protanomaly: Red color perception is defective.

• Deuteranomaly: Green color perception is defective.

• Tritanomaly: Blue color perception is defective.

Achromatopsia: No color perception due to the absence of cones. It may also occur in the lesion of area V4 or V8 of the visual cortex.

questions.question: Majority of the energy requirement in the lens is met by the ______________.
questions.explanation:
Majority of the energy requirement of the lens is met by glycolysis.

90–95 % of the glucose that enters the lens is converted to glucose 6 phosphate by hexokinase. The remaining 5% is converted to sorbitol and gluconic acid.

The glucose-6-phosphate formed is metabolized in 3 ways:

• Glycolysis: 80 %

• Pentose phosphate pathway: 10%

• TCA cycle: 3%

Energy in the lens is stored in the form of ATP.

questions.question: What is the angle subtended by the optotype on the second line of Snellen’s chart when viewed from a distance of 6 meters?
questions.explanation:
The angle subtended by the optotype (individual letters on the chart) on the second line of Snellen’s chart in the above case would be 30 minutes of arc.

The second line on Snellen’s chart corresponds to a distance of 36 meters. When viewed from a 6m distance, it is denoted as visual acuity 6/36. Where,

• The numerator (6) denotes the distance from which the patient is actually viewing it

• The denominator (36) denotes the distance at which it should be ideally viewed. It denotes the distance at which each stroke of the letter would subtend the minimum angle of resolution (MAR) of one minute of arc.

MAR = 1/Visual acuity

Each letter is shaped such that it can be placed in a square, the sides of which are five times the breadth of individual limbs of the letters. Hence, the angle subtended by the optotype= MAR x 5

For eg: At exactly 6 meters distance from the patient, the letters on the 6/6 line shall subtend 5 minutes of arc (such that the individual limbs of the letters subtend 1 minute of arc).

The equation to calculate the minimum angle of resolution (MAR) is given as follows:

For the given question,

MAR = 1/ 6/36
MAR = 36/6
MAR = 6 minutes of arc

Hence, the angle subtended by the entire letter is 6 × 5 = 30 minutes of arc.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man with monocular aphakia wears contact lenses. What is the approximate percentage of aniseikonia in his eyes?
questions.explanation:
The approximate percentage of aniseikonia in a person with monocular aphakia wearing a contact lens would be 8%.

Aniseikonia is defined as the difference in image size between the two eyes and can lead to disturbances in stereopsis. The tolerable limit of aniseikonia is 5–8%. It is reduced with contact lens (8%) compared to glasses (25–30%) in aphakia.

However, the percentage of aniseikonia is least with an intraocular lens (IOL) (1–3%), thus secondary IOL implantation is the most preferred management of unilateral aphakia.

questions.question: Which cerebellar nucleus controls the ocular saccade?
questions.explanation:
The Floccular nucleus of the cerebellum controls ocular saccades.

A saccade is a rapid ballistic movement to change the point of fixation. It is the fastest of all eye movements and is initiated by the contralateral frontal lobe. Smooth pursuit is a slow tracking movement to keep the target on the fovea. It is controlled by the ipsilateral parieto-occipital lobe.

Following an object from the right to left is left pursuit and is controlled by ipsilateral (left) parieto-occipital lobe, and the corrective movement is a saccade (in this case, left to right) termed right saccade and is controlled by the contralateral (left) frontal lobe.

The floccular nucleus is found in the lobule HX of the cerebellar vermis. Its functions include matching pulse-step, gaze holding, and sustained smooth pursuit. Bilateral lesions of the flocculus result in the following:

• Post-saccadic drift- saccadic movements do not stop, but there is a brief, several hundred milliseconds drift of the eyes after each saccade.

• Saccadic pursuit- smooth tracking is replaced by simultaneous rapid jerking motions of the eye to follow an object toward the ipsilateral visual field.

• Gaze-evoked nystagmus- impaired ability to hold the eyes in the eccentric position, resulting in gaze-evoked nystagmus towards the affected side of the cerebellum.

Emboliform and globose nuclei: Generation of vertical saccades

Fastigial nuclei: Pursuit initiation

questions.question: Purely depolarizing cells in the optic pathway are ________.
questions.explanation: Amacrine cells are the cells that produce purely depolarizing potential and spikes.

questions.question: Most afferent fibers from the lateral geniculate body terminate in the primary visual cortex in ______.
questions.explanation:
Most afferent fibers from the lateral geniculate body (LGB) terminate in the primary visual cortex in layer 4.

Both the magnocellular and parvocellular pathways from the LGB terminate in layer 4 of the visual cortex. Only the interlaminar pathway terminates in layers 2 and 3.

questions.question: What is the mean value for outflow facility of the aqueous in the normal eye?
questions.explanation:
The aqueous outflow facility is about 0.28 µL/min/mmHg. Aqueous humor is produced at an average rate of 2.0–2.5 µL/min.

The ease with which the aqueous humor leaves the eye is called an aqueous outflow facility.

• The outflow facility is measured using tonography.

• The normal range is between 0.22–0.28 µL/min/mmHg.

• A juxtacanalicular portion of the trabecular meshwork is the primary limiting factor for the outflow facility.

• Uveoscleral outflow accounts for 10% of the total aqueous outflow facility.

• Aqueous outflow facility decreases with aging.

• Trabecular outflow facility is reduced in glaucoma.

• Laser trabeculoplasty reduces intraocular pressure (IOP) in open-angle glaucoma by increasing the trabecular outflow facility.

questions.question: The term ametropia refers to all except_____.
questions.explanation:
The term ametropia refers to conditions of refractive error.

Emmetropia refers to an optically normal eye.

The term ametropia includes conditions such as

• Myopia (shortsightedness)

• Hypermetropia (longsightedness)

• Astigmatism

questions.question: A small kid is brought for examination due to difficulty reading from the board at school. Visual acuity was 20/60 in both eyes. His vision got corrected with concave lens spectacles. Which of the following is the most common cause of this refractive error?
options: Increased anteroposterior diameter of the eye ball
Increase in the refractive index of lens
questions.answer: A. Increased anteroposterior diameter of the eye ball
questions.explanation:
Poor vision for distance (difficulty reading from board) that is corrected with concave lens spectacles suggest that the child has myopia. The most common cause of myopia (shortsightedness) is increased anteroposterior length of the eyeball.

Myopia is a type of refractive error seen when the parallel rays of light from infinity are focused in front of the retina when accomodation is at rest.

questions.question: Which of the following range defines moderate myopia?
questions.explanation:
Moderate myopia is defined when the refractive error is between -3D and -6D.

Note: Myopia according to age of onset:

• Congenital: Present at birth

• Youth onset: 2–20 years of age

• Early adult onset: 20–40 years of age

• Late adult onset: >40 years of age

questions.question: Which of the following myopias is not associated with high degree of refractive error?
questions.explanation:
School myopia or simple myopia is associated with a low to moderate degree of refractive error.

Simple myopia is the most common type of myopia. It results from a normal biological variation in the development of the eye i.e. increased anteroposterior diameter of eyeball or increased curvature of the cornea.

Other options:

Options A and D: Pathological/Degenerative/Progressive myopia occurs due to degenerative changes in the retina, leading to a high degree of refractive error.

Option B: Congenital myopia is associated with congenital anomalies of the eye, and a high degree of refractive error.

Note: Other types of myopia include:
1. Nocturnal myopia: Accommodation is induced by low contrast in dim illumination
2. Induced myopia: Temporary and reversible myopia due to external agents (e.g., pilocarpine-induced accommodation spasm)/variations in blood sugar levels
3. Pseudomyopia: Inappropriately excessive accommodation due to overstimulation/ciliary spasm.

questions.question: A woman comes to the ophthalmology OPD because of having vision difficulties for the last 3 months. On fundoscopic examination, the following findings are seen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a fundus typical of pathological myopia due to the stretching of the retina.

The tigroid appearance or tessellated appearance of the fundus can be appreciated. As the eye enlarges, the retinal pigment epithelium becomes thinner, resulting in:

• A tessellated (checkered) appearance of the fundus

• Increased visibility of the choroidal vasculature

Other features of the myopic fundus are as follows:

• Lacquer cracks are spontaneous ruptures of the elastic lamina of Bruch’s membrane. It appears yellowish-white. it is usually located in the posterior pole.

• Annular gray shadow around the optic disc

• Lattice degeneration

• Foster Fuchs spots

• Cystoid degeneration

• Total retinal atrophy

questions.question: A woman with pathological myopia visits the ophthalmology OPD for an annual eye check-up. What is the least likely finding to be seen on her ophthalmologic examination?
questions.explanation:
The shallow anterior chamber is not a feature of pathological myopia.

Signs of pathological myopia include the following:

• Prominent eyeballs

• Large cornea

• Deep anterior chamber (AC)

• Fundus picture

• Large, pale optic disc with the temporal myopic crescent

• Degenerative changes in retina and choroid

• Foster Fuchs spots (blackish spots due to retinal pigment epithelial hyperplasia)

• Lattice degeneration

• Cystoid degeneration

• Total retinal atrophy

• Posterior staphyloma

• Degenerative changes in the vitreous—posterior vitreous detachment

questions.question: Which of the following is true about degenerative myopia?
options: It is seen in less than 6 dioptres of myopia.
It is more common in males than in females.
Myopic degeneration can lead to retinal detachment.
The condition has no racial prediliction.
questions.answer: C. Myopic degeneration can lead to retinal detachment.
questions.explanation:
The statement that is true for degenerative myopia is that myopic degeneration can lead to retinal detachment.

Degenerative myopia is seen in more than 6 dioptres of myopia. It is more common in females as compared to males. The condition has a racial predilection; it is more common in Jews and Japanese people, and most cases are of genetic origin.

Changes seen in degenerative myopia are myopic crescent, rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (due to degenerative changes in the periphery of the retina with subsequent tear) and floaters (due to degenerative changes in the vitreous).

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common complication of pathological myopia?
questions.explanation:
Macular degeneration is the most common complication of myopia, followed by rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Complications of pathological myopia include the following:

• Macular degeneration

• Retinal detachment

• Complicated cataract

• Vitreous hemorrhage

• Choroidal hemorrhage

• Strabismus fixus convergence

• Primary open-angle glaucoma, which is not a complication, but reported to occur in association with pathological myopia.

questions.question: While performing the following procedure on a 35-year-old male at a distance of 1 meter, you found out that the red reflex was not moving with the movement of the instrument. How will you interpret your findings?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows the procedure of retinoscopy (skiascopy) being performed. As the red reflex is not moving with the movement of the retinoscope, the patient is interpreted as having myopia of 1D.

Retinoscopy is an objective method of determining the error of refraction. It is based on the principle that when light is reflected from a mirror into the eye, the direction in which tlhe light will travel across the pupil depends upon the refractive stale of the eye. Interpretation of retinoscopy done at 1m is:

• No movement of red reflex: Myopia of 1D

• Movement of red reflex with retinoscope: Emmetropia, hypermetropia, myopia less than 1D

• Movement of red reflex against the retinoscope: Myopia more than 1D

questions.question: A worried mother brought her son for vision examination when she noticed him reading a book too closely. She says he also narrows his eyes while watching television. Examination revealed myopia. Which of the following lens should be prescribed to correct this child's vision?
questions.explanation:
Concave lenses are used for correcting myopic errors.

Other options:

Option A: Convex lenses are used in the correction of hypermetropic eye and presbyopic eye.
Option C: Cylindrical lenses are used in the correction of astigmatism.

questions.question: Which of the following statement about the management of myopia is false?
options: In high myopia, it is better to slightly under-correct for distance.
Concave lens is used to correct myopia.
Contact lens provides a wider field and larger image size as compared to glasses.
Myopia must never be under-corrected with spectacles.
questions.answer: D. Myopia must never be under-corrected with spectacles.
questions.explanation:
The false statment is that myopia must never be under-corrected with spectacles. In fact, it is better to slightly under-correct cases of high myopia.

Concave lens are used to correct myopia. In high myopia, it is better to slightly under-correct to avoid the problem of near vision and that of minification of images. Contact lens are preferred in high myopia as they provide a wider field and larger image size as compared to glasses.

questions.question: A college student is fed up with wearing spectacles for her myopia. During her annual eye checkup, she asks the ophthalmologist for eye surgery to get rid of the glasses. Which of the following is not a surgical option to correct her refractive error?
questions.explanation:
Conductive keratoplasty is a cornea-based surgical procedure used in the correction of hypermetropia.

Surgical procedures are undertaken after the stabilization of myopia which usually occurs after 18 years of age.

questions.question: Which of the following laser is used in the treatment of myopia?
questions.explanation:
Excimer laser is used in the treament of myopia.

Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) is the most popular treatment modality for myopia. It is performed using an excimer laser. Surgical correction is only done in individuals who have a stable refractive error for at least 1 year. Corneal thinning disorders must be ruled out prior to this procedure.

questions.question: A mother asks for LASIK surgery for the correction of her 15-year-old daughter's myopia. Which of the following is not an eligibility criterion for this procedure?
options: Stable refraction for the past 1 year
questions.explanation:
Age of 15 years is not a criterion for LASIK surgery. LASIK surgery is performed after 18 years of age.

Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) is performed using excimer laser in individuals aged > 18 years who have a stable refractive error for 1 year. It is done in individuals who have had unsatisfactory results with non-surgical treatment. Corneal-thinning disorders such as keratoconus must be ruled out before this procedure.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about the refractive error in which the image is formed behind the retina?
questions.explanation:
Hypermetropia is the refractive error where the image is formed behind the retina. In hypermetropia, near point becomes distant.

The near point or punctum proximum is the nearest point at which small objects can be seen clearly. It recedes with age.

Hypermetropia is also called long-sightedness since patients are able to focus distant objects more easily than near objects. Accommodative convergent squint in children is a complication of uncorrected long-standing hypermetropia. The fundus may show pseudopapillitis.

Hypermetropia is classified into the following types:

• Latent hypermetropia: Masked by the tone of the ciliary body

• Facultative hypermetropia: Masked by the voluntary accommodative effort of the person

• Absolute hypermetropia: Apparent/manifest

questions.question: You have been asked to perform fundoscopy by your senior resident in one of his patients diagnosed with hypermetropia. Which of the following options represent the findings that could be seen in this patient?
questions.answer: B. Shot silk appearance with pseudopapillitis.
questions.explanation:
Shot silk appearance with pseudopapillitis can be seen on fundal examination of the hypermetropic eye.

Hypermetropia is a refractive error of the eye in which parallel rays of light from infinity focus behind the retina when accommodation is at rest. Fundoscopy findings in hypermetropia include shot silk appearance (retina may shine due to the greater brilliance of light reflections) and pseudopapillitis (optic disc is small, hypervascular, with ill-defined margins without disc edema).

Other signs of hypermetropia include small eyeball, small cornea and short anteroposterior length of the eyeball.

Convex lens (plus lens) is used for the correction of hypermetropia.

questions.question: Which of the following grades of error defines high hypermetropia?
questions.explanation: High hypermetropia is defined as an error of >5D.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man wants to undergo surgery for hypermetropia. All of the following are options to treat his refractive error except?
questions.explanation:
Photorefractive keratectomy is not the surgical modality of the treatment of hypermetropia.

Photorefractive keratectomy is a laser ablation technique for the correction of myopia. An excimer laser is used to cause flattening of the central cornea.

questions.question: A boy was brought by his parents for an eye exam. He has been having headaches, nausea, and visual discomfort since he started school. His ophthalmological examination revealed a refractive error of + 2D in the right eye and -1 D in the left eye. His fundus appears to be normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A child with refractive error of + 2D in the right eye and -1 D in the left eye has anisometropia.

Anisometropia is the condition wherein the total refractive power of the two eyes is unequal. A difference of up to 2.5 D between two eyes is well tolerated. If the anisometropia exceeds 2.5D, ambylopia may develop. Contact lenses are preferred for treatment due to less optical defects as compared to glasses.

questions.question: What is aniseikonia?
options: Difference in the axial length of the two eyes
Difference in the size of the image formed by the two eyes
Difference in the size of the pupil in the two eyes
Difference in the curvature of the cornea in the two eyes
questions.answer: B. Difference in the size of the image formed by the two eyes
questions.explanation:
Aniseikonia is a condition in which there is a difference in the size of the image formed by the two eyes.

Up to 5–8% aniseikonia is well tolerated. Treatment includes contact lens in patients with phakia and intraocular lens implantation in patients with aphakia.

questions.question: A 20-year-old girl started having frequent headaches and blurring of vision while studying for college exams. She says she feels better when she closes her eyes. On examination, she is found to have astigmatism. Which of the following is the most common cause responsible for this condition?
options: Irregularity of the curvature of the cornea
Irregularity of the curvature of the lens
questions.answer: A. Irregularity of the curvature of the cornea
questions.explanation:
Abnormalities of the curvature of the cornea is the most common cause of astigmatism.

Astigmatism is a refractive error in which the rays of light entering the eye are refracted differently in different meridia of the eye. Meridia of the eye correspond to the lines of longitude on a globe.

There are two types of astigmatism. In regular astigmatism, refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another. In irregular astigmatism, there is irregular change of the refractive power in different meridia. It can be caused by corneal scars.

Etiology of regular astigmatism:

• Corneal: Most common cause. Occurs due to abnormalities of curvature of the cornea

• Lenticular: Occurs due to abnormalities of lens curvature and position

• Curvatural: Seen in lenticonus

• Positional: Due to tilting or oblique placement of the lens or subluxation of lens

• Retinal: Due to oblique placement of the macula

Note: Spherical aberration is a high-order refractive error of the eye. It is seen when light rays passing through the periphery of the cornea and lens focus at a slightly different location than light rays passing through the center of the cornea and lens. It improves on using a pinhole.

questions.question: Which among the following is normal astigmatism seen in eyes due to the pressure of the eyelids?
questions.explanation:
With-the-rule astigmatism is normally seen in the eyes due to the pressure of the eyelids.

In with-the-rule astigmatism, the vertical meridian is more curved. This is more common and often occurs due to the pressure of eyelids on the eye. In against-the-rule astigmatism (ATR) (option B), the horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian. In both these types, the principal meridia are vertical and horizontal (90 and 180 degrees) and are at right angles to each other.

The other types of astigmatism include oblique and bi-oblique astigmatism. In oblique astigmatism (option C), the two principal meridians are not the horizontal and vertical meridians, although they are at right angles to each other. In bi-oblique astigmatism (option D), the two principal meridians are not at right angles to each other; for example, one may be at 40 degrees and the other, at 100 degrees.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding with-the-rule astigmatism?
options: The horizontal meridian is more myopic.
The vertical meridian is more myopic.
The vertical meridian is more hyperopic.
The horizontal meridian is more hyperopic.
questions.answer: B. The vertical meridian is more myopic.
questions.explanation:
In with-the-rule astigmatism, the curvature of the vertical meridian is more than the horizontal meridian. Greater the curvature of the meridian, more the myopia of that meridian. Hence, the vertical meridian is more myopic in with-the-rule astigmatism.

With-the-rule astigmatism is the type of astigmatism wherein the vertical curvature is always more than the horizontal curvature. Thus, irrespective of the type or cause of with-the-rule astigmatism, the vertical meridian is always more myopic (curved) than the horizontal meridian.

questions.question:
Match the images shown with the refractive errors they represent.

Image
Refractive error

1
a. Mixed astigmatism

2
b. Simple myopic astigmatism

3
c. Compound myopic astigmatism

4
d. Simple hypermetropic astigmatism

e. Compound hypermetropic astigmatism
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is 1 - d, 2 - b, 3 - c, 4 - a.

Image
Refractive error

1
d. Simple hypermetropic astigmatism

2
b. Simple myopic astigmatism

3
c. Compound myopic astigmatism

4
a. Mixed astigmatism

Astigmatism is a refractive error in which the rays of light entering the eye are refracted differently in different meridia of the eye. Meridia of the eye correspond to the lines of longitude on a globe. There are two types of astigmatism - regular and irregular.

In regular astigmatism, refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another. Thus, two principal meridia are present. The rays of light from infinity form two focal points due to the difference in curvature of the two principal meridia. Based on the relation of the two focal points to the retina, regular astigmatism has the following types:

1. Simple astigmatism: One focal point lies on the retina. In simple myopic type, the second focal point lies in front of the retina while in simple hypermetropic type, the second focal point lies behind the retina.

2. Compound astigmatism: In compound hypermetropic type, both focal points lie behind the retina. In compound myopic type, both focal points lie in front of the retina.

3. Mixed astigmatism: One focal point lies in front of while the second focal point lies behind the retina.

questions.question: In compound myopic astigmatism, with parallel rays of light entering the eye in relaxed accommodation, the image(s) formed is/are __________.
options: One focal point in front of the retina
Two focal lines in front of the retina
Two focal lines behind the retina
Two focal lines, one behind and the other in front of retina
questions.answer: B. Two focal lines in front of the retina
questions.explanation:
In compound myopic astigmatism, parallel rays of light entering the eye in relaxed accommodation form two focal lines in front of the retina.

Option A: One focal point in front of retina describes myopia.

Option C: Two focal lines behind the retina describes compound hypermetropic astigmatism.

Option D: Two focal lines, one behind and one in front of the retina describes mixed astigmatism.

questions.question: The PARK procedure is used in the correction of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
PARK is a technique used for correcting astigmatism.

Photo-astigmatic refractive keratotomy (PARK) is performed using excimer laser for the correction of astigmatism. The other surgical procedures used for correction of astigmatism are astigmatic keratotomy, LASIK and SMILE.

questions.question: An 80-year-old man is reading a newspaper in his backyard. His accommodation while reading a newspaper is due to______.
questions.answer: B. Contraction of the ciliary muscle
questions.explanation:
Near vision accommodation is due to the contraction of the ciliary muscle.

Accommodation is the phenomenon of increasing the convergence power. This occurs by increasing the refractive power of the lens and increasing its curvature. The capsule of the lens is more elastic than the lens itself and plays a role in increasing the curvature of the lens. When the circular fibres of the ciliary muscles contract, the ciliary body approaches the lens. This slackens the zonules so that the capsule, relieved of its tension, is able to mould the lens to its accommodative form.

questions.question: During a routine school eye examination camp, a 5-year-old boy is able to read everything written on the board. Which of the following mechanisms aids in establishing normal distant vision in this child?
options: Shortening of the focal length of the lens
questions.answer: A. Relaxation of the ciliary muscles
questions.explanation:
Relaxation of the ciliary muscles would aid in establishing a normal distant vision.

Relaxation of the ciliary muscles keeps the zonules in a taut state and maintains the radius of curvature of the anterior lens surface at 10 mm. Thus, the focal length is maximum and distant objects are most clearly visualized.

Option B: The pupils constrict during accommodation to increase the depth of focus.

Option C: During accommodation, ciliary muscles contract causing relaxation of zonular fibers, rounding of the lens, and shortening of the focal length.

Option D: The radius of curvature of the anterior lens surface becomes 6 mm i.e rounder during accommodation.

questions.question: The condition of the accommodative power being significantly less than the normal physiological limits for the patient's age is called _________.
questions.explanation:
The condition in which accommodative power is significantly less than normal physiological limits for the patient's age is called insufficiency of accommodation

Anomalies of accommodation:

Presbyopia
Insufficiency of accommodation

Paralysis of accommodation

(cycloplegia)

Spasm of accommodation

Failing near vision due to age-related decrease in the amplitude of accommodation or increase in near point
Inadequacy of the accommodative power. It is significantly less than normal physiological limits for the patient's age
Complete absence of accommodation
Exertion or abnormally excessive accommodation

Causes:

• Age-related change in the lens- decreased elasticity and sclerosis.

• Age-related decline in ciliary muscle power

Causes:

• Premature sclerosis of the lens

• Weakness of the ciliary muscles due to systemic causes like anemia and malnutrition.

• Weakness of the ciliary muscles associated with primary open-angle glaucoma

Causes:

• Drug-induced

• Internal ophthalmoplegia due to diphtheria, diabetes mellitus, etc.

• As a component of 3rd nerve palsy

Causes:

• Drug-induced spasm, e.g., ecothiophate, pilocarpine

• Spontaneous spasm: Found in children who use eyes for excessive near work in conditions of bad illumination.

questions.question: What is the accommodative amplitude of a patient with a near point at 20 cm and a far point at infinity?
questions.explanation:
The amplitude of accommodation for the above patient would be 5.

Near point of accommodation (NPA) is the closest distance at which the near object is clearly focussed without blur. Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum power of the lens that permits clear near vision without blur. Its unit is dioptre (D). The amplitude of accommodation is the reciprocal of NPA in meters. 20 cm is 1/5th of a meter. Therefore, accommodative amplitude is its inverse, that is, 5D.

The NPA is measured clinically using a scale device such as the Prince, Berens, or Royal Air Force (RAF) ruler.

questions.question: A 45 year old woman complains of an inability to read books and stitch garments for the past few months. Which of the following is false regarding her condition?
options: Decrease in elasticity and plasticity of the crystalline lens
Age-related decrease in the power of ciliary muscles
It is corrected with a concave lens
questions.answer: D. It is corrected with a concave lens
questions.explanation:
A 45 year old woman presenting with an inability to do near vision work (reading, stitching) likely has presbyopia. Presbyopia is corrected by the use of a convex lens (weakest convex lens).

Presbyopia can be caused by an age-related decline in the ciliary muscle power or age-related change in the lens including:

•

• Hardness (sclerosis) of the lens substance, which is less easily molded

• Decrease in the elasticity of lens capsule

questions.question: A 51-year-old woman comes for an ophthalmological examination. She says she is unable to thread a needle and is facing difficulty making a sweater for her grandson. She never had vision problems in her youth. What power of glasses would roughly correct her vision difficulties?
questions.explanation:
The power of prescription glasses for a 51-year-old woman should be +1.5D.

Presbyopia is the condition of decreased near vision. It is due to an age-related decrease in the amplitude of accommodation or an increase in punctum proximum (near point). For correction of presbyopia, convex lenses are used.

Roughly, the power of prescription glasses age-wise is as follows:

Age
Power

45 years
+1 to +1.25D

50 years
+1.5 to 1.75D

55 years
+2 to +2.25D

60 years
+2.5 to +3D

questions.question: During your morning jogging routine, you found a pair of spectacles lying on the sidewalk. The spectacles are shown below. What type of presbyopic lens is present in these spectacles?
questions.explanation: The given lens in the image is a typical example of progressive lenses. Progressive lenses are identified as such due to the absence of the line of demarcation on the lens. They are gradually optimized for reading vision, distant vision, and for intermediate vision, such as computer work.

questions.question: A 55-year-old male with limbal scar presents to the ophthalmology clinic with marked defects in both near and far vision. Clinical examination reveals a wide and deep anterior chamber, iridodonesis, and a dark pupillary reflex. A vision of 6/6 is achieved with correcting lens of +11D. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A limbal scar with defective near and distant vision, a wide and deep anterior chamber, iridodonesis, and dark pupillary reflex suggests aphakia.

Aphakia is the condition in which the lens is absent from the pupillary area. Signs of surgical aphakia include limbal scar, deeper anterior chamber than normal, iridodonesis (tremulousness of the iris), jet black color of the pupil. On Purkinje's test, only the first and second images are seen. A small disc is seen on fundus examination and high hypermetropia is seen on retinoscopy.

The best treatment option is secondary intraocular lens (IOL) implantation.

questions.question: Which of the following is used to differentiate pseudophakia from aphakia?
questions.explanation:
Pseudophakia shows 4 images in the Purkinje image test, whereas aphakia shows only 2 images. Other features can be seen in both.

When aphakia is corrected with an intraocular lens implant (IOL), the condition is referred to as pseudophakia. Signs of pseudophakia with posterior chamber IOL include:

• Surgical scar

• Anterior chamber slightly deeper than normal

• Mild iridodonesis (tremulousness) of the iris

• Purkinje image test shows 4 images

• Pupil blackish in color but when the light is thrown in the pupillary area, shining reflex is observed

Purkinje images are reflections of objects from the structure of the eye. They are also known as Purkinje reflexes or Purkinje–Sanson images. Normally, 4 images are formed from four different reflecting surfaces i.e.

Image
Location
Direction

Image 1
Anterior surface of the cornea
Erect

Image 2
Posterior surface of the cornea
Erect

Image 3
Anterior surface of the lens
Erect

Image 4
Posterior surface of the lens
Inverted

In aphakia, as the lens is absent, image 3 and image 4 are absent.

questions.question: Roving–ring scotoma is seen after the correction of aphakia by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Roving-ring scotoma is seen in the correction of aphakia with spectacles due to prismatic effects at the edge of the lens.

The difficulties in the correction of aphakia by spectacles include the following:

• Image magnification by 25–30%

• Spherical aberrations producing a “pin cushion effect”

• Jack-in-the-box phenomenon from the prismatic effects at the edge of the lens

• Reduced visual fields

• Physical inconvenience

For aphakia, the best correction is obtained by an intraocular lens (IOL).

Roving-ring scotoma:

The edge of a convex lens acts as a prism. The greater the angle of the prism, the more will be the bending. In aphakic spectacles, the angle of the lens is large. Thus, the light falling at the edge of the lens bends towards the center of the lens and does not reach the pupil. This results in a ring-shaped scotoma as this prismatic effect is present all around the edges of the lens. The position of this scotoma is not fixed in the visual field because the eye keeps moving (or roving) in relation to the aphakic spectacle. Hence, the result is a roving ring scotoma.

questions.question: Soft contact lenses are made of _____.
questions.explanation: Soft lenses are made up of hydroxyethyl methyl acrylate (HEMA).

questions.question: Which among the following is not an advantage of contact lens?
options: It helps in eliminating peripheral aberrations.
It is helpful in dry eye.
questions.answer: D. It improves corneal oxygen supply.
questions.explanation:
Contact lenses decrease corneal oxygen supply.

The cornea obtains its O2 supply from the atmosphere. The use of contact lenses decreases the O2 supply from the atmosphere. Contact lens eliminate peripheral aberrations and can correct irregular astigmatism. Although dry eye is caused by wearing contact lenses, lenses made of hydrogel which are high in water content are beneficial in dry eye.

Rigid gas-permeable/semi-soft contact lens are used for keratoconus. Toric contact lens are used for astigmatism.

questions.question: Which of the following characteristic features would you expect to see in a histopathology slide of conjunctiva?
options: Amacrine cells within non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Goblet cells within non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Goblet cells within keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Amacrine cells within keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
questions.answer: B. Goblet cells within non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
questions.explanation:
The presence of goblet cells within the non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium would help identify the conjunctiva. Goblet cells are involved in the secretion of mucin.

Amacrine cells are a type of retinal interneuron, and hence would be found in the retina, not the conjunctiva.

questions.question: A child presents with irritation and redness of the left eye at a primary health center. There are no previous immunization records. Examination showed a greyish-white membrane over the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva which bled on peeling. What is the likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
The of a child with irritation and redness of the eye with no previous vaccination records is suggestive of a case of membranous conjunctivitis and among the given options, Corynebacterium diphtheriae is the most likely etiological agent.

Membranous conjunctivitis presents with irritation and redness of the eye and is characterized by the formation of a greyish-white membrane that bleeds on peeling. Vaccines are routinely used to prevent diphtheria infection and hence, unvaccinated status increases his susceptibility to the bacteria. Moreover, the bacteria thrive in crowded populations and poor hygienic surroundings, hence a background of low socioeconomic context, such as an orphanage, acts as a risk factor in this case.

This condition is associated with the formation of fibrinous exudates on the surface and into the substance of the conjunctival epithelium. The causes include beta-hemolytic streptococci, Streptococcus pneumonia, Haemophilus aegyptius, Corynebacterium diphtheria, and Neisseria gonorrhea

The image given below shows the eye of a patient with pseudomembranous conjunctivitis. It differs from membranous conjunctivitis in that the membrane can be easily peeled off in this condition leaving an intact underlying epithelium.

questions.question: A child with pharyngitis, and fever subsequently develops conjunctivitis. Initially, the left eye was affected, followed by the right eye's involvement in 2 days. Epiphora, conjunctival hyperemia, and chemosis are noted. What is its most likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
This child with pharyngitis and subsequent involvement of the eyes most likely has pharyngoconjunctival fever. This condition is commonly caused by adenovirus serotypes 3, 4, and 7.

Pharyngoconjunctival fever is an acute and highly infectious illness characterized by fever, pharyngitis, acute follicular conjunctivitis, and regional lymphoid hyperplasia with tender, enlarged preauricular adenopathy. Within the classical triad, symptoms may vary in severity. It is usually bilateral, with one eye typically having onset 1-3 days prior to the second eye. It is a self-limiting disease and treatment is mainly symptomatic, as follows:

• Cold compresses several times per day for 1-2 weeks.

• Artificial tears 4-8 times per day for 1-3 weeks.

Newcastle conjunctivitis is usually clinically indistinguishable from this condition and is derived from contact with diseased fowls. Another conjunctivitis caused by adenovirus serotypes 8, 19 and 37 is known as epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.

The image given below shows the eye of a patient with pharyngoconjunctival fever. Significant conjunctival hyperemia, petechial subconjunctival hemorrhages, and conjunctival follicles are noted.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?
options: The condition is commonly associated with a benign course.
It can occur spontaneously in elders with systolic hypertension.
The blood gets absorbed gradually in 6-8 weeks time without treatment.
Use of NSAIDs and aspirin to treat the condition should be avoided.
questions.answer: C. The blood gets absorbed gradually in 6-8 weeks time without treatment.
questions.explanation:
The image given above shows a subconjunctival haemorrhage in the eye. In this condition, the blood gets absorbed gradually in 1-3 weeks time without treatment.

A subconjunctival hemorrhage is also called subconjunctival ecchymosis. It is due to the rupture of small blood vessels and can occur spontaneously in elders with systolic hypertension or after local trauma. The condition is commonly associated with a benign course but, if the posterior limit of the hemorrhage is not seen, one should check for the base of the skull fracture.

Recurrent episodes warrant investigations for a bleeding diathesis or leukaemia. The use of NSAIDs and aspirin to treat the condition should be avoided.

questions.question: A UNICEF volunteer presented with a bilateral red eye of 2 days duration beginning on a return flight from Ghana. The infection spread among all her family members within a day of her return. Initial examination revealed lid edema, serous discharge, and severe sub-conjunctival hemorrhage. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a patient with bilateral red-eye and a rapid spread of infection to family members points towards a likely diagnosis of hemorrhagic conjunctivitis. Examination findings of lid edema, serous discharge, and subconjunctival hemorrhage further consolidate this diagnosis.

Causes:

• Enterovirus 70 (most important)

• Coxsackievirus 24

• Echovirus 34

• Adenovirus

• Pneumococcus

• Haemophilus

There is no treatment currently available. The infection generally resolves itself within a five to seven-day period. The use of steroids can actually cause a corneal microbial superinfection which then requires antimicrobial therapy to eliminate.

The image given below shows the eyes of a patient with acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.

questions.question: A tribal farmer, presented with a three-day history of right eye redness with pain. He had spent the prior week trekking up a mountain in order to travel to the nearby town and takes such trips frequently. The following lesion was observed on examination. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of right eye redness with pain, and findings of a raised whitish-yellowish lesion surrounded by mild erythema, points toward a likely diagnosis of pinguecula. A history of trekking, along with chronic sunlight exposure as a farmer, acts as a risk factor because it increases the exposure to the stronger UV radiation in the mountains.

Pinguecula has a fatty appearance and is usually bilateral. They are more often located nasally than temporally. It has horizontally oriented areas of bulbar conjunctival thickening that adjoin the limbus in the palpebral fissure area. They are associated with a 2- to 3-fold increased incidence of age-related macular degeneration. It is seen in most eyes by 70 years of age and in almost all by 80 years of age.

Pingueculitis responds to a brief course of NSAIDs or topical corticosteroids. Simple excision may be warranted in rare cases, wherein pingueculae may be chronically inflamed or cosmetically unsatisfactory.

questions.question: The excision of a pinkish, triangular tissue growth at the 1 o’clock position of the eye is being performed. The patient had a history of blurry vision and persistent redness in both eyes for a month. In order to secure the graft in the scleral bed, which of the following will not be used?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette, with symptoms of blurry vision and persistent redness, along with findings of an abnormal triangular mass of thickened conjunctiva, is suggestive of pterygium. Cyanoacrylate is not used for pterygium surgery.

The various glues used in ophthalmology are as follows:

• Cyanoacrylate glue- Mainly used as a corneal patch to seal acute corneal perforations and improve visual outcomes, with reduced enucleation rates and need for tectonic keratoplasty

• Fibrin glue- It is a biological adhesive, which reduces the total surgical time. It is used in corneal and conjunctival surgeries, squint surgeries, cataract (to fix the haptics of intraocular lens [IOL] to the tissue in place of sutures in glued IOL), refractive surgeries, trabeculectomy, and even retinal surgeries.

• Newer tissue adhesives like bio-dendrimers and photo-cross-linkable adhesives-

1. Bovine serum albumin-based bioadhesives: used in squint surgery

2. Riboflavin-based bioadhesive activated on exposure to ultraviolet A: used in post-LASIK ectasia, infectious keratopathy, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy

3. Hyaluronic acid-based photocatalytic glue activated with argon LASER: used in the repair of corneal lacerations

questions.question: A man presented with red eyes associated with a sandy, gritty sensation. He was diagnosed with conjunctivitis last week, however, his symptoms persisted. He has had multiple sexual partners in the past. Examination revealed palpable preauricular nodes and a follicular reaction involving the bulbar conjunctiva and semilunar folds. Conjunctival scrapings were sent for culture. What is the likely organism involved?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of red eyes, along with the examination findings of palpable preauricular nodes and follicular reaction involving the bulbar conjunctiva and semilunar folds, is suggestive of inclusion conjunctivitis. It is also known as chlamydial conjunctivitis, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D–K. It is a sexually transmitted disease occurring commonly in young adults.

The modes of transmission include orogenital activities and hand-to-eye spread of infective genital secretions. Hence, it is important to treat all sexual partners simultaneously to prevent re-infection and to rule out other venereal diseases, such as gonorrhoea and syphilis. Treatment includes a single 1g dose of azithromycin or doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 7 days.

The image given below shows the eye of a patient with chlamydial conjunctivitis.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is closely related to mucus fishing syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Mucus fishing syndrome is closely related to giant papillary conjunctivitis.

In Mucus fishing syndrome, patients develop a chronic papillary reaction due to repetitive manual removal of mucus. The severe form of mechanically induced papillary conjunctivitis is known as giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC). It is most frequently encountered with contact lens (CL) wear; in such cases, it is termed contact lens-associated papillary conjunctivitis (CLPC).

The increased risk in contact lens users is because of the build-up of proteinaceous deposits and cellular debris on the contact lens surface. It may be also be caused by ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, and scleral buckles, corneal surface irregularity, or filtering blebs.

questions.question: A young man presented with watering, redness and photophobia. He had similar complaints in the past which improved with self-medicated topical drops. His best-corrected visual acuity is 6/36 improving to 6/24. Slit-lamp examination revealed a 3 mm × 2 mm epithelial defect in the paracentral part of the cornea that stained positive with fluorescein dyes. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of spring catarrh. Slit-lamp examination finding of shield ulcer is typical of vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) or warm weather conjunctivitis (another name of VKC).

Shield ulcers are transverse ulcers seen in the upper cornea due to epithelial macroerosions in VKC. It is a rare complication of VKC and should always be kept in mind for patients suffering from vernal conjunctivitis.

Corneal signs in VKC:

• Shield ulcers

• Vernal plaques

• Subepithelial scarring

• Pseudo-gerontoxon- resembles arcus senilus; has a cupid's bow outline

Treatment of VKC is mainly with allergy avoidance and lid hygiene. Cool compresses, topical antihistamines, topical NSAIDs and topical steroids can be used to reduce the intensity of symptoms.

The image given below shows a shield ulcer in a patient with VKC.

questions.question: While browsing through the news channels, Geeta came across a panel discussion on public health diseases celebrating the elimination of a peculiar condition of the eye. It was known as the most important cause of corneal blindness in India and shows the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given sago-grain appearance of the conjunctiva is seen in trachoma. It was the most important cause of corneal blindness in India affecting young children.

Conjunctival appearance:

1. In trachoma

• Sago-grain appearance

• A follicular reaction

2. In vernal keratoconjunctivitis

• Cobblestone appearance

• A papillary reaction seen in palpebral conjunctiva

3. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis

• White-pinkish nodule in the bulbar conjunctiva

4. Xerophthalmia

• Epithelial xerosis

• Bitot spot in bulbar conjunctiva

questions.question: Which of the following will not be seen as a corneal sign in a 6-year-old patient with trachoma?
questions.explanation:
Arlt’s line is a conjunctival sign of trachoma.

Corneal signs
Conjunctival signs

• Superficial keratitis

• Follicles in the limbal area

• Pannus- superior limbus

• Corneal ulcer

• Herberts pits- near Limbal area

• Corneal opacity

• Congestion- On upper tarsal, fornix

• Follicles (containing Leber cells on histopathology)- On upper tarsal, fornix

• Papillary hyperplasia

• Arlt’s line- Linear scarring in sulcus subtarsalis

• Concretions- Inspissated mucus, dead epithelial cells in the glands of Henle

questions.question: A young girl has been brought in by her grandmother because she has constant pain, photosensitivity and discharge from her eyes. From the notes, you see that the child has had multiple presentations for prior eye infections. You observe severe scarring on the palpebral conjunctiva, as well as trachomatous trichiasis. Which McCallan stage will this be classified under?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette of a young child with pain, photosensitivity and discharge, having repeated infections, along with findings of scarring and trichiasis is suggestive of trachoma. Cicatrising trachoma is stage 3 of trachoma and is characterized by scarring of the palpebral conjunctiva.

Cicatricial trachoma is the end result of scarring that occurs in individuals who suffer from severe, persistent infections in childhood. Trachomatous scarring is recognized by the presence of easily visible white bands on the underside of the upper eyelid. Severe scarring can result in contraction of the tarsal conjunctiva which causes the lid margin to roll inwards. This results in buckling of the lid so the lashes rub on the eye known as trachomatous trichiasis. These lashes can lead to corneal opacities and scarring and eventually blindness.

The four stages of trachoma according to McCallan are as follows:

• Stage 1: Incipient - Immature follicles are present, but clinical symptoms are not obvious.

• Stage 2: Established - Typical trachomatous lesions without scarring.

• Stage 3: Cicatrising - Scarring along with active infection.

• Stage 4: Healed - Only scarring, the disease is either cured or quiet.

The image below shows trachomatous trichiasis with severe scarring-

questions.question: What is the drug of choice under the SAFE strategy for trachoma management?
questions.explanation:
Oral azithromycin is the drug of choice in the SAFE strategy of trachoma management. The adult dose is 1 g while 20 mg/kg body weight is given for children.

Oral azithromycin is slowly replacing tetracycline eye ointment as the first line drug used in trachoma treatment. The experience of Morocco, the first country that used azithromycin in a large-scale, nationwide elimination programme, has paved the way for the worldwide application of azithromycin as part of the SAFE strategy.

questions.question: A 21-year-old man presented with the following lesion in his eye. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image depicts Bitot's spot, a pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia. Hence, the likely diagnosis in this 21-year-old man presenting with the above lesion is xerophthalmia.

Bitot's spot is a triangular, silvery-white, foamy patch on the bulbar conjunctiva which is usually bilateral. The most common site is temporal.

questions.question: A 10 year old malnourished boy is brought with a 2-month history of diminished night vision. His dietary history revealed a restricted diet, consisting of mainly chips and nuggets, and he would refuse to eat green leafy vegetables. What is the conjunctival change seen in this deficiency?
questions.answer: D. Hyperkeratosis of the squamous epithelium
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario indicates that this patient has nyctalopia (diminished night vision) most likely due to vitamin A deficiency, suggested by his poor consumption of vegetables. Changes seen in the conjunctiva in vitamin A deficiency is hyperkeratosis of the squamous epithelium.

This occurs due to the metaplasia of the non-keratinized epithelium to keratinized epithelium.

questions.question: Ophthalmia nodosa occurs due to which of the following?
questions.answer: D. Irritation due to caterpillar hair
