questions.explanation:
Ophthalmia nodosa occurs due to irritation due to caterpillar hair.

It is often mistaken for tuberculosis. On examination, small, semitranslucent, reddish and yellowish-grey nodules are formed in the conjunctiva, cornea, and iris. Microscopy contains caterpillar hair surrounded by giant cells and lymphocytes. Treatment includes excision of the nodules in the conjunctiva.

The image below shows a patient's eye infected with ophthalmia nodosa.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with redness and photophobia of the left eye was seen in the OPD. An image of a characteristic lesion of her eye is as shown below. Identify the lesion.
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a white-pinkish nodule surrounded by hyperemia on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus with associated symptoms of redness and photophobia most likely has phlyctenular conjunctivitis. The given finding is referred to as a phlycten.

 Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction due to endogenous allergens like Staphylococcus aureus (most common) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

It is characterized by the following:

• Phlycten that may eventually form ring ulcers

• Shallow marginal ulcer due to the breakdown of limbal phlycten known as scrofulous ulcer

• Fascicular ulcer with a prominent parallel leash of blood vessels that heals leaving a band-shaped opacity

Treatment: Topical steroids; atropine if the cornea is involved.

Note: This can be differentiated from pinguecula by the following points:

Pinguecula is a yellow triangular patch on the conjunctiva near the limbus. It usually remains free from conjunctival congestion. The following image shows a yellow patch with tortuous blood vessels. There is no congestion as seen with a phlycten.

questions.question: Which of the following should not be considered in the differential of a patient who presents with the following finding?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows symblepharon, which is not seen in phlyctenular conjunctivitis. It is a partial or complete adhesion of the palpebral conjunctiva of the eyelid to the bulbar conjunctiva of the eyeball.

Causes of symblepharon:

1. Chemical injuries (especially alkalis)

2. Burns

3. Ocular cicatrical pemphigoid (OCP)

4. Steven–Johnson syndrome

5. Erythema multiforme

6. Pemphigus bullosa

7. Membranous conjunctivitis

Management:

• Lubrication

• Sweeping of fornices

• Symblepharon ring

• Symblepharon release and amniotic membrane graft

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy had to miss school because the matting of his eyelids made it difficult to open them in the morning and caused severe pain. His agonized mother rushed him to the hospital and reported that he had a fever and red eye for 4 days. Which group of lymph nodes is likely to be enlarged?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of fever and red eyes, associated with matting of eyelids and pain, is suggestive of conjunctivitis. Lymph from the conjunctiva drains directly into the submandibular and preauricular nodes and hence, these group of lymph nodes are likely to be enlarged.

The lymphatic drainage of the conjunctiva is as follows-

• From the medial side, one-third of the superior and medial two-thirds of the inferior conjunctiva → Submandibular nodes

• From the lateral side, two-thirds of the superior conjunctiva and lateral one-third of the inferior conjunctiva → Preauricular nodes

Specialized collections of T and B lymphocytes underlying a modified epithelium is known as conjunctiva-associated lymphoid tissue (CALT) present in the stroma (substantia propria). It is critical in the initiation and regulation of ocular-surface immune responses.

 Note:

The stroma also consists of the accessory lacrimal glands of Krause and Wolfring which are exocrine glands responsible for the basal secretion of the middle aqueous layer of the tear film.

The image given below shows the lymphatic drainage of the conjunctiva.

questions.question: The image of the eye of a 32-year-old woman having superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis is given below. Which of the following is commonly associated with it?
questions.explanation:
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis has a definite association with thyroid dysfunction. It affects one or both eyes of middle-aged women and about 65% of patients have abnormal thyroid function (usually hyperthyroidism).

It is a chronic disease of the superior limbus and the superior bulbar and the tarsal conjunctiva.

Clinical features:

• Papillary hypertrophy of the superior tarsal plate, often having a diffuse velvety appearance.

• Hyperemia of a radial band of the superior bulbar conjunctiva that stains with rose bengal.

•

• Superior filamentary keratitis that develops in about one-third of cases.

Management:

• Preservative-free lubricants

• Topical acetylcysteine 10% to 20%, four times daily to break down filaments

• Topical rebamipide

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not characteristic of pterygium?
options: Abnormal activity of p53 is seen in the pterygium tissue.
Decreased activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases is seen.
Destruction of Bowman's layer occurs when the pterygium invades the cornea.
Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.
questions.answer: D. Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.
questions.explanation:
Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the conjunctival connective tissue occurs in pinguecula (and not pterygium).

In pterygium, there is elastotic degeneration of collagen with fibrovascular proliferation.

It is important to distinguish a pterygium from a pinguecula. A pterygium, while histologically similar to a pinguecula, is distinguished by fibrovascular tissue that grows onto the cornea. Pingueculae do not have vascularized tissue and do not cross the limbus.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy complains of intense lacrimation, associated with photophobia. On examination, the following finding is seen in his upper tarsal conjunctiva. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above image depicts cobblestone appearance, which is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva seen in vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC). No follicular reaction is seen.

Vernal conjunctivitis is also called spring catarrh or warm weather conjunctivitis. It primarily affects boys, and the onset is generally from the age of 5 years. It is primarily a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction that is IgE mediated. It also involves a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction.

Classical features of the conjunctiva in VKC:

Palpebral VKC - Cobblestone papillae are present in the upper tarsal conjunctiva associated with ropy discharge. Maxwell–Lyon sign is present which is a pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

Limbal VKC - Horner – Trantas spots are white dots consisting of eosinophils and epithelial debris in the limbal area.

The image given below shows Horner-Trantas spots.

Treatment of this condition is with topical steroids and mast cell stabilizers such as cromolyn sodium. Topical cyclosporine can be used in patients who do not respond to first line treatment modalities.

questions.question: Your professor has assigned you to proofread a seminar on the anatomy of the conjunctiva made by a junior. In the explanation of conjunctival follicles, you spot a wrong statement that needs revision. What is that statement?
options: Conjunctiva of new born does not produce follicles before 2-3 months of age.
Slit lamp may be necessary to differentiate between follicles and papillae.
Follicles are a hyperplasia of the normal vascular system.
Follicles are found in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer of the conjunctiva.
questions.answer: C. Follicles are a hyperplasia of the normal vascular system.
questions.explanation:
Papillae (not follicles) are hyperplasia of the normal vascular system, with glomerulus-like branches of capillaries growing into the epithelium in inflammatory conditions. On the other hand, follicles are yellowish-white, round elevations of 1-2 mm diameter. Follicles are a localized aggregation of lymphocytes present in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer of the conjunctiva.

Image: Conjunctival papillae (hyperplastic epithelium and capillaries) shown in the first image followed by conjunctival giant follicles (round yellowish-white elevations) shown in the second image.

questions.question: In the grading of trachoma, the follicular stage is defined by the presence of which of the following?
options: 5 or more follicles in the lower tarsal conjunctiva
3 or more follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva
5 or more follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva
3 or more follicles in the lower tarsal conjunctiva
questions.answer: C. 5 or more follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva
questions.explanation:
In the grading of trachoma, follicular stage is defined by the presence of 5 or more follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva.

Trachoma is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide. It is caused by an obligate intracellular bacterium called Chlamydia trachomatis Serotypes A–C. The infection is transmitted by direct or indirect transfer of eye and nose discharges of infected people, particularly young children who harbour the principal reservoir of infection.

The image below shows the follicular stage of trachoma -

questions.question: What is the innermost layer of the sclera?
questions.explanation:
Lamina fusca is the innermost layer of the sclera.

Lamina fusca faces the choroid. It is the transition zone between the sclera and the choroid. It consists of a delicate meshwork of elastic fibres, fibrocytes and melanocytes, traversed by long posterior ciliary nerves and vessels.

Layers of the sclera from outside to inside include episclera, sclera proper, and lamina fusca, in that order.

questions.question: The sclera is the thinnest at which of the following locations?
options: Anterior to attachment of the superior rectus
Posterior to attachment of the superior rectus
questions.answer: D. Posterior to attachment of the superior rectus
questions.explanation:
The sclera is the thinnest posterior to the insertion of the rectus muscles.

The sclera is 1mm thick posteriorly, with maximum thickness around the optic nerve, 0.66 mm at the insertions of the rectus muscles and 0.33 mm beneath the rectus muscles and thinnest behind their insertions

questions.question: A patient sustained a severe blow to the right eye from the lateral side during a fistfight. The eyeball is soft to touch and a rupture of the sclera is suspected. What is the least likely site of rupture?
questions.explanation:
The lateral limbus is the least likely site to be involved in a traumatic scleral rupture.

Traumatic scleral rupture, or globe rupture, occurs after blunt-force trauma. It usually occurs due to the compression force of the trauma. It therefore likely occurs at the insertion of rectus muscles, at the equator, or in an area parallel to the limbus opposite from the site of the impact. Rupture at the site of trauma, in this case lateral limbus, is rare.

The major signs of scleral rupture are conjunctival edema and subconjunctival hemorrhage, hyphema, ocular hypotony, impairment or dislocation of the lens, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment.

questions.question: What is the predominant type of collagen in the sclera?
questions.explanation:
Collagen type I is the predominant type of collagen found in the sclera.

Collagen forms 50 to 75% of the dry weight of the sclera. Type II is absent in the sclera. It is found in the vitreous body of the eye.

questions.question: Staphyloma involves ______.
questions.explanation:
Staphyloma (a bunch of grapes) is a clinical condition characterized by ectasia (dilation or bulging) of the outer coats (cornea or sclera or both) of the eye with the incarceration (trapping) of the uveal tissue.

The image given below shows the anatomical types of staphyloma.

The above image shows an anterior staphyloma.

questions.question: The ciliary staphyloma is due to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Ciliary staphyloma is due to scleritis.

Ciliary staphyloma is the ectasia (bulging) of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. This affects the ciliary zone that includes the region up to 8 mm behind the limbus. It can be caused by scleritis, absolute glaucoma or trauma to the ciliary region of the eye.

The image below shows ciliary staphyloma with scleritis.

questions.question: A 50-year-old female complaining of irritation in her left eye has the following finding. Which of the following condition commonly causes this?
questions.explanation:
Irritation in the eye associated with areas of scleral thinning through which the uvea shines is suggestive of scleromalacia perforans. It is commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

Scleromalacia perforans is a specific type of progressive scleral thinning without inflammation. Despite the term 'scleromalacia perforans', perforation is extremely rare as the integrity of the sclera is maintained by a thin layer of fibrous tissue.

Other collagen disorders associated with it are as follows:

• Wegener’s granulomatosis (option B)

• Polyarteritis nodosa (option A)

• Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

• Ankylosing spondylitis

• Relapsing polychondritis

questions.question: The most common type of scleritis is ______.
questions.explanation:
Non-necrotizing anterior scleritis is the most common type of scleritis.

Scleritis can be classified into anterior and posterior scleritis. Anterior scleritis affects the sclera in front of the equator, while posterior scleritis affects the sclera behind the equator of the eye. Anterior scleritis is further classified into the following types:

1. Non-necrotizing

1. Diffuse: The most common variety

2. Nodular: Scleral nodules are present. Annular scleritis is a variant in which the scleral nodules are arranged in a ring around the limbus.

2. Necrotizing

1. With inflammation

2. Without inflammation: Also known as scleromalacia perforans. It is seen in elderly females with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.

The image below shows anterior nodular scleritis.

questions.question: All the following statements are true for a 40-year-old diagnosed with scleritis except-
options: Scleromalacia perforans is associated with systemic disease.
Pain is not a prominent feature.
Retinal detachment is a known complication.
questions.answer: B. Pain is not a prominent feature.
questions.explanation:
Pain is a prominent feature of scleritis.

Scleritis is an inflammation of the sclera. Patients present with moderate to severe eye pain, redness, lacrimation and photophobia. Anterior scleritis affects the sclera in front of the equator and may lead to the following complications:

• Acute infiltrative stromal keratitis

• Sclerosing keratitis

• Peripheral ulcerative keratitis

• Uveitis

• Glaucoma

• Hypotony (rarely phthisis)

• Perforation of the sclera

Posterior scleritis involves the sclera behind the equator and may lead to uveal effusion with choroidal detachment, disc edema, proptosis or exudative retinal detachment.

Scleromalacia perforans is a type of anterior scleritis. It typically occurs in elderly women with rheumatoid arthritis (systemic disease). There is ischemia and necrosis of the sclera; however, there is no inflammation. Clinically, it is a painless condition with a white eye. Areas of thinned out sclera through which the uvea shines are seen in such patients.

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of gradually worsening sharp and stabbing left eye pain with redness. The severe pain kept her awakened during the night. On investigation, B-scan ultrasound shows the 'T' sign due to fluid accumulation in sub-tenon space. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of severe worsening eye pain with redness and a B-scan showing T sign due to fluid accumulation in sub-tenon space is suggestive of posterior scleritis.

Posterior scleritis is the inflammation involving the sclera behind the equator. Ultrasonography in posterior scleritis may show the following:

• Increased scleral thickness

• Scleral nodules

• Separation of tenon capsule from the sclera

• Disc oedema

• Choroidal folds

• Retinal detachment

• Fluid in the sub-tenon space may give a characteristic "T" sign. The stem of the "T" is formed by the optic nerve and the cross-bar by the fluid-containing gap.

The image given below shows a B-scan ocular ultrasound of the eye.

questions.question: A patient develops surgically induced necrotising scleritis following an ocular surgery. The patient most likely underwent any of the following surgeries except:
questions.explanation:
Surgically induced necrotizing scleritis (SINS) may occur following any ocular surgery involving the creation of a scleral wound. Tarso-frontalis sling surgery is a lid surgery and does not involve the sclera.

SINS is a condition of scleral inflammation and necrosis that may occur as a complication of the following surgeries:

• Pterygium excision

• Cataract surgery (especially with sclero-corneal tunnel)

• Trabeculectomy

• Vitreo-retinal surgeries

• Squint surgery

SINS is more likely to develop in those with rheumatoid arthritis, connective tissue disorders or following intra-operative use of mitomycin C. It is treated with NSAIDS and systemic steroids.

questions.question: As a first-year ophthalmology resident, you come across a child with the following presentation. Which of the following disorders is it associated with?
questions.explanation:
The child has blue sclera which is associated with osteogenesis imperfecta.

Blue scleral discoloration is due to scleral thinning. The underlying uvea thus becomes prominent and visible. Osteogenesis imperfecta (types I and IIA) and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (type VI) are the most commonly associated diseases. Both diseases are inherited disorders of collagen formation.

Other options:

Option A: Hemochromatosis occurs due to iron deposition in various tissues. Rusty-brown perilimbal conjunctiva and scleral discoloration are seen.

Option C: Congenital ocular melanocytosis occurs due to an increase in the number, size and pigmentation of melanocytes. Sclera is multifocal slate-grey pigmented.

Option D: Rheumatoid arthritis may present with extraarticular manifestations such as secondary Sjögren’s syndrome where keratoconjunctivitis sicca can be seen.

questions.question: The sclera is thick in all the following conditions except-
questions.explanation:
The sclera is not thick in buphthalmos.

The sclera is 1mm thick posteriorly, 0.66mm thick at the insertion of recti and 0.33mm thick beneath the recti. In buphthalmos, the sclera is stretched and thinned out, resulting in “blue sclera.” Buphthalmos refers to an enlarged eyeball due to congenital glaucoma.

questions.question: An intern comes across a 7-year-old girl with the following features. All the following are components of her condition except-
questions.explanation:
The given scenario of a young girl with facial asymmetry, deviation of angle of the mouth, flat nasal bridge, preauricular tags and limbal dermoid (lenticular yellow tumour at the limbus) of the eye is suggestive of Goldenhar syndrome. Lung hypoplasia is not a component of this syndrome.

Goldenhar syndrome or oculoauriculovertebral spectrum is a congenital developmental anamoly affecting structures derived from the first branchial arch. It has the following features:

• Systemic:

• Hypoplasia of the malar, maxillary, and mandibular regions

• Macrostomia and microtia

• Preauricular and facial skin tags

• Hemivertebrae (usually cervical)

• Mental handicap

• Cardiac, renal, and central nervous system (CNS) anomalies.

• Ocular:

• Dermoid

• Upper lid notching or coloboma

• Microphthalmos

• Disc coloboma

chapters.chapter: Basics Of Cornea And Infectious Keratitis

questions.question: What is the corneal epithelium normally composed of?
questions.explanation:
The corneal epithelium is made up of stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium.

Layers of the cornea:

• Epithelium (Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium)

• Bowman’s membrane - Acellular; does not regenerate

• Stroma (Thickest layer) - The stroma can scar, but cannot regenerate

• Dua’s layer (Newly discovered, toughest layer)

• Descemet’s membrane- Ends peripherally as Schwalbe’s ring; has regenerative potential

• Endothelium (Most metabolically active layer)- does not regenerate

Note: Limbal stem cells are located at the corneoscleral limbus, in the palisades of Vogt. Deficiency may result in chronic epithelial defects and "conjunctivalization" of the cornea

questions.question: What is the average density of corneal endothelial cells?
questions.explanation:
The density of corneal endothelial cells in adults is about 2500–3000 cells/mm².

Variation in corneal endothelial density with age:

• At birth- 3,500–4,000 cells/mm2 at birth

• Young adults- 2500–3000 cells/mm²

• Old age (about 80 years)- 2000 cells/mm²

Corneas stored in eye banks are assessed for their quality and viability using a variety of parameters. Donor tissues are screened for stress lines, mechanical trauma, scarring, corneal edema, and infiltrates that could indicate poor tissue quality. They are further evaluated for thickness and endothelial cell density (a surrogate for endothelial function) which are important determinants of successful graft transplantation.

Endothelial cell density (ECD) and morphology are assessed using a specular microscope or by a bright-field/phase-contrast light microscope.

Note: The number of cells decreases at about 0.6% per year, and the neighboring cells enlarge to fill the space as the cells cannot regenerate. At a density of about 500 cells/mm2, corneal edema develops and transparency is impaired. This is known as critical endothelial density.

questions.question: Below what horizontal diameter can a diagnosis of micro-cornea be made?
questions.explanation:
To make a diagnosis of microcornea, in this child, the diameter of the cornea should be less than 10 mm.

Micro-cornea

• Horizontal corneal diameter is 10 mm or less (over 2 years of age) or less than 9 mm (in the newborn).

• There may be hypermetropia and a shallow anterior chamber but other dimensions are normal.

Megalocornea

• Horizontal corneal diameter is 12 mm or more (up to 2 years of age) or 13 mm or more (if age >2 years)

• There is typically high myopia and astigmatism, but normal corrected visual acuity.

• Usually X-linked recessive; 90% of affected individuals are male.

Cornea plana

• The cornea is flatter than normal, i.e., the radius of curvature is larger.

• There is a corresponding reduction in refractive power, resulting in high hypermetropia.

Keratectasia

• It is characterized by a protuberance between the eyelids caused by a severely opacified, and sometimes vascularized, cornea.

• It is often associated with raised intraocular pressure as well as intrauterine keratitis.

• Usually unilateral

Microphthalmos

• Microphthalmia is a condition in which the entire eye is small, with an axial length at least two standard deviations below the mean for age.

• It may or may not be associated with ocular dysgenesis.

Nanophthalmos

• In nanophthalmos (simple microphthalmos), the entire eye is small, but is structurally normal;

• It is usually associated with hypermetropia and strabismus

Anophthalmos: Anophthalmos (anophthalmia) refers to the complete absence of any visible globe structure.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms are capable of invading the intact cornea?
questions.explanation:
Gonococcus can invade an intact cornea.

Organisms that can penetrate the intact epithelium of the cornea can be remembered with the mnemonic- CHaNNeLS

• Corynebacterium diphtheria

• Haemophilus influenza;Haemophilus aegypticus

• Neisseria gonorrhea; Neisseria meningitidis

• Listeria

• Shigella

questions.question: A patient with a history of uncomplicated cataract surgery 1 year back, presents with pain, redness, and purulent discharge from his right eye. A greyish-white serpiginous ulcer was noted over the lower third of the cornea. The anterior chamber showed a 4 mm hypopyon and a moderate flare reaction. A smear from the ulcerated area is likely to demonstrate which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Hypopyon corneal ulcer with a characteristic serpiginous description (ulcus serpens) is typically caused by Pneumococcus. The bacterial hypopyon is sterile.

Ulcus serpens is a greyish-white or yellowish disc-shaped ulcer occurring near the centre of the cornea. The ulcer has a tendency to creep over the cornea in a serpiginous fashion.

Risk factors include both surgical and non-surgical ocular trauma, dry eye, chronic corneal disease, immune alterations and contact lenses.

An examination may reveal the following signs:

• Swelling of lids and blepharospasm

• Conjunctival hyperemia

• Ciliary congestion, hypopyon and anterior chamber flare reaction

• Iridocyclitis

Image given below shows ulcus serpens.

questions.question: A young woman presents with sudden onset, rapidly progressing ocular pain, photophobia, and blurred vision in her right eye for 1 day. A deep, 4 mm diameter corneal ulcer, surrounded by stromal infiltrates was visualized. The anterior chamber has small amounts of mucopurulent discharge. She mentions using a cosmetic contact lens which she forgot to remove before sleeping 2 days ago. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
The sudden onset and rapid progression of ocular symptoms and ulceration in this patient along with the history of improper contact lens usage are suggestive of a Pseudomonas infection.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common gram-negative organism isolated from corneal ulcers and is a frequent cause of contact lens–associated keratitis. Other risk factors include chlorinated swimming pools, hot tubs, ventilators, nebulizer, and vaporizer solutions, and ophthalmic solution bottles.

Pseudomonas keratitis has a rapid and fulminant course if left untreated and are associated with a worse visual prognosis than that caused by most other common bacterial pathogens. Pseudomonas spp. can cause corneal perforation in just 48 hours. Treatment is mainly by topical NSAIDs and topical antipseudomonal antibiotic eye drops such as tobramycin 1.3% and fluoroquinolone eye drops.

questions.question: A young woman comes with sudden onset ocular pain, tearing, and photophobia in the left eye. You suspect a bacterial corneal ulcer. What concentration of cephazolin drops would you prescribe for this patient?
questions.explanation:
The concentration of fortified cephazolin used to treat uncomplicated bacterial keratitis is 5% ( 50 mg/mL)

Treatment of uncomplicated bacterial keratitis:

• Antibiotic eyedrops (broad-spectrum)

• If not responding, fortified antibiotic eye drops are used

• Fortified cephazolin (5%)

• Fortified tobramycin (1.3%)

• Fortified vancomycin (5%)

• Cycloplegic drugs- Preferably 1% atropine eye ointment or drops to prevent pain due to ciliary spasm. Also, it prevents the development of posterior synechiae.

• Oral vitamin A and vitamin C help in the healing of the epithelium

• Systemic analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs

Management of non-healing ulcers:

• Debridement

• Chemical cauterization- 10–20% trichloroacetic acid, carbolic acid

• Conjunctival flapping

Management of impending perforation:

• Decrease intraocular pressure (IOP) by antiglaucoma drugs

• Tissue adhesive glue such as cyanoacrylate

• Bandage contact lens

• No strain

questions.question: A non-sterile hypopyon is seen in______.
questions.explanation:
Fungal keratitis can cause non-sterile hypopyon.

Unlike bacterial ulcer, the hypopyon may not be sterile as the fungi can penetrate into the anterior chamber without perforation.

Aspergillus spp. are the most common cause.

Hypopyon in a fungal ulcer is fixed, non-sterile and contains fungal filaments.

questions.question: A farmer presents with blurring of vision in his left eye. He has a history of injury with a bush to the same eye while working. An ulcer is seen in his cornea with feathery margins. Slit-lamp examination shows infiltrates in the corneal stroma in a circular fashion. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction causes these infiltrates?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical situation points towards a fungal corneal ulcer and the infiltrates of stroma in a circular fashion are suggestive of the immune ring of Wessely. This immune ring is due to type 3 hypersensitivity reaction (antigen-antibody complex).

The immune ring of Wessely can be made out as a deep stromal haze in a slit lamp. It occurs as a result of the deposition of antigen-antibody complexes in the stroma. Once deposited it draws the immune cells, inciting further inflammation.

The given shows an ulcer in the cornea and the adjacent immune ring of Wessely.

questions.question: Steroids are contraindicated in_______.
questions.explanation:
Steroids are contraindicated in fungal corneal ulcer

Steroids make the fungi facultative pathogens when they are otherwise symbiotic saprophytes. Therefore, the use of these drugs predisposes the patients to fungal infections and perforation.

questions.question: A 41-year-old female presented with a one-month history of photophobia and foreign body sensation in her right eye. A slit-lamp examination showed a corneal ulcer. The culture of the corneal scrapings grew a filamentous organism identified as a fusarium species. What would be the drug of choice in this case?
questions.explanation:
This patient with a one-month history of eye foreign body sensations and photophobia and slit lamp exam showing an ulcer that had fusarium growth most likely has a fungal corneal ulcer. Natamycin 5% suspension is the drug of choice for filamentous fungal keratitis caused by fusariam species.

Surface debridement is also done as it helps to remove slough, reduce the load of infection and enhances drug penetration. Amphotericin B is particularly effective against yeasts but less effective against filamentous fungi. Also, its penetration through an intact epithelium is less than natamycin.

Amphotericin B is the first agent of choice against yeasts. Amphotericin B (0.15%) drops can be considered alone or in combination with natamycin in refractory cases.

Treatment of specific fungal corneal ulcers:

Topical antifungal drops

• Aspergillus and Fusarium- Natamycin 5%, amphotericin B, fluconazole (0.2%)

• Candida- Amphotericin B (0.15%) or econazole (1%)

Systemic antifungals such as itraconazole and voriconazole are used for severe non-responding cases or if the location of the ulcer is near the limbus or if there is a risk of perforation leading to endophthalmitis.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of the given condition?
questions.explanation: The above image shows a dendritic ulcer caused by herpes simplex virus. Corneal guttata are not seen in HSV infection. They are droplet-like accumulations of non-banded collagen on the posterior surface of Descemet's membrane. It is a feature of corneal dystrophies.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the given condition?
options: It is related to Hutchinson’s triad
There is usually a history of primary HSV infection as a child
High dose topical acyclovir is the treatment of choice
questions.answer: C. Can lead to neurotrophic keratitis
questions.explanation:
The image shows a unilateral painful, vesicular rash suggestive of herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) within the ophthalmic nerve. Neurotrophic keratitis is a complication of HZV infection.

Keratitis occurs due to corneal nerve damage by the virus leading to decreased sensation, frequent infections, persistent epithelial defect, thinning and even perforation.

Corneal lesions in HZO (zoster keratitis):

• Epithelium- superficial punctate keratitis and pseudo-dendritic ulcer

• Stroma- nummular keratitis and disciform keratitis

Other ocular lesions in herpes zoster:

• Uveitis

• Episcleritis and scleritis

• Conjunctivitis

• Acute retinal necrosis

• Secondary glaucoma

• Anterior segment necrosis and pthisis bulbi

Other options:

Option A: Hutchinson’s rule is related to herpes zoster ophthalmicus. It states that if the tip of the nose is involved, there will be a significant risk of ocular involvement. This is due to the involvement of the nasociliary nerve. Hutchinson's triad is seen in congenital syphilis.

Option B: There is primary HZV infection (chickenpox/varicella) not HSV infection.

Option D: Systemic acyclovir is the treatment of choice; not topical antiviral drops. Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times a day for 7-10 days, ideally initiated within 72 h of the onset of symptoms is the usual regimen.

The image shows Hutchinson's sign in a patient with herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

questions.question: A 17-year-old boy presented with blurred vision, photophobia, and increasing pain in his right eye. He has been using contact lenses for the past 2 years. He mentions swimming with his cousins 2 weeks back in a local pond. A close-up image of the eye is given below. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation:
The history of a patient with contact lens use with swimming in freshwater ponds with the image depicting a ring lesion (stromal infiltrate) makes acanthamoeba keratitis the likely diagnosis.

Acanthamoeba keratitis is a rare protozoal infection of the cornea. It is more common in soft contact lens users. The organism exists either as active, motile trophozoites or dormant, double-walled cysts. Suspicious sources of infection can be swimming or use of the hot tub while wearing contact lenses, homemade saline solution to wash contact lenses, exposure to standing groundwater etc.

Pain is disproportionate to the degree of keratitis due to perineural invasion. It presents as ring lesion (most common), pseudo-dendrites and as a reticular pattern.

Diagnosis:

• Confocal microscopy - may reveal bright trophozoites with pseudopodia in the basal epithelium and double-walled cyst forms

• Histopathology - double-walled cysts are seen on H&E. Other stains for Acanthamoeba include calcofluor white, acridic orange, Giemsa-Wright, Wheatly trichrome or periodic acid-Schiff

• Culture - Acanthamoeba can be grown on a bed of E. coli plated on a non-nutrient agar

questions.question: A 39-year-old contact lens user with a corneal ulcer, showing no improvement to tobramycin drops, was referred to a tertiary care centre. Corneal biopsy revealed double-walled cysts within the stroma. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
This patient with a corneal ulcer whose biopsy showed double walled cysts in the stroma most likely has acanthamoeba keratitis. Polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) is the treatment of choice for acanthamoeba keratitis.

Combination therapy with chlorhexidine is most effective against trophozoites and cysts. This is recommended as the first line of therapy.

Other topical anti-amoebic agents:

• Diamidines- Propamidine isethionate (0.1 %), Hexamidine

• Aminoglycosides- Neomycin, Paramomycin

• Imidazoles- Clotrimazole, Miconazole

questions.question: Which of the following does not cause interstitial keratitis?
questions.explanation:
Diphtheria is not a cause of interstitial keratitis.

Interstitial keratitis is a non-ulcerating, inflammatory reaction of the corneal stroma that is characterized by non-suppurative infiltration and often stromal vascularization. The epithelium and endothelium are not affected. Scarring due to stromal inflammation and vascularization, in interstitial keratitis, can result in decreased vision.

Interstitial keratitis (IK) is a common endpoint of any keratitis that predominantly involves the corneal stroma. So there is a wide range of potential etiologies.

Immune-mediated etiologies
Infectious etiologies

• Cogan syndrome:

•

• Interstitial keratitis + deafness + vertigo

• Sarcoidosis

• Mycosis fungoides

Bacterial causes:

• Syphilis; Lyme disease

• Tuberculosis; Leprosy

• Brucellosis; Leptospirosis.

Viral causes:

• Herpes simplex (HSV), Herpes zoster (VZV)

• Epstein-Barr (EBV), mumps, rubella (measles)

• influenza, and vaccinia

Parasitic causes:

• leishmaniasis

• onchocerciasis

• trypanosomiasis

• plasmodium

• acanthamoeba

Treatment for IK typically involves the use of topical corticosteroids, as well as appropriate systemic medications for the associated systemic disease.

questions.question: Which of the following infections is classically associated with salmon patch appearance of the cornea?
questions.explanation:
Salmon patch appearance of the cornea is classically associated with syphilitic infection.

This is because, syphilis causes deep vascularization of the cornea, leading to a radial bundle of brush-like vessels.

Stages of interstitial keratitis in congenital syphilis:

• Progressive stage - ground-glass appearance

• Florid stage - salmon patch appearance

• Stage of regression - ghost vessels

questions.question: A patient with recurrent corneal epithelial erosions is diagnosed with limbal stem cell deficiency. She has been enrolled on a research trial for corneal epithelial stem cell transplant. All are markers that can be used to identify stem cells from an ex-vivo culture except?
questions.explanation:
Connexin 50 is not a limbal stem-cell marker.

The major markers proposed for epithelial stem cells can be categorized into at least three groups:

• Nuclear proteins such as transcription factor p63

• Cell membrane or transmembrane proteins

• Integrins (integrin ß1, α6, and α9),

• Receptors (epidermal growth factor [EGF] receptor and transferrin receptor CD71)

• Drug-resistance transporters (ABCG2—a universal stem cell marker)

• Cytoplasmic proteins such as

• Cytokeratins (cytokeratin 14 - exclusively at LSC)

• Alpha-enolase

questions.question: For her final year thesis, an ophthalmology resident is studying endothelial cell loss due to phacoemulsification surgery. The image is taken during the pre-op evaluation of one of the cataract patients. What does this show?
questions.explanation:
The given image is a specular microscopy view of endothelial cells of different shapes (pleomorphism) and large surface area (polymegathism). These are indicators of endothelial dysfunction.

A normal endothelium has a regular hexagonal shape. Because these cells are terminally differentiated cells, they do not divide, and when they die, the remaining cells have to stretch to cover more area, resulting in polymegathism and pleomorphism.

Taking an endothelial cell count can be helpful before taking patients up for cataract or refractive surgery so that any potential endothelial dysfunction or thinning is recognized before they have the surgical intervention.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of herpetic keratitis?
questions.explanation:
Corneal guttata are seen in corneal dystrophy.

Peripheral guttata are seen in old age—Hassall–Henle bodies. Central guttata, on the other hand, are found in Fuch's endothelial dystrophy.

questions.question: A corneal foreign body was removed from a 53-year-old man. He was sent home with chloramphenicol and steroid eye drops. Two days later he came back with a corneal ulcer and a hypopyon. The ulcer scraping under microscopy revealed branched septate hyphae. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given history of trauma and worsening with antibiotic-steroid drops suggests a fungal corneal ulcer. Out of the given options, Aspergillus is the fungus with branched septate hyphae.

Clinically, fungi are classified on a morphological basis into filamentous, yeast, and dimorphic forms:

• Filamentous organisms are multicellular with branched hyphae. It can be septate or aseptate.

• Septate filamentous organisms, such as Fusarium and Aspergillus, have hyphae that are divided by cell walls.

• Non-septate filamentous fungi, include Mucor and Rhizopus.

• Yeasts, such as Candida and Cryptococcus, are unicellular fungi that reproduce by budding, but in tissue, they might develop elongated buds (pseudohyphae).

• Dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma, Coccidioides, and Blastomyces demonstrate both a yeast phase that occurs in tissues and a mycelial phase that appears on culture media and saprophytic surfaces.

Image: Branched septate hyphae of Aspergillus spp.

questions.question: Corneal sensation is lost in____.
questions.explanation:
Corneal sensation is lost in herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection.

The pathognomic feature of viral keratitis is decreased corneal sensation. Decreased corneal sensation is also seen in diabetes mellitus and leprosy.

questions.question: Deposition of which of the following is responsible for band-shaped keratopathy?
questions.explanation:
Band-shaped keratopathy is caused by pathological calcium deposition on the cornea in the form of a band.

On exam, there is a white band-like formation of calcium across the corneal surface with irregular borders and a peripheral clearing of cornea between the calcium deposits and the limbus. The calcium deposition is typically found beneath the epithelial layer within Bowman’s layer but may extend into the anterior stroma.

Once the visual axis starts to get involved, there will be progressive loss of vision. Recurrence is common unless the predisposing cause is identified and treated.

Local causes such as chronic ocular irritation or inflammatory conditions and systemic diseases that elevate serum calcium levels are the main causes for band-shaped keratopathy. It can rarely have hereditary causes as well.

Image given below shows band-shaped keratopathy.

questions.question: A patient was with the given finding has been having painless and slowly progressive vision loss for the past 10 years. Which of the following diseases is not associated with the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Based on the given clinical scenario and ocular finding depicted here, it is suggestive of band-shaped keratopathy, and systemic lupus erythematosus is not associated with this condition.

Band-shaped keratopathy (BSK) is due to calcium deposition, primarily in the form of hydroxyapatite, in the epithelial basement membrane, Bowman's layer, and the anterior stroma. Initially, these deposits are grey but may become chalky-white as the degeneration progresses.

lt typically presents as a band-shaped opacity in the interpalpebral zone with a clear interval between the ends of the band and the limbus. The condition begins at the periphery and gradually progresses towards the centre. The surface of this opaque band is stippled due to holes in the calcium plaques in the area of nerve canals of Bowman's membrane.

Causes of band-shaped keratopathy include local causes such as chronic ocular irritation or inflammatory conditions and systemic diseases that elevate serum calcium levels:

Local causes
Systemic diseases

• Chronic anterior uveitis (especially in Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

• Interstitial keratitis

• Superficial keratitis

• Phthisis bulbi

• End-stage glaucoma

• Silicone oil left in the aphakic eye

• Hyperparathyroidism

• Sarcoidosis

• Multiple myeloma

• Hypophosphatemia

• Paget disease

• Chronic renal failure

Treatment:

• Medical management- Chelation using topical ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) 1.5–3.0%

• Surgical management- Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) using excimer laser or manual superficial keratectomy

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman was brought by her son, during a cataract outreach camp. She gives a history of trauma to her left eye, one year back and a complete loss of vision in that eye since then. Her image is given below. Which of the following statement is true about her condition?
options: Corneal tattooing is a treatment option in this lady.
The given lesion is an adherent leucoma.
It is due to scars involving Bowman's layer and superficial stroma.
Excimer laser phototherapeutic keratectomy is the current treatment of choice.
questions.answer: A. Corneal tattooing is a treatment option in this lady.
questions.explanation:
The above image shows a dense white opacity, which results from the scarring of more than half of the stroma, characteristic of leucoma.

Corneal tattooing is a treatment option in patients with corneal opacities, who have lost their vision or who do not expect to recover it. It improves cosmetic appearance by altering the white colour of the opacity and blending it to normal eye colour.

Depending on the density, corneal opacities are graded as nebula, macula and leucoma.

• Nebular corneal opacity (fog or mist):

• Hard-to-see corneal scar, due to superficial scars involving Bowman's layer and superficial stroma.

• Slit-lamp detection is required.

• A thin, diffuse nebula covering the pupillary area interferes more with vision than the localised leucoma away from the pupillary area. Nebula produces more discomfort due to blurred image (irregular astigmatism).

• Macular corneal opacity:

• Semi-dense opacity that can be seen with proper illumination.

• Due to scarring involving about half the corneal stroma.

• Leucomatous corneal opacity (leucoma simplex):

• White scar that is easily seen just by looking at the eye.

• Due to scarring of more than half of the stroma

• Adherent leucoma:

• It results when healing occurs after perforation of the cornea with incarceration of iris

Secondary changes in corneal opacity which may be seen in long-standing cases include hyaline degeneration, calcareous degeneration, pigmentation and atheromatous ulceration.

Treatment:

• Keratoplasty is the treatment of choice in leucomatous corneal opacities.

• Optical iridectomy may be performed in cases with central adherent leucomas

• Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) performed with excimer laser is useful only in superficial (nebular) corneal opacities.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is least likely to be associated with bilateral corneal opacities in a neonate?
questions.explanation:
Keratoglobus is least likely to be associated with bilateral corneal opacities in a neonate. Here, the cornea is clear.

Keratoglobus is a rare noninflammatory, familial disorder marked by generalised thinning and globular protrusion of the cornea. It can be congenital or acquired. The thinning is usually greatest at corneal periphery or midperiphery. It can cause refractive errors, otherwise, cornea is clear, normal angle of anterior chamber, normal intraocular pressure with no optic disc cupping.

Intrastromal ring segments and cross-linking can be used for management.

Other options:

Option B: Birth injuries resulting in Descemet's membrane tears can also cause corneal opacities.

Option C: Peter's anomaly, also known as iridocorneal adhesions or keratolenticular adhesions, is a posterior corneal defect with an overlying stromal opacity.

Option D: Sclerocornea is a congenital disorder in which the cornea is opaque and resembles the sclera, making the limbus indistinct. The central cornea is clearer than the periphery.

questions.question: What causes neurotrophic keratopathy?
questions.explanation:
Neurotrophic keratopathy is caused by trigeminal nerve palsy.

Lesions of the fifth cranial nerve from the trigeminal nucleus to the cornea may lead to abnormalities of the normal corneal sensation and trophic stimulation.

Causes:

• Varicella-zoster (most common cause)

• Herpes simplex keratitis

• Trauma

• Irradiation to the eye

• Aneurysm/stroke

• Multiple sclerosis

Mackie characterized three stages of neurotrophic keratitis.

• Stage I is characterized by an irregular corneal surface, which later develops into an easily recognized punctate keratitis.

• Stage II is characterized by a frank epithelial defect, which is typically associated with mild anterior stromal oedema and inflammation.

• Stage III involves stromal melting and occasionally perforation.

questions.question: Paralysis of which of the following nerves is responsible for exposure keratopathy?
questions.explanation:
Exposure keratopathy is caused by paralysis of the facial nerve.

It is the result of incomplete lid closure (lagophthalmos) resulting in drying of the cornea (despite normal tear production).

Causes:

• Neuroparalytic, e.g., facial nerve palsy

• Reduced muscle tone as in parkinsonism

• Mechanical such as lid scarring

• Proptosis

Note: Neurotrophic keratopathy is due to loss of trigeminal nerve innervation resulting in partial or complete loss of sensation.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs is least likely to cause the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Erythromycin is least likely associated with cornea verticillata/vortex keratopathy, a whorl-like opacity in corneal epithelium, as shown in the image above.

Vortex keratopathy occurs due to corneal deposits in the basal epithelium. They are almost always bilateral and are readily recognisable by their distinct appearance as fine, golden-brown or grey opacities that branch out from a central whorl, usually across the inferior cornea. Opacity due to drugs is reversible upon stopping the drug.

Causes:

• Amiodarone (most common) (Option A)

• Tamoxifen (Option C)

• Indomethacin

• Chloroquine (Option D)

• Chlorpromazine (rarely)

• Fabry’s disease

questions.question:
A 30-year-old albino woman presents with a characteristic finding as shown below. Which of the following statements are true regarding the suspected condition?

1. It is due to the deposition of copper in the Descemet's membrane

2. It requires screening for underlying lipid disorder

3. It is seen in patients with the neurological form of Wilson’s disease

4. If seen unilaterally it is suggestive of ipsilateral carotid stenosis

5. It is also called limbus sign
questions.explanation:
A 30-year-old individual with corneal changes, as shown above, known as gerontoxon or arcus lipoides, may require screening for underlying lipid disorder.

Arcus senilis (AS), also known as gerontoxon, arcus lipoides or arcus cornealis, is usually an age-related lipid degeneration of the peripheral cornea that forms a light grey or bluish ring. It is the most common peripheral corneal opacity, typically benign, occurring bilaterally and prevalent among the elderly.

However, when observed in individuals under 50, termed arcus juvenilis, it may indicate underlying lipid disorder and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, warranting lipid profile screening. Unilateral cases of arcus senilis may indicate contralateral carotid artery stenosis due to decreased ophthalmic blood flow on the ipsilateral side, resulting in protection from forming arcus in the ipsilateral eye.

The condition results from the leakage of lipoproteins (phospholipids and cholesterol) from limbal capillaries into the corneal stroma, initiating deposition at the superior and inferior cornea. Over time, the ring progresses circumferentially, sparing a clear corneal zone adjacent to the limbus called the interval of Vogt.

The following opacities and rings can resemble arcus senilis:

• Kayser- Fleischer (KF) ring: A dark brown ring caused by the deposition of excess copper in Descemet's membrane, classically seen in Wilson's disease. It may also be seen in certain chronic, cholestatic liver conditions such as primary biliary cirrhosis.

• Limbus sign: Caused by dystrophic calcification, seen as a "milky precipitate" at the corneal limbus. It can sometimes be confused with AS in the elderly population.

• Pseudo-gerontoxon: A greyish peri-limbal band of superficial scarring adjacent to a previously inflamed segment of the limbus resembling AS, seen in vernal keratoconjunctivitis.

The image below depicts the Kayser–Fleischer ring and anterior capsule of the crystalline lens (Sunflower cataract) seen in Wilson's disease.

questions.question: A young male labourer presents to the casualty with severe bilateral eye pain that woke him from sleep. He reports welding the previous afternoon without a face shield and symptoms of photophobia, blurry vision, tearing, and worsening pain in bright light. Examination reveals mild conjunctival injection and diffuse punctate epithelial erosions on the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The described corneal findings, with his classic history of welding less than 12 hours prior to presentation, are suggestive of photophthalmia.

Photophthalmia is produced due to exposure to short-wavelength ultraviolet (UV-B) rays. The cornea absorbs the majority of UV light (especially 311 to 290 nm). It results in desquamation of the epi­thelium leading to multiple painful corneal erosions. Causes of of UV keratitis:

Artificial causes
 Natural causes

• Arc welding

• Flash from short-circuits,

• Damaged metal halide lamps

• Tanning beds

• UV germicidal lamps.

• Exposure to strong solar radiation at high altitudes especially on snow-covered terrain (snow blindness)

• Prolonged viewing of a solar eclipse without proper eye protection.

The symptoms appear characteristically after a latent period of 4- 5 hours of exposure to ultraviolet light. There is intense burning pain, foreign body sensation, and watering of the eyes. There may be associated marked photophobia and blepharospasm. On slit-lamp examination, corneal epithelium shows a breach in continuity and takes up fluorescein stain.

Management comprises cold compresses, lubricant eye drops and bandaging eyes for 24 hours with antibiotic eye ointment and cycloplegic. Avoid local surface topical anaesthesia. Crooke’s glass is a prophylactic aid consisting of a spectacle lens combined with metallic oxides to absorb ultraviolet or infrared rays and should be used by those who are prone to exposure.

Note: Photoretinitis and macular burns are often a result of infrared radiation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a method for long-term preservation of cornea?
questions.explanation: Cryopreservation is used for long-term preservation of cornea, up to 1 year.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of infection following corneal transplantation in India?
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common cause of infectious keratitis after corneal transplantation in developing countries.

Pneumococcus spp. and Staphylococcus aureus have been found to be the most common causes of post-corneal transplant infections in developed countries.

questions.question: Which of the following techniques is the gold standard for assessing corneal thickness?
questions.explanation:
The gold standard technique for assessing corneal thickness is ultrasound pachymetry, which uses a corneal pachymeter.

Measurement of the corneal thickness (pachymetry) indirectly reflects endothelial function. The average central corneal thickness is around 0.5 mm, which gradually increases toward the periphery to around 0.7 mm. Normally, as a diurnal variation, corneas tend to be slightly thicker just after a person awakes in the morning.

Other options:

Option A: Confocal microscopy is an imaging technique that allows in vivo examination of corneal structures at high magnification and resolution. It is used to assess corneal nerve morphology and corneal endothelium.

Option B: Keratometry measures the anterior corneal curvature and is traditionally performed with a manual keratometer, also known as an ophthalmometer.

Option D: Corneal topography is used to assess the anterior corneal surface, its shape and thickness.

The image below shows a corneal pachymeter.

questions.question: Your aunt recently shared that it is becoming cumbersome for her to frequently change her glasses. You suggested a referral and the rapid change in power was diagnosed to be due to keratoconus. The following image shows the results of one of the investigations done on her. What is the name of the investigation?
questions.explanation:
The investigation shown in the image is corneal topography, and it is used for conditions like keratoconus, as seen in this clinical scenario.

Corneal topography captures the shape of the cornea by projecting concentric rings of light onto its anterior surface, forming a Placido disc pattern. the reflected light is analyzed with specialised software to create a detailed map of the corneal curvature.

Uses:

• Detection of corneal ectasia, mainly keratoconus

• To measure corneal thickness

• Prior to refractive surgery

• Sometimes prior to contact lens fitting

The image shows a Placido or Keratoscopic disc which is used for corneal surface assessment.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old girl with high myopia was referred by the optometrist for further evaluation. She has a history of recurrent allergic conjunctivitis and persistent eye rubbing. An image is given below. Which of the following statements are true about the given condition?

1. It is usually associated with regular astigmatism

2. Corneal topography is the primary diagnostic tool

3. Keratoplasty is the treatment of choice

4. Vogt's striae and Rizzuti sign are both findings

5. The area of protrusion is mostly inferotemporal
questions.explanation:
Keratoconus is a progressive bilateral corneal ectatic disorder. It manifests as characteristic cone-like steepening of the cornea associated with irregular stromal thinning, resulting in a cone-like bulge (protrusion) and significant loss of vision.

The pathogenesis is not fully known. Several associations have been identified, which include rigid contact lens wear, chronic eye rubbing, Down's syndrome, atopic disease, Leber's congenital amaurosis, and connective tissue disease.

It is a non-inflammatory disease. With the exception of the significant loss of vision, other classic signs of inflammation are not usually present. The asymmetrical thinning and the highly irregular corneal topography often causes significant myopia and irregular astigmatism.

Corneal topography is the primary diagnostic tool for KCN detection.

Whereas keratoplasty, historically has been the mainstay of treatment for keratoconus, it is now generally reserved for eyes that are unable to achieve functional vision with other surgical or non-surgical modalities and is only considered only as a last resort, in very advanced disease. It is the definitive treatment for keratoconus, not the treatment of choice.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a treatment option in advanced keratoconus?
questions.explanation:
Vision correction with spectacles with spherical/toric soft contact lenses is suboptimal and only applicable to the early stages of keratoconus, not in the advanced stages.

Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory, bilateral corneal ectasia characterized by cone-like steepening due to irregular stromal thinning. This leads to a conical corneal protrusion, significant vision loss, myopia and irregular astigmatism.

The available options for the management of keratoconus are highly dependent on the stage of the disease and its progression. If the disease is stabilized (no progression), the emphasis is given to correcting the vision. If the disease is progressing, the emphasis is on slowing (arresting) the progression.

Treatment options in moderate-to-advanced keratoconus:

• Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses and vaulting scleral lenses are the mainstays of vision treatment for moderate to advanced KCN. Their main advantage is the creation of a tear pool between the lens and the cornea, which naturally neutralizes the ocular aberrations associated with keratoconus. (Option B and C)

• Intra-corneal ring segments (INTACS)- small curved PMMA ring or set of rings that are implanted in the cornea to help flatten corneal curvature to improve vision.

• Corneal transplantation- Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) and penetrating keratoplasty (PKP)

Corneal collagen cross-linking with riboflavin (CXL or C3R) and ultraviolet-A rays arrest the progression of the disease. (Option D)

questions.question: A 40-year old male with progressive loss of vision in his left eye was diagnosed with against-the-rule astigmatism. Examination revealed peripheral corneal thinning, but there was no inflammation. Which of the following is least likely to be the cause?
questions.explanation:
The examination in a 40-year-old male revealed peripheral corneal thinning with no inflammation, making peripheral ulcerative keratitis, an inflammatory condition, the least likely cause.

Peripheral ulcerative keratitis is a destructive inflammatory disease involving the peripheral cornea. It is associated with signs and symptoms of inflammation. The other options are causes of peripheral thinning in a quiet eye.

Other options:

Options A and B: Terrien's and Pellucid marginal degeneration are noninflammatory corneal degenerations. Pellucid degeneration causes bilateral, inferior corneal thinning that leads to marked, irregular, against-the-rule astigmatism. Terrien's degeneration usually begins in the superior cornea.

Option C: Dellen is a localized thinning of the peripheral cornea associated with the drying of a focal area. Usually associated with an adjacent elevated lesion (e.g., pinguecula or a large subconjunctival haemorrhage) that impairs physiological lubrication.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman presented with tearing, irritation, and photophobia of the left eye. On examination, a paracentral, crescent-shaped corneal melt was noted. Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) was suspected. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis is commonly associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK). It is also the most common cause.

PUK is a group of destructive inflammatory diseases involving the peripheral cornea, characterized by the sloughing of corneal epithelium and keratolysis (corneal melting). It can lead to corneal perforation. The causes can be divided into:

• Infectious- bacterial, viral, protozoal, fungal.

• Non-infectious- rheumatoid arthritis, Wegener's granulomatosis, SLE, rosacea, psoriasis etc.

Ophthalmologic manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis (due to type III and IV hypersensitivity reactions):

• dry eye

• scleritis

• stromal keratitis

• peripheral ulcerative keratitis

• paracentral keratolysis

Treatment of PUK includes protection of the surface from drying and exposure; systemic corticosteroids and immunomodulatory; use of adjuncts such as amniotic membrane grafts to promote healing; and in some situations, tectonic keratoplasty.

questions.question: A 54-year-old school teacher presented with a chief complaint of pain in the eyes and intermittent blurry vision which was worse in the mornings. Generalized corneal haze was noted in both eyes but was more significant in the left. Examination findings are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario along with beaten metal appearance on slit lamp and reduced endothelial cell density with coalescing guttata on specular microscopy is suggestive of Fuch's endothelial dystrophy.

Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is a bilateral, slowly progressive, often asymmetric corneal disease. It is characterized by deterioration of endothelial cells and development of guttata, which are excrescences of Descemet’s membrane (seen on specular or confocal microscopy). Females are affected more than males. It is more common in the 4th decade or later.

Endothelial layer dysfunction causes loss of corneal deturgescence, and bilateral oedema of the stroma, leading to ocular pain, glare, halos, and decreased visual acuity. Patients have a worse vision in the morning because of the eyes being closed during the night causing a buildup of corneal oedema.

Stages of Fuch’s endothelial dystrophy:

• Stage 1: Central corneal guttata that spreads peripherally

• Stage 2: Corneal oedema - beaten metal-like appearance

• Stage 3: Bullous keratopathy

• Stage 4: Subepithelial scarring and superficial vascularization

Treatment:

• Conservative option- topical hypertonic (saline sodium chloride 5% drops or 6% ointment) and bandage contact lenses.

• The definitive treatment is endothelial keratoplasty: Descemet’s stripping endothelial keratoplasty (DSEK/DSAEK) or Descemet membrane Endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK).

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about macular corneal dystrophy?
questions.explanation:
Macular dystrophy does not spare the peripheral cornea.

It is the least common corneal dystrophy. It has an autosomal recessive inheritance. Most other corneal dystrophies are autosomal dominant. It is associated with mucopolysaccharidoses and is characterized by the deposition of glycosaminoglycans in the stroma and staining by Alcian blue. It develops in childhood and is progressive, resulting in profound visual impairment in early adult life.

Clinical examination reveals superficial whitish fleck-like opacities. These opacities extend peripherally to the limbus and the deep stroma down to Descemet’s membrane. The intervening corneal stroma develops a progressive and diffuse haze.

Note:

• Most common dystrophy overall- Microcystic/fingerprint/map-dot dystrophy

• Most common stromal dystrophy- Lattice dystrophy

• Dystrophy with corectopia- Posterior polymorphous dystrophy

• Autosomal recessive dystrophy- Macular dystrophy

questions.question: Which of the following stains is used in identifying granular dystrophy of the cornea?
questions.explanation:
Masson trichrome stains stromal hyaline deposits in granular dystrophy of the cornea.

Granular corneal dystrophy belongs to the stromal dystrophy of the cornea. It is of autosomal dominant inheritance and is caused by a defect in the TGFB1 gene.

Granular corneal dystrophy is characterized by milky, granular, hyaline deposits in the anterior stroma, which may coalesce into irregular shapes. The peripheral cornea and the area between the opacities/deposits remain clear. Early symptoms may involve light sensitivity, glare, ocular discomfort, pain, and watering. As opacification progresses with age, visual acuity decreases.

The following image shows numerous irregularly shaped discrete crumb-like corneal opacities of Granular dystrophy, which stain bright red with Masson trichrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is implicated in the pathogenesis of oil-droplet keratopathy?
options: Deposition of lipid in the anterior stroma
questions.explanation:
Oil-droplet keratopathy occurs due to exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays.

Climatic droplet keratopathy (CDK), alternatively known as oil droplet keratopathy/spheroidal degeneration/Labrador keratopathy, is an acquired corneal degenerative disorder. Clumps of variably sized golden-yellow globules accumulate in the superficial corneal stroma and are thought to be derived from photochemical degradation of plasma proteins, by UV radiation.

The image shows Labrador keratopathy.

Other options:

Option A: Lipid keratopathy involves the accumulation of whitish or yellow fat deposits, mainly cholesterol and fatty acids, which begin intracellularly and later move extracellularly due to necrosis of corneal stromal cells. It can be primary (rare, in the cornea free of vascularization) or secondary (common, in the vascularized cornea).

Option C: Exposure keratopathy results from lagophthalmos (incomplete eyelid closure), causing corneal dryness despite normal tear production. Causes include neuroparalytic conditions (like facial nerve palsy), reduced muscle tone in Parkinsonism, lid scarring, post-blepharoplasty and proptosis.

Option D: Neurotrophic keratopathy results from loss of trigeminal nerve innervation to the cornea, affecting both sensation and healing. This disruption can cause corneal dryness, ulceration, exfoliation, and edema. It is commonly linked to conditions such as trigeminal ganglion surgical ablation for neuralgia, stroke, diabetes, herpes simplex and herpes zoster keratitis.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding intracorneal ring segment (ICRS) implantation is false?
options: It is used in the management of keratoconus.
Corneal perforation is a very common complication.
It is made of polymethyl methacrylate.
questions.answer: C. Corneal perforation is a very common complication.
questions.explanation:
Corneal perforation may occur but is quite rare in intracorneal ring segment (ICRS) implantation.

Salient points on ICRS:

• These segments are made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) and are implanted into the mid-peripheral corneal stroma.

• These are used in the management of keratoconus and low myopia.

• Improvement in visual acuity and refraction after ICRS implantation is accomplished by a shortening of collagen lamellae along the arc length of the ring. There is a redistribution of corneal stress due to a change in the curvature of the cornea after implantation of the ICRS.

• Decreased corneal sensation can be a postoperative complication.

• More than 90% of patients have <1 D change in refraction at 1-year postoperative follow-up.

 The image shows the intrastromal corneal ring segment.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with normal visual acuity undergoes a routine eye exam. Slit-lamp examination reveals numerous crumb-like centrally dense deposits in the anterior corneal stroma, bilaterally symmetrical, with clear intervening stroma. Which of the following statements is likely to be true?
options: Histopathology specimen will stain positive with alcian blue
Histopathologic review will reveal amyloid deposits on congo red staining
Histopathologic review will reveal hyaline deposits on the Masson trichrome stain
questions.answer: C. Histopathologic review will reveal hyaline deposits on the Masson trichrome stain
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario, with the given image showing multiple breadcrumb-like deposits, is suggestive of granular corneal dystrophy, where histopathology reveals hyaline deposits on the Masson trichrome stain.

Granular corneal dystrophy belongs to the stromal dystrophy of the cornea. It is of autosomal dominant inheritance and is caused by a defect in the TGFB1 gene.

In granular corneal dystrophy, opacities form due to the abnormal accumulation of hyaline protein, assuming a discrete granular form and subsequently coalescing into various irregular shapes. The cornea between the opacities and the peripheral cornea remains clear. The condition is characterised by milky granular hyaline deposits in the anterior stroma.

In many patients, no symptoms occur, whereas some patients develop recurrent erosions. In the fifth decade or later, some patients develop sufficient visual difficulties to require keratoplasty. Treatment is usually keratoplasty for severe visual handicaps.

Note: The beaten metal appearance on the slit lamp and reduced endothelial cell density with coalescing guttata on specular microscopy is suggestive of Fuch's endothelial dystrophy.

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant is brought with a history of diffuse, ground glass-like corneal haze in both eyes. The corneas are thickened with normal diameters and associated nystagmus. Which one of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
options: Intraocular pressure (IOP) is likely to be elevated.
The corneal stroma shows abnormal deposits that stain with amyloid.
It could be a bilateral choristoma.
Descemet’s membrane may be thickened due to an abnormal endothelium.
questions.answer: D. Descemet’s membrane may be thickened due to an abnormal endothelium.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario most likely suggest congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED), where Descemet’s membrane is abnormally thickened.

CHED is a rare disorder characterized by focal or diffuse thickening of the Descemet membrane and endothelial degeneration. The key features of this condition include corneal thickness, which is two to three times the normal, normal intraocular pressure (IOP) and normal corneal diameter. Associated features are corneal pannus, nystagmus, and esotropia.

Treatment usually involves corneal transplantation (lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty) for visual rehabilitation.

Other options:

Option A: As the corneal diameters are normal, and there are no typical symptoms, congenital glaucoma is ruled out.

Option B: Amyloid deposits in the corneal stroma are seen in Lattice stromal dystrophy.

Option C: Choristomas are congenital lesions representing normal tissue(s) in an abnormal location. They are the most common epibulbar and orbital tumors in children. It usually arises at the limbus of the eye and may include dermoid tissue, lipodermoid or other tissues.

Note: The combination of congenital endothelial dystrophy and progressive neural deafness, is known as Harboyan syndrome. This disorder must be distinguished from another autosomal recessive disorder, congenital endothelial dystrophy, in which deafness does not occur.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about Mooren's ulcer?
options: Painless superficial ulcer that can perforate
Associated with autoimmune and rheumatological conditions
Characterized by a steep, overhanging edge
Ulcerative process begins centrally and then moves circumferentially
questions.answer: C. Characterized by a steep, overhanging edge
questions.explanation:
Moorens’s ulcer/ulcus roden is characterized by a steep, overhanging edge.

It is described as a chronic serpiginous ulcer of the cornea. It is a subtype of peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK). It is defined as an idiopathic condition without associated systemic or rheumatological conditions and hence is a diagnosis of exclusion. The pathophysiology is thought to be due to autoimmune.

Clinical features include redness, tearing, and photophobia, but pain is typically the outstanding feature. The pain often is incapacitating and may well be out of proportion to the inflammation. There may also be a complaint of decreased visual acuity, which may be secondary to associated iritis or central corneal involvement.

Initially, the ulcerative process spreads circumferentially. Later, it moves centrally to involve the entire cornea. In contrast to other forms of PUK, the limbus is involved. The end-stage result is typically a scarred, vascularized cornea that may be thinned to less than half of its original thickness.

Treatment involves corticosteroids and excision of a strip of adjacent conjunctiva, which eliminates the conjunctival sources of collagenase and proteoglycanase.

The image shows a perforated Mooren's ulcer.

questions.question: Which layer of the cornea is affected in Reis–Buckler dystrophy?
questions.explanation:
The corneal layer involved in Reis–Buckler dystrophy is Bowman’s membrane.

Corneal dystrophies are primarily a bilateral, inherited, non-inflammatory condition specific to the cornea.

Reis–Buckler dystrophy, an autosomal dominant disorder, is an anterior variant of granular stromal dystrophy, characterised by the replacement of the Bowman layer with connective tissue bands, primarily affecting the Bowman layer and superficial stroma. Several recurrent corneal erosions may occur in childhood along with visual impairment.

In this condition, there are grey-white, geographic subepithelial opacities (that are most dense centrally and increase over time, eventually forming a reticular pattern. Additionally, corneal sensation is reduced as the disease progresses.

The image below shows Reis–buckler corneal dystrophy on slit-lamp examination:

chapters.chapter: Lens Introduction, Types Of Cataract And Clinical Features

questions.question: What is the embryonic origin of the lens?
questions.explanation:
The lens of the eye originates embryonically from the surface ectoderm.

Surface ectoderm gives rise to lens, conjunctival and corneal epithelium and epithelial lining of lacrimal glands and tarsal glands.

questions.question: Where are the youngest fibers of the lens present?
questions.explanation:
The youngest fibers of the lens are the peripheral part, the cortex.

The nucleus of the lens is the central part containing the oldest fibers.

The lens fibers are produced by mitosis of the epithelial cells in the pre-equatorial zone. As the lens fibers elongate and the new ones are formed, the older ones are pushed towards the depth of the lens so that the youngest fibers are the most superficially located.

questions.question: At a routine ophthalmological check-up, a patient was found to have bilateral, Y-shaped lens opacities as shown below. He was diagnosed with suture cataracts. Which zone of the lens nucleus is not involved here?
questions.explanation:
The primary fibers in the embryonic nucleus of the lens do not form Y-shaped sutures.

The image shows bilateral cataracts in the Y-shaped sutures of the lens. These are very slowly progressive congenital cataracts and do not require any surgical intervention.

 Types of lens nucleus and their age of development:

• Embryonic nucleus: Innermost nucleus formed at around 1–3 months of gestation

• Fetal nucleus: From 3 months of gestation till birth

• Infantile nucleus: From birth to puberty

• Adult nucleus

As lens fibers grow anteriorly and posteriorly, a pattern emerges where the ends of the fibers meet. These patterns of cell association are known as sutures.

Y-shaped sutures are recognizable at about 8 weeks of gestation.

questions.question: What is the ligament of Weigert?
options: Attachment of the vitreous to the posterior capsule of the lens
Attachment of the lens to the ciliary muscles
questions.answer: A. Attachment of the vitreous to the posterior capsule of the lens
questions.explanation:
The hyaloideo-capsular ligament of Weigert is the attachment of the vitreous to the posterior capsule of the lens.

It is the annular region (1–2 mm in width and 8–9 mm in diameter) where the vitreous is attached to the posterior aspect of the lens.

Erggelet’s or Berger’s space is at the centre of the hyaloideo-capsular ligament, a potential space between the vitreous and the lens. The canal of Cloquet arises from this space and courses posteriorly through the central vitreous, which is the former site of the hyaloid artery in the embryonic vitreous.

Posteriorly, Cloquet’s canal opens into a funnel-shaped region anterior to the optic disc, whch is known as the area of Martegiani.

questions.question: Where does the crystalline lens derive its nutrition from?
questions.explanation:
The crystalline lens derives its nutrition from the aqueous humor.

The lens is an avascular structure. It receives nutrition mostly from the aqueous humor and, to some extent, from the vitreous humor as well. Glucose is the main energy source. Major intrinsic protein 26 (MIP 26)/Aquaporin 0 in the lens is responsible for maintaining transparency by transporting water and glycerol across the lens.

Anti-oxidant mechanisms in the lens:

• Reduced glutathione (most important)

• Glutathione peroxidase

• Superoxide dismutase

• Catalase

• Vitamin C, Vitamin E, carotenoids.

questions.question: While studying the histological anatomy of the lens, you are measuring the thickness of the lens capsule in various areas. At which of the following zones would you get the lowest measurement?
questions.explanation:
