The lens capsule is the thinnest at the posterior pole, measuring 4 µm.

Other options:

Option A: At the anterior pole, the thickness of lens capsule is 14 µm.

Option C: In the pre-equator region, lens capsule is the thickest, measuring 23 µm.

Option D: At the equator, as shown in the illustration below, the thickness is 17 µm.

questions.question: You are observing the given slide in a histology examination. Where is the marked structure absent?
questions.explanation:
The slide shows the histology of the lens and the structure marked in the subcapsular epithelium. The epithelium of the lens is absent on its posterior surface.

The lens epithelium is a single layer of cells on the anterior surface of the lens. There is no epithelium on the posterior surface, as these cells are used up in filling the central cavity of the lens vesicle during the development of the lens. The anterior epithelial lining creates new lens fibers throughout a person's life.

questions.question: Ascorbate and alpha-tocopherol are maintained in the lens in the reduced state by _______.
questions.explanation:
Ascorbate and alpha-tocopherol are maintained in the lens in the reduced, functional state by glutathione.

Glutathione is present in high concentrations in the lens, particularly in the epithelial layer. One of its key functions is to maintain protein thiols in their reduced state, which preserves the lens transparency by preventing the formation of high molecular weight crystalline aggregates and protects the lens from oxidative stress.

The lens is highly prone to photochemical reactions from continuous exposure to ultraviolet rays (295–400 nm), leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Its defence relies heavily on superoxide dismutase, ascorbate, catalase and glutathione peroxidase.

With ageing or cataracts, levels of glutathione and ascorbic acid (in reduced form) significantly decrease.

questions.question: As part of a public health initiative, screening for cataract is being carried out. What is the most common cause of this healthcare issue in the population?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of cataracts is ageing, specifically senile (age-related) cataract.

Important causes of cataract:

• Aging (Most common)

• Congenital cataract (crystallin gene - CRYAA, CRYAB, CRYGC, CRYGS) (Option A)

• Diabetes mellitus (Option B)

• Syndermatotic- atopic dermatitis is the most common skin condition associated with cataract

• Galactosemia- reversible cataract

• Radiation- UV rays, X-rays, gamma rays, infrared

• Toxic agents- Corticosteroids, miotics (long-acting anticholinesterases, e.g., echothiophate) (Option C)

• Obesity

Senile cataract is the most common type of acquired cataract and is also known as age-related cataract. The two types of senile cataracts are cortical (soft cataract)-75% and nuclear (hard cataract)-25%. In cortical cataract, the cuneiform type (70%) is the most common, and the cupuliform type is the most visually handicapping.

questions.question: You are compiling a literature review on congenital cataracts diagnosed in the last few years. Which of the following is the most common type?
questions.explanation:
The most common type of congenital cataract is the blue-dot cataract.

Cataracta-punctata-caerulea, commonly known as blue dot cataract, is a prevalent type of congenital cataract. It typically develops during the first two decades of life. This condition is characterized by distinctive rounded bluish opacities located in the peripheral region of the adolescent nucleus and the deeper cortical layers of the lens. While these opacities are generally stationary and do not impair vision, larger ones may cause slight visual disturbance.

questions.question: The parents of a child have been informed at a PTA meeting that he has a lot of incomplete classwork. On being questioned, the child complains that he is unable to see things clearly and is having difficulty in reading and writing. On ophthalmic examination, he is found to have a cataract. Which type of congenital cataract most commonly presents with these findings?
questions.explanation:
Lamellar or zonular cataract is the most common type of congenital cataract presenting with visual impairment.

The etiology may be either genetic or environmental in origin.

• Genetic- familial autosomal-dominant

• Environmental form is associated with:

• Vitamin D deficiency

• Hypocalcemia

• Sometimes, maternal rubella infection contracted between the 7th and 8th week of gestation may also cause lamellar cataract.

The main mass of the lens internal and external to the zone of cataract is clear.

Small linear opacities like spokes of a wheel (riders) may be seen towards the equator.

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman delivers a baby girl with a congenital rash, as shown below, and patent ductus arteriosus. What type of cataract is commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario showing blueberry muffin rash, combined with patent ductus arteriosus in a baby girl, suggests a diagnosis of congenital rubella syndrome, which is typically associated with a progressive, pearly white nuclear cataract.

Ocular effects of rubella:

• Microphthalmia

• Rubella keratitis

• Angle-closure glaucoma

• Nuclear pearly cataract

• Salt and pepper fundus (a most common ocular feature of rubella) due to diffuse chorioretinitis.

questions.question: The following finding is found on the ophthalmologic examination of an 18-year-old girl. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image above characteristically depicts a Christmas tree cataract, featuring multiple refractile colors commonly observed in myotonic dystrophy.

Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by difficulty relaxing skeletal muscles after contraction. The initial symptoms typically manifest during adolescence or early adulthood.

Cataracts are an early and prominent feature in 90% of patients with myotonic dystrophy. They typically present as fine, dust-like opacities interspersed with iridescent, polychromatic spots in the cortical layer beneath the anterior and posterior lens capsule, resembling a Christmas tree. These cataracts may remain stable or progress.

Surgical outcomes are generally favourable.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmology OPD with the findings shown below. She has been diagnosed with a right-sided senile cataract. Identify the stage of the cataract.
questions.explanation:
The above image represents an advanced stage of cataract progression characteristic of a Morgagnian hyper-mature cataract.

Morgagnian hyper-mature cataracts are characterized by liquefaction of the entire cortex. The lens is converted into a bag of milky fluid. The small, brownish nucleus settles at the bottom, its position altering with a change in the position of the head.

Senile cataract is the most common type of acquired cataract and is also known as age-related cataract. The two types of senile cataracts are cortical (soft cataract)-75% and nuclear (hard cataract)-25%.

Cortical cataract is further divided into the cuneiform and cupuliform types.

Cuneiform (70%)
Posterior subcapsular/Cupuliform (5%)

Radial spoke-like opacity starting in the periphery and extending centrally

Central saucer-shaped opacity in the posterior cortex just below the capsule

Late visual loss

Early loss of visual acuity; most visually handicapping senile cataract

Nuclear cataracts: These may be pigmented due to the deposition of urochrome pigments. These are cataracta brunescens (brown), cataracta nigra (black), cataracta rubra (red).

questions.question: Where is polychromatic luster noted?
questions.explanation:
Polychromatic luster is seen in complicated cataracts.

Due to disturbances in nutrition of the lens due to inflammatory/degenerative disease of other parts of the eye like iridocyclitis and ciliary body tumors. In inflammations/degenerations affecting the posterior segment, a characteristic opacification is seen in the posterior part of the cortex in the axial region (posterior subcapsular cataract).

These cataracts present with a breadcrumb appearance and polychromatic luster. Even in the early stages, vision is impaired.

questions.question: Who among the following patients can potentially develop drug-induced cataracts?
questions.answer: C. 36 year old male on Dexamethasone
questions.explanation:
Patients taking dexamethasone (corticosteroid) are prone to drug-induced cataracts, predominantly presenting as discoid posterior subcapsular cataracts.

Drugs causing cataracts:

Drugs
Type of cataract

Corticosteroids
Discoid, posterior subcapsular

Anticholinesterases
Anterior subcapsular

Chlorpromazine
Yellow-brown anterior capsular granules/stellate/anterior polar

Busulfan
Posterior subcapsular

Chloroquine
White, flaky, posterior subcapsular

Amiodarone
Anterior subcapsular

Other options:

Option A: Zoledronate, a bisphosphonate drug can cause orbital inflammation, uveitis, and scleritis.

Option B: Hydroxychloroquine, a drug used in malaria and rheumatoid arthritis, does not cause cataracts, chloroquine does. It can rarely cause retinal toxicity.

Option D: Ethambutol is used in anti-tubercular therapy and its use has been shown to cause optic neuritis.

questions.question: The ophthalmologic examination on a 23-year-old college student revealed the following image. What disease is commonly associated with this ocular finding?
questions.explanation:
The given picture of a slit-lamp biomicroscope examination depicts the anterior lenticonus, which is associated with Alport syndrome.

In Alport’s syndrome, both anterior and posterior lenticonus are seen, but anterior lenticonus is more common. The diagnosis of lenticonus is typically confirmed through slit-lamp examination.

Note: Lowe’s syndrome is an oculo-cerebro-renal syndrome characterized by congenital cataract, glaucoma, and posterior lenticonus

questions.question: A 60-year-old man, diagnosed with bilateral cataracts two months ago, reports being able to read better without prescription glasses. However, he complains that his distant vision has become blurrier. Which type of cataract typically causes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
The phenomenon described is the second sight of old age, seen in nuclear cataracts.

Due to nuclear sclerosis, there is an increase in the refractive index, causing progressive myopia. A patient with presbyopia may be able to read again, without the aid of spectacles. This improvement in vision is termed second sight.

questions.question: A 38-year-old lady is a known case of diabetes and is on insulin for the last 8 years. Her sugars are poorly controlled and now she complains of hazy vision. What type of cataract will be characteristically noted in her eyes?
questions.explanation:
The typical appearance of a diabetic cataract is a snowflake cataract.

Hyperglycemia is reflected in a high level of glucose in the aqueous humor, which diffuses into the lens. Here, glucose is metabolized into sorbitol, which accumulates within the lens, resulting in secondary osmotic overhydration.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents with an inability to see objects in bright light. On examination, she is diagnosed with a cataract. In which of the following cataract is this characteristic finding not seen?
questions.explanation:
The inability to see objects in bright light is not a feature of cuneiform cataract, as the lens opacity is peripheral, allowing visibility in bright light during miosis.

The loss of the ability to see objects in bright light is a feature of posterior subcapsular cataract (visually handicapping), cupuliform cataract and nuclear cataract as these present with central opacities.

When a person is exposed to bright light, the pupil undergoes miosis (constriction). These central opacities come to lie directly in the path of axial rays, allowing no transmission of rays. Therefore, there is an inability to see objects in bright light. However, in dim light, when there is mydriasis (dilatation of the pupil), some rays may pass around the opacity, leading to an improvement in dim-light vision.

Furthermore, the complicated cataract, steroid-induced cataract, radiation-induced mainly present with a posterior subcapsular cataract and therefore have a similar clinical picture.

questions.question: You are counseling the parents of Nisha, a 1-month-old child diagnosed with a congenital lamellar cataract in both eyes. What is the course of treatment you would advise?
options: Cataract surgery with intraocular lens (IOL) implant
Pars plana lensectomy with no IOL implant
questions.answer: C. Cataract surgery with intraocular lens (IOL) implant
questions.explanation:
Cataract surgery with an intraocular lens (IOL) implantation is the treatment of choice in congenital cataracts.

It involves an extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) with primary posterior capsulorhexis and anterior vitrectomy. After removal of the cataractous lens, a posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL) is implanted.

The critical period for the development of the fixation reflex in both unilateral and bilateral visual deprivation disorders is 2–4 months of age. Thus, any cataract dense enough to impair vision must be dealt with before this age, and the earliest possible time is preferred.

• Bilateral dense cataract- early surgery by 4-6 weeks of age

• Unilateral dense cataract or involving visual axis- urgent surgery within days

Intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE) is contraindicated in children.

questions.question: A 28-year-old girl is being evaluated for an aortic root aneurysm. She says her mother died of an aortic dissection at the age of 43. She is tall and slim. A musculoskeletal system finding is shown below. What is the most common lens subluxation noted in the genetic disease she is suffering from?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette of a girl with tall, slim stature, an aortic arch aneurysm, Steinberg sign (positive thumb sign), and similar family history suggest a diagnosis of Marfan’s syndrome. It is most commonly associated with a superotemporal subluxation of the lens.

The image below shows a subluxated lens in a patient with Marfan's syndrome.

Congenital subluxation of the lens is called ectopia lentis.

Types of ectopia lentis are as follows:

• Simple type

• Ectopia lentis et pupillae (pupil also displaced in opposite direction)

• Ectopia lentis associated with syndromes

• Marfan’s syndrome- superotemporal subluxation of lens

• Homocystinuria- inferonasal subluxation of the lens

• Weill–Marchesani- downward, forward subluxation of the lens.

• Ehler–Danlos syndrome

questions.question: Which of the following diseases does not show a specific pattern of cataract?
questions.explanation:
A specific pattern of cataract is not seen in leprosy.

A specific pattern of cararact is seen in the following:

• Juvenile diabetes: Snowflake cataract

• Myotonic dystrophy: Christmas tree cataract

• Wilson's disease: Sunflower cataract

chapters.chapter: Lens Cataract Surgery, Complications And Iols

questions.question: A child has congenital cataract involving the visual axis, which was detected at birth. When should the child be operated up on?
options: At 1 year of age, when the globe attains normal size
At 4 years, when ocular and orbital growth is complete
questions.explanation:
The child should be operated at 4-6 weeks of age.

When a child has unilateral or bilateral cataract impairing vision (involving the visual axis), the cataract surgery must be performed before 2-4 months of age. This is because 2-4 months is the critical period for visual maturation and development of the fixation reflex in children. A unilateral cataract is more dangerous than a bilateral cataract because the risk of amblyopia is greater. Under-correction of intraocular lens (IOL) power is needed in children.

In children < 2 years of age:

• In unilateral cases, primary implantation is indicated as soon as the patient is fit for anesthesia, ideally between 2 and 3 months of age. The power is undercorrected by 20%.

• The earlier the surgery is done, the better the chance that deep amblyopia can be overcome.

• After the cataract has been aspirated, an elective posterior capsulectomy–anterior vitrectomy is performed. The posterior chamber IOL is inserted through a scleral tunnel, which is prepared in advance.

• Sulcus implantation is indicated in neonates and infants less than 1 year of age.

In children between 2 and 8 years of age:

• An IOL is implanted but power is undercorrected by 10%.

• An in-the-bag IOL is chosen for children above 1 year of age because they are less likely to need an IOL exchange.

Beyond 8 years, IOL power is the same as the calculated value.

questions.question: In which of the following cataract surgeries is a self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel incision used?
questions.explanation:
The self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel incision is made in small-incision cataract surgery (SICS).

SICS is a type of extracapsular cataract extraction techniques (ECCE). In these techniques, the major portion of the anterior capsule with the epithelium, nucleus, and cortex are removed, leaving behind the intact posterior capsule.

Note: Newer cataract surgeries include femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS), micro-incision cataract surgery (MICS) and Phaconit. FLACS is a microincision cataract surgery or a micro-phacoemulsification where a femtosecond laser is used to make the corneal incisions, perform capsulorhexis and fragment the lens. MICS refers to the phacoemulsification techniques that can be performed through a microincision (<2 mm). Phaconit is the term for the bimanual micro-phacoemulsification done with the needle incision technique through an incision of <1mm.

questions.question: In which of the following patients is an intracapsular cataract extraction indicated?
questions.explanation:
At present, the only indication of intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE) is markedly subluxated and dislocated lens.

In ICCE, the entire cataractous lens along with the intact capsule is removed by rupturing the zonules. Therefore, weak and degenerated zonules are a prerequisite for this method. Methods of lens delivery include cryoextraction (best method), forceps extraction (Arruga forceps), wire vectis method and Indian Smith method. ICCE is no longer used for cataract treatment due to the large incision required, inability to implant an IOL and a high rate of complications like vitreous loss, retinal detachment and cystoid macular edema.

questions.question: What is the length of the incision used in phacoemulsification?
questions.explanation:
The length of the incision in phacoemulsification varies from 1.5 to 2.4 mm. The option closest to this answer is B, i.e., 2 to 2.5 mm.

In phacoemulsification, the nucleus of the lens is emulsified and aspired. This is done by the phacoemulsifier. It acts through a hollow 1-mm titanium needle, which vibrates by at an ultrasonic speed of 40000 times a second. The steps of phacoemulsification are given below:

• Step 1 - Small clear corneal incision

• Step 2 - Continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis

• Step 3 - Hydro dissection

• Step 4 - Hydro delineation is done in some cases.

• Steps 5 and 6 - Emulsification and aspiration of the nucleus

• Step 7 - Removal of the cortical lens matter using an irrigation-aspiration technique

• Step 8 - Implantation of a foldable lens

Length of the incision in various cataract surgeries:

• Phacoemulsification- 1.5–2.4 mm.

• Micro-phacoemulsification- 1–1.5 mm.

• Intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE)- 12–14 mm.

• Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE)- 8–12 mm.

questions.question: What is the most common late complication following cataract surgery?
questions.explanation:
The most common late complication following cataract surgery is posterior capsule opacification.

Posterior capsule opacification, known as after or secondary cataract, is the most common late postoperative complication. It may be caused by residual opaque lens matter or proliferation of left out anterior epithelial cells.

questions.question: In a patient undergoing cataract surgery, which of the following is the most important strategy in the prevention of postoperative endophthalmitis?
options: One week antibiotic therapy prior to surgery
questions.answer: A. Preoperative preparation with povidone iodine
questions.explanation:
The most important factor in the prevention of postoperative endophthalmitis is preoperative preparation with povidone-iodine.

Postoperative endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis. Flora of the eyelids and conjunctiva are the most frequent source. Other potential sources include contaminated solutions and instruments, environmental air, and the surgeon and other operating room personnel.

Prophylaxis for postoperative endophthalmitis includes:

• Instillation of 5% povidone-iodine into the conjunctival fornices and leaving this undisturbed for at least 3 minutes prior to surgery. This is the most important factor.

• Scrupulous preparation of the surgical site

• Treatment of pre-existing infections such as blepharitis

• Antibiotic prophylaxis

• Intracameral cefuroxime (1 mg in 0.1 mL) injected into the anterior chamber (AC) at the end of surgery.

• Post-operative subconjunctival injection can achieve bactericidal levels in the AC for at least 1–2 hours.

• Preoperative topical fluoroquinolone antibiotics are frequently given in regimens from 1 hour to 3 days before surgery

Patients present with ocular pain, diminished vision, circumciliary congestion and hypopyon. The differential diagnosis for postoperative endophthalmitis includes retained lens material in the AC, vitreous hemorrhage, postoperative uveitis and toxic reaction to the use of inappropriate or contaminated irrigating fluid or viscoelastic.

questions.question: What is the treatment of choice for after cataract?
questions.explanation:
Nd:YAG laser is the treatment of choice for after cataract.

Thin membranous after-cataract, thickened posterior capsule and Elschnig's pearls are treated with Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy. Dense membranous after-cataract requires capsulotomy using a vitreous cutter. Sommering's ring, if the central posterior capsule is clear, requires no treatment.

Other options:

Option A: Intra-capsular cataract extraction (ICCE) is currently used for the treatment of markedly subluxated and dislocated lens.

Option B: Intravitreal steroids may be used for the treatment of acute endophthalmitis, an early postoperative complication of cataract surgery.

Option C: Anterior vitrectomy is performed for the treatment of cystoid macular edema with vitreous incarceration. This is a late post-cataract surgery complication.

questions.question: What is the cause of late-onset endophthalmitis after cataract surgery?
questions.explanation:
Late-onset endophthalmitis after cataract surgery is caused by Propionibacterium acnes.

Late or delayed-onset endophthalmitis following cataract surgery develops when an organism of low virulence such as P. acnes, becomes trapped within the capsular bag (saccular endophthalmitis). Organisms can become sequestered within macrophages, protected from eradication but with continued expression of bacterial antigens. Patients present with symptoms between 4 weeks to years (mean 9 months) postoperatively following an uneventful cataract surgery.

questions.question: An elderly male residing in an old-age home is brought to the hospital with senile cataracts in both eyes. He says he had difficulty in seeing objects for a few years, but never went to the clinic. He is posted for surgery in 3 weeks. Which of the following is a complication is he unlikely to develop in the 3 weeks until his surgery?
questions.explanation:
Hypopyon is not a complication of senile cataracts.

Hypermature, or senile cataracts, can lead to the following complications.

• Phacoanaphylactic uveitis: The lens proteins may leak into the anterior chamber. They may act as an antigen and induce antigen–antibody reaction, leading to phacoanaphylactic uveitis.

• Lens-induced glaucoma:

• Phacomorphic glaucoma: Most common, seen in intumescent cataract. The lens swells and causes secondary angle closure glaucoma.

• Phacolytic glaucoma: Seen in hypermature cataract. The leaked lens proteins are engulfed by macrophages, which clog the trabecular meshwork and cause secondary open-angle glaucoma.

• Phacotopic glaucoma: Seen in hypermature cataract. The lens may subluxate or dislocate and block the angle of the anterior chamber.

• Subluxation or dislocation of the lens: It may occur due to degeneration of zonules in the hypermature stage.

questions.question: What is the best irrigating fluid for cataract surgery?
questions.answer: D. Balanced salt solution plus glutathione
questions.explanation:
The best irrigating fluid for cataract surgery is balanced salt solution plus glutathione (BSS plus).

In the early days of phacoemulsification, the only irrigating solutions available were normal saline, plasmalyte, and lactated Ringer’s solution. Their main adverse effects were endothelial cell toxicity. The buffer in BSS Plus is bicarbonate, which is an improvement over the sodium acetate and citrate buffers in BSS.

questions.question: How many weeks following surgery are spectacles prescribed?
questions.explanation: Spectacles are prescribed 6 weeks after cataract surgery after the course of steroids is over. It is the time required for the incison to heal. Then visual acuity is checked and glasses are prescribed.

questions.question: A 72-year-old diabetic who underwent uncomplicated cataract extraction with PCIOL implant 15 days back presents with painless, decreased vision in the operated eye. His visual acuity is 6/12 and does not improve with a pinhole. On examination, the anterior chamber is deep, and PCIOL is well-centered in the capsular bag. Dilated fundus exam reveals clear media, and optic nerve with a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.4, a few peripheral microaneurysms, and a dull foveal reflex. The rest of the fundus exam is unremarkable. Which test would be of least benefit?
questions.explanation:
In the above case scenario, gonioscopy would be the least helpful.

A painless decrease in vision after cataract surgery could be due to:

• Posterior capsular opacification (most commonly, after 1-3 months)

• Cystoid macular edema (early)

• Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (delayed)

In the given question, the media is clear (rules out posterior capsular opacification). Also, there are no symptoms nor signs of retinal detachment (RD), hence it is ruled out. Decreased vision not improving with a pinhole in the presence of clear media is attributable to macular pathology. Also, there is a dull foveal reflex. The diagnosis in this patient is cystoid macular edema (CME).

The incidence of clinical CME is about 1% to 2% following uncomplicated cataract surgeries. The incidence of angiographic evidence of CME is 10 times greater at around 10% to 20%.

Optical coherence tomography (option A) is useful in identifying cystoid macular edema and evaluating the vitreomacular interface. It is also useful in the measurement of retinal thickening, thus allowing the assessment of the therapeutic response. On fluorescein angiography (option B), the classic petaloid leakage in the fovea is seen in the case of CME. Amsler’s grid (option D) is a macular function test.

Hence, the least useful in this scenario is gonioscopy.

questions.question: Two months after undergoing cataract surgery, a 45-year-old man is found to have after cataract. He is planned for an Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy. What is the principle behind the use of this laser?
questions.explanation:
The principle of the Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm) is photodisruption.

Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy is used for treatment of thin membranous after-cataract, posterior capsular opacification and Elschnig's pearls. The plasma produced at the laser target expands and disrupts the tissues, creating an opening. Double frequency Nd:YAG laser is used in posterior segment photocoagulation.

questions.question: Which of the following complaints in a patient presenting to your OPD would prompt you to perform a Fincham's test?
questions.explanation:
Fincham's test is used to distinguish whether the colored halos are due to cataract or glaucoma.

Colored halos are rainbow-colored rings seen around lights at nighttime. It may be caused by cataracts, acute congestive glaucoma and mucopurulent conjunctivitis. These conditions lead to prismatic disruption of light.

questions.question: As part of the pre-operative evaluation of a patient posted for cataract surgery, you are asked to calculate the power of the IOL to be implanted. What investigation do you perform?
questions.explanation:
The power of the intraocular lens (IOL) to be implanted after cataract surgery is calculated by a biometer and the procedure is termed as biometry.

Biometry consists of keratometry and axial length measurement. The most common method of determining IOL power uses a regression formula called modified Sanders–Retzlaff– Kraff (SRK) formula, which is given below:

 E = A - 2.5L - 0.9K

Where,

• E is the emmetropic power designated for the eye

• A is a predetermined constant, which is specific for each intraocular lens type

• L is the axial length of the eyeball in millimeter, determined by using the "A" scan ultrasonography

• K is the average corneal curvature, which is determined by keratometry.

 The image given below shows a biometer.

questions.question: In the SRK formula for intraocular lens power calculation 'E=A-2.5L-0.9K', the value of L is estimated using__________
questions.explanation:
In the SRK formula, the value of L is calculated using the A-scan ultrasonographic biometry.

The most widely used formula for intraocular lens power calculation is the modified Sanders-Retzlaff-Kraff (SRK) formula, given by:

 E = A - 2.5L - 0.9K

Where,

• E: Emmetropic power designated for the eye

• A: Predetermine constant which is specific for each intraocular lens type.

• L: Axial length of eyeball in millimeters, determined using the A scan ultrasonography.

• K: Average corneal curvature determined by keratometry.

Given below is an image of A scan ultrasonography.

questions.question: What is a rigid intraocular lens made of?
questions.explanation:
Rigid IOLs are made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA).

Depending on the type of material of manufacturing, 3 types of posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOLs) are available:

• Rigid IOLs are made entirely from polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA).

• Foldable IOLs are made of silicone, hydrogel, acrylic, and Collamer. These are implanted through a small incision.

• Rollable IOLs are ultra-thin IOLs made of acyrlic or hydrogel. These are implanted through a 1-mm incision after micro-incision cataract surgery technique.

questions.question: A patient, on follow-up after cataract surgery, has the lens shown below. What is the type of lens implanted in the patient?
options: Modified C loop posterior chamber IOL
questions.explanation:
The image depicts Singh and Worst’s iris claw lens.

This lens is an iris-supported lens, which is fixed with the help of sutures, loops or claws. They are associated with a high incidence of postoperative complications and are thus only used if posterior chamber IOLs cannot be implanted.

Note: Kelman multiflex type of anterior chamber intraocular lens (ACIOL) is the most commonly used ACIOL. Anterior chamber IOLs lie entirely in front of the iris and are supported in the angle of the anterior chamber. These are associated with a higher incidence of bullous keratopathy. Thus, they are currently used only for correction of aphakia in cases where posterior chamber IOLs cannot be used (eg: rupture of posterior capsule).

questions.question: An 80-year-old man is posted for cataract surgery. The given lens is chosen to be used for implantation. Identify the lens.
options: Modified C loop posterior chamber IOL
Singh and Worst's iris claw lens
questions.answer: B. Modified C loop posterior chamber IOL
questions.explanation:
The above image depicts a modified C-loop type of posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL).

A PCIOL rests entirely behind the iris. They may be supported and fixed by capsular bag fixation of PCIOL (most ideal method), ciliary sulcus fixation or scleral fixation.

The PCIOL consists of a central part overlying the optic axis is called the optic and the peripheral arms used for placement and stabilization called the haptics.

questions.question: Identify the intraocular lens shown below.
questions.explanation:
The given image is of a toric IOL used to correct pre-existing astigmatism. The dotted markings on the optic of the IOL indicate the axis of IOL, and it is aligned to coincide with the steep axis of the patient’s eye.

For every, one degree of misalignment, about 3 percent of the lens cylinder power is lost.

questions.question: What is the normal aqueous production rate?
questions.explanation:
The rate of formation of aqueous humor is 2-3 μL/min.

Formation of aqueous humor involves the following:

• Ultrafiltration

• Secretion- Na/K ATPase of non-pigmented epithelium of the ciliary process

• Diffusion

questions.question: What is the critical angle of the air-cornea interface?
questions.explanation:
The critical angle of the air–cornea interface is 46 degrees. Gonioscopy is a method of evaluating the anterior chamber (AC) angle.

Direct goniolenses include the Koeppe, Medical Workshop, Barkan, and Swan–Jacob. Indirect goniolenses include Goldmann, Zeiss, and Posner.

Structures seen on gonioscopy from anterior to posterior are:

• Schwalbe line: represents the posterior limit of Descemet's membrane

• Trabecular meshwork

• Scleral spur

• Ciliary body and root of the iris

Shaffers grading of angle width:

Grade 4 (35–45°) is the widest angle, characteristic of myopia and pseudophakia; the ciliary body can be visualized without tilting the lens.
Grade 3 (25–35°) is an open-angle in which the scleral spur is visible.
Grade 2 (20°) is an angle in which the trabeculum but not the scleral spur can be seen.
Grade 1 (10°) is a very narrow-angle in which only the Schwalbe line, and perhaps the top of the trabeculum, can be identified.
A slit angle is one in which there is no obvious iridocorneal contact but no angle structures can be identified.
Grade 0 (0°) is closed due to iridocorneal contact.

questions.question: Which statement regarding the depth of the anterior chamber is false?
options: Depth is less in women than men
questions.explanation:
The depth of the anterior chamber decreases with age.

Anterior chamber depth

• The anterior chamber is shallow in very young and in old age.

• At other periods of life, it is normally about 2.5 mm deep.

• Depth is less in women than in men.

• Depth is more in myopes.

• Depth is less in hypermetropia and in angle-closure glaucoma

questions.question: A neonate is brought with complaints of photophobia and watering. Clinical examination shows normal tear passages and clear but large cornea. Investigation reveals Haab’s striae seen in the eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This neonate with complaints of photophobia and watering with large cornea and Haab's striae is suggestive of buphthalmos. Haab’s striae are horizontal/circumferential breaks in Descemet’s membrane seen in buphthalmos.

Buphthalmos (Bull-like eyes) is an enlargement of the eyeball seen in true congenital and infantile glaucoma, usually when the disease onset is before 3 years.

The image given below shows Haab's striae and a child having buphthalmos in congenital glaucoma.

Note: Vogt's striae are vertical, fine, whitish lines (folds/tears) in Descemet's membrane commonly found in patients with keratoconus.

The image given below shows Vogt's striae.

questions.question: A patient presents to the clinic for a change of her presbyopic glasses. This is the third time that she is coming in 2 months. What is the likely underlying diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Frequent changes in presbyopic glasses in this patient is a symptom of open-angle glaucoma (OAG).

This is due to increasing accommodative failure as a result of constant pressure on the ciliary muscle and nerve supply.

In intumescent cataracts, patients report difficulty with distance vision and frequent change of spectacle prescription. However, it is not associated with frequent changes of presbyopic glasses.

questions.question: Normal cup-to-disc ratio is up to_______.
questions.explanation: Normal cup-to-disc ratio is up to 0.6. Although the average cup-to-disc ratio is around 0.3 to 0.4, a ratio of up to 0.6 may be found in healthy individuals. This larger ratio is frequently seen in cases of large discs, myopic discs or physiological cupping. A cup-to-disc ratio of > 0.6 is suggestive of glaucoma.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man, who is a known case of diabetes mellitus, presents with headache and eye pain. He also reports difficulty with driving at night. Examination showed a laminar dot sign. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a patient with headache and eye pain along with the finding of a laminar dot sign is suggestive of glaucoma.

The laminar dot sign is an advanced glaucomatous change in the optic disc. This occurs because the pores in the lamina cribrosa are slit-shaped and are visible up to the margin of the disc.

Glaucomatous changes in the optic disc

Early glaucomatous changes:

• Slit defects of the retinal nerve fiber layer

• Splinter hemorrhages on disc margin

• Large cup - 0.7 or more

• Asymmetry of the cups: A difference equal to or more than 0.2 between two eyes is significant

• Vertically oval cup

Advanced glaucomatous changes:

• Marked cupping (Beanpot cupping)

• Thinning of neuroretinal rim

• Bayonetting sign - Sharp angulation of vessel at the margin of the excavated cup

• Laminar dot sign

questions.question: What is the last visual field to be affected in glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
The temporal visual field is the last field to be affected in glaucoma.

The pattern of visual field progression in glaucoma from early to severe is predictable in light of the pattern of thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer, which usually begins with the superior and inferior arcuate fibers, then the papillomacular bundle and finally, the nasal fibers.

Since the nasal fibers are the last to be involved, the temporal field is the last to be affected in glaucoma.

questions.question: Which of the following is a late visual field defect in open-angle glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
Bjerrum scotoma (arcuate) is a late and clinically significant visual field defect.

Progression of visual field changes seen in glaucoma:

Early non-specific changes

• Isopter contraction

• Baring of a blind spot: Exclusion of blind spot from the central field

Early significant changes

• Peripheral nasal step (may be early or late)

• Paracentral scotoma in Bjerrum's area.

• Siedel’s scotoma: Paracentral scotoma joins the blind spot

Late significant changes

• Arcuate or Bjerrum scotoma

• Ring or Double arcuate scotoma: When 2 arcuate scotomas join together

• Roenne’s central nasal step

Advanced glaucomatous field defects

• Tubular vision

• No light perception: Complete visual field defect.

questions.question: A 70-year-old patient presents with progressive deterioration of vision. The pupillary reaction is sluggish and the IOP is elevated. Fundoscopy shows a large and deep cup and the visual field reveals paracentral scotoma. What is the first line of treatment for this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of deterioration of vision, sluggish pupils, elevated IOP and paracentral scotoma is suggestive of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). Timolol is one of the first-line agents used in the treatment of primary open-angle glaucoma.

First-line agents for the treatment of glaucoma are:

• Prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost and bimatoprost

• Topical beta-blockers such as timolol, betaxolol, and levobunolol

• Selective alpha 2 adrenergic agonist brimonidine

Adjunctive therapy: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

Laser trabeculoplasty: In cases where intraocular pressure (IOP) is uncontrolled despite maximal tolerated medical therapy.

Note: Since prostaglandin (PG) analogs are not included in the options, the next best option to choose is timolol.

Historically, beta-blockers were the most common first-line agents used in the medical treatment of POAG. However, with an increase in our experience with newer agents, specifically the prostaglandin analogues that facilitate outflow, they were recognized as being more efficacious in lowering IOP and systemically safer than beta-blockers. As a result, now they are the first-line agents in glaucoma treatment.

questions.question: A patient with a known case of MI on aspirin comes with shortness of breath. She has an active history of asthma and uses inhalational bronchodilators, her last attack was 7 months ago. She was recently prescribed medications for increased intraocular pressure. What is the likely cause of her current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
This patient with a history of asthma now presenting with shortness of breath after starting medications for increased intraocular pressure was most likely diagnosed with glaucoma. The drug she was likely prescribed was timolol, a non-selective beta blocker.

Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that is used in glaucoma. Non-selective beta-blockers can cause precipitation of bronchial asthma in susceptible individuals (beta-2 block on bronchi). They cause bronchospasms and are therefore contraindicated in patients with asthma (e.g. timolol, levobunolol). Ocular beta-blockers reduce intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous formation by blockade of β2 receptors. Timolol is specifically associated with allergic blepharoconjunctivitis and punctal stenosis

Side effects: Systemic: Bronchospasm, bradycardia, decreased cardiac output, hypotension, depression, impotence, and altered lipid profile.

Contraindications: Asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, congestive heart failure, sinus bradycardia, and atrioventricular blocks

Other options:

Option A: The patient has been stable on aspirin for the past three years which is unlikely to be the cause of her current symptoms.

Option B: Betaxolol is a beta 1 selective blocker that is used in glaucoma and has a lower propensity to precipitate bronchial asthma.

Option C: Latanoprost is a prostaglandin (PGF2 alpha) analog and does not precipitate bronchial asthma.

questions.question: As a first-year ophthalmology resident, you have been referred a case of glaucoma. He complaints that his current medication is causing excessive drowsiness and is interfering with his work. Which of the following anti-glaucoma medications can cause drowsiness?
questions.explanation:
Brimonidine is an anti-glaucoma medication that can cause drowsiness.

It is a selective alpha-2 agonist. It can cross the blood-brain barrier and, hence, causes drowsiness and CNS depression; it is contraindicated in infants and children.

A new class of glaucoma drugs, Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitors, promises to act specifically on the trabecular meshwork, a main outflow and blockage site in glaucoma. ROCK inhibitors are not yet approved and available for glaucoma patients. Two US companies, Aerie and Altheos, are currently in early clinical research development with topical ROCK inhibitors to lower IOP.

questions.question: A 55-year-old female, who is a known case of sickle cell anemia, comes to the casualty with a history of severe eye pain, redness, and diminution of vision. On examination, the visual acuity is 6/60, and there is circumcorneal congestion, corneal edema, and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the drug of choice from the given options?
questions.explanation:
This patient with complaints of severe headache, corneal congestion, and edema with a shallow anterior chamber most likely has acute angle closure glaucoma. Since this patient has a past history of sickle cell disease, intravenous mannitol is the drug of choice for this patient

Acetazolamide is contraindicated in cases of sickle-cell anemia since these drugs tend to increase sickling of erythrocytes.

questions.question: A 50-year-old female presents with an acute painful red-eye. An image of her eye is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario, supported with the image of the mid-dilated and vertically oval pupil is suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma. The pupil is non-reactive to both light and accommodation.

Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma refers to the occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris (iridotrabecular contact [ITC]), obstructing aqueous outflow.

Angle closure can be primary, when it occurs in an anatomically predisposed eye or secondary to another ocular or systemic factor.

Classification:

Primary angle-closure suspect (PACS)

• Gonioscopy shows posterior meshwork ITC in three or more quadrants but no peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).

• Intraocular pressure (IOP), optic disc, and visual field are normal.

• No PAS are seen

• The risk of PACG at 5 years may be around 30%.

Primary angle closure (PAC)

• Gonioscopy shows three or more quadrants of ITC with raised IOP and/or PAS or excessive pigment smudging on the TM.

• Normal optic disc and field.

Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG)

• ITC in three or more quadrants, with glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

• Optic nerve damage from an episode of severe IOP elevation, such as acute angle closure, may not appear as typical glaucomatous cupping.

Symptoms: Pain, redness, photophobia, impaired vision, watering

Signs:

• Corneal edema- colored halos

• Conjunctiva- congestion, chemosis

• IOP- elevated 40–70 mm Hg

• AC very shallow

• Pupil- vertically oval, mid-dilated

• Angle- completely closed, Grade 0

Treatment:

• Immediate- Intravenous mannitol, intravenous acetazolamide followed by oral dose, topical beta-blockers, brimonidine, latanoprost

• Definitive- Laser peripheral iridotomy, filtration surgery

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman develops pain in the eye after dark-room/prone-provocative test. Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
questions.explanation:
Pain after dark-room prone-provocative test indicates occludable angles. Hence, atropine is contraindicated as it is a long-acting mydriatic and can precipitate angle closure.

Dark-room/prone-provocative test (DRPPT)- The patient sits in a dark room, face down for one hour without sleeping (sleep induces miosis). The intraocular pressure (IOP) is checked (immediately after the test, as IOP can normalize very rapidly), and an IOP rise of 8 mmHg or more is frequently considered significant.

questions.question: A young female presents with sudden onset severe pain in the left eye after watching a movie. She rushes to the hospital as there is a progressive loss of vision. She has ciliary injection and a shallow anterior chamber. The pupil is semi dilated and the cornea appears oedematous. What is the procedure of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of sudden onset severe pain in the eye, progressive loss of vision, shallow anterior chamber, semi-dilated pupil, and edematous cornea is suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Laser iridotomy is the procedure of choice especially in emergency situations.

The attack may have been precipitated by pupillary dilation, which may result from activities such as going to a movie theater. Laser iridotomy re-establishes the communication between the posterior and anterior chamber, bypassing the pupillary block; hence, it immediately relieves crowding of the angle.

Various surgical and laser modalities used in glaucoma:

Angle-closure glaucoma:

• Laser iridotomy by Nd:Yag along with prophylactic iridotomy of the other eye → Treatment of choice.

• Trabeculectomy → Filtration surgery

Congenital glaucoma:

• Goniotomy

• Trabeculotomy

Primary open-angle glaucoma:

• Laser trabeculoplasty: Argon or diode (if not controlled medications)

• Trabeculectomy: Filtration surgery (if not controlled medications)

Absolute glaucoma:

• Cyclocryotherapy

• Nd:Yag lasercyclo destruction

questions.question: What is Glaukomflecken?
questions.answer: B. Lens opacity due to glaucoma
questions.explanation:
Glaukomflecken is anterior subcapsular lenticular opacity and a component of Vogt's triad seen in patients after an acute angle closure glaucoma attack.

The Vogt's triad comprises of:

• Glaukomflecken

• Patches of iris atrophy

• Slightly dilated nonreactive pupil

questions.question: A 25-year-old patient presents with painless white eye with an intraocular pressure of 60 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario fits the description of glaucomatocyclitic crisis.

Glaucomatocyclitic crisis/Posner–Schlossman Syndrome [PSS]) describes recurrent attacks of unilateral acute raised intraocular pressure (IOP) associated with mild anterior uveitis. The mechanism is thought to be acute trabeculitis, and there is evidence that infection, possibly cytomegalovirus (CMV) or Helicobacter pylori, may play a role. PSS typically affects young to middle-aged adults. Males are affected more frequently than females.

Signs:

• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy typically shows a few anterior chamber cells and one to several fine white central keratic precipitates.

• Mydriasis is common; posterior synechiae are not a feature.

• IOP is typically raised to over 40 mmHg, out of proportion to iritis severity.

• Gonioscopy shows an open-angle.

Treatment:

• Topical steroids are used to control inflammation, with aqueous suppressants to lower the IOP.

• Topical or oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents may also be beneficial.

Note: In PSS, the rise in IOP is out of proportion to the pain felt. There is often a mild discomfort and pain may even be absent.

questions.question: An ophthalmologist evaluating a patient with glaucoma identifies the following finding on slit-lamp examination. What is the finding?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a pattern of the deposition of pigments on the back of the cornea in pigmentary glaucoma. They are called Krukenberg spindles.

Pigmentary glaucoma is an open-angle glaucoma having the following features:

• Krukenberg spindles

• Gonioscopy shows pigment accumulation along the Schwalbe line inferiorly, and this accumulation is called the Sampaolesi line.

• Radial transillumination defect in the iris is a pathognomonic feature.

• Pigment granules may be deposited on the anterior surface. There may be a Scheie line or Zentmayer ring of pigment on the peripheral/equatorial surface around the zonular insertions.

Other options:

Option A: Ferry line: Corneal epithelial iron line at the edge of filtering blebs of glaucoma surgery

Option B: Fleischer line/ring: Epithelial iron deposits at the base of the cone in keratoconus

Option C: Hudson–Stahli line: Iron deposition line in the corneal epithelium, which is commonly seen in the junction between middle and lower third cornea. This finding is mainly age-related.

questions.question: Malignant glaucoma is seen in __________.
questions.explanation:
Malignant glaucoma is seen after intra-ocular surgery (usually after trabeculectomy).

Ciliary block glaucoma is also called malignant glaucoma/inverse glaucoma. It can be seen after any intraocular surgery. Forward flow of the aqueous is blocked as tips of ciliary processes rotate forward and press against the lens/intraocular lens (IOL)/anterior hyaloid of the vitreous. Hence, aqueous humor starts collecting in the vitreous cavity.

Signs:

• High intraocular pressure (IOP) and absent bleb.

• Negative Seidel test.

• Shallow anterior chamber (AC)

Treatment:

• Initial treatment is with cycloplegics (atropine 1%) to dilate the ciliary ring and push the vitreous-lens-iris posteriorly.

• Subsequent treatment if medical therapy fails is with Nd:YAG laser hyaloidotomy.

• Pars plana vitrectomy can be considered in conditions that don't respond to the above treatment modalities.

questions.question: What is iridocorneal endothelial syndrome associated with?
options: Progressive atrophy of the iris stroma
Bilateral stromal edema of the iris
Deposition of glycosaminoglycans in Descemet's membrane
questions.answer: A. Progressive atrophy of the iris stroma
questions.explanation:
Progressive atrophy of iris stroma is a clinical entity of iridocorneal endothelial syndrome (ICE).

ICE syndrome is a proliferative endotheliopathy, which leads to secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

It includes three clinical entities:

1. Progressive iris atrophy

2. Chandler’s syndrome - corneal edema

3. Cogan–Reese syndrome - nodules and nevus on the iris; hence, it is known as iris nevus syndrome.

questions.question: What is seen in hypersecretory glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
Hypersecretory glaucoma is associated with epidemic dropsy.

Epidemic dropsy occurs due to Argemone mexicana poisoning. Here, glaucoma is due to excessive production of aqueous humor.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the progression of ocular hypertension to primary open-angle glaucoma?
options: Reducing IOP is effective in delaying the onset of POAG
Thin cornea is a risk factor for POAG development
Family history is not a risk factor for POAG development
Increased cup disc ratio is a risk factor for POAG development
questions.answer: C. Family history is not a risk factor for POAG development
questions.explanation:
Family history is a risk factor for the development of primary open-angle glaucoma.

Ocular hypertension (OHT) is characterized by only raised intraocular pressure (IOP). Optic disc and normal visual field are normal, with no evidence of angle closure.

Risk factors for the progression of ocular hypertension to primary open-angle glaucoma include the following:

• African American race

• Thin cornea

• Increasing age

• Increased cup-disc ratio

• Increased IOP

• Family history of POAG

questions.question: Identify the instrument given in the image below.
questions.explanation:
The given image shows Baerveldt implant which is a glaucoma drainage device (GDD)/seton/aqueous shunt.

It consists of a scleral plate that is sutured to the sclera and a tube connecting it into the anterior chamber. It is valveless, and hence, it carries the risk of postoperative hypotony due to excessive aqueous drainage.

Glaucoma drainage devices are devices that allow aqueous outflow by establishing a communication between the anterior chamber and sub-Tennon's space/sub-conjunctival space. The glaucoma valve implant is also known as a seton.

The commonly used devices are as follows:

1. Shunts using episcleral explants

• Ahmed glaucoma valve: Silicone

• Molteno implant- Polypropelene plate and silicone plate

• Baerveldt implant- Silicone

2. Mini-shunts

• Ex-Press™ Mini-Shunt: Stainless steel

• iStent®- Titanium

questions.question: What is the drug of choice for inverse glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
The drug of choice for inverse glaucoma is atropine.

Inverse glaucoma is a type of secondary angle-closure glaucoma caused by the flow of aqueous humour posteriorly to the posterior segment instead of the posterior chamber. The increased pressure in the posterior segment pushes the lens forward leading to the shallowing of the anterior chamber.

Miotics are contraindicated as they can cause the ciliary zonules to slack, the lens to move forward and further shallowing of the anterior chamber. So mydriatic and cycloplegic agents such as atropine are administered.

Inverse glaucoma is also called:

• Malignant glaucoma

• Ciliary block glaucoma

• Aqueous misdirection.

Note:

Pilocarpine is the drug of choice in angle-closure glaucoma but is contraindicated in inverse glaucoma.

Whereas, atropine is the drug of choice in inverse glaucoma but is contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.question: An elderly male who is a known case of diabetes presents with blurry vision near the center of his field of vision. He also informs that colours appear washed out or faded. His IOP was found to be elevated. Which of the following drugs should not be used to control IOP in this diabetic patient?
questions.explanation:
This diabetic patient with new onset central loss of vision and reports of colors appearing faded or washed out most likely has macular edema. Prostaglandin analogs have a high propensity to cause and further exacerbate cystoid macular edema and hence are not preferred in this patient.

Drugs associated with cystoid macular edema (CME):

1. Prostaglandin analogues

2. Epinephrine

3. Dipivefrine (only the non-selective alpha agonists, in aphakic eyes)

4. Tamoxifen

5. Timolol

6. Docetaxel

7. Interferons

8. Fingolimod

9. Thiazolinediones

10. Niacin (pseudo-CME)

questions.question: In a 55-year-old patient presenting with secondary open-angle glaucoma, what is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Pseudoexfoliation (PEX) syndrome is the most likely cause of secondary open-angle glaucoma.

Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is an ocular manifestation of an age-related systemic disorder of the extracellular matrix, characterized by the production and progressive accumulation of fibrillar extracellular material in many ocular and systemic tissues. The clinical hallmark of PEX syndrome is the deposition of whitish abnormal pseudoexfoliative debris on the anterior lens capsule.

A deposition is also noted on:

• Zonules (causing zonulolysis and phacodonesis, lens subluxation)

• Pupillary margin

• Trabecular meshwork (causing the secondary open-angle glaucoma)

questions.question: A 48-year-old lady was started on an ocular medication that she was instructed to take daily. She develops redness of the eye. Examination reveals a colour change of the iris and orbital fat atrophy. Which of the following medications was she likely prescribed?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history of a patient that has iris pigmentation and redness of the eye, was most likely started on latanoprost.

Drug
Side Effects

Latanoprost

Allergic conjunctival hyperemia, permanent increase in iris pigmentation, orbital fat atrophy.

Timolol
Exacerbation of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bradycardia, depression, impotence

Scopolamine
Photosensitivity, blurred vision

Pilocarpine
Corneal edema, miosis, induced myopia, decreased vision, brow ache, retinal detachment

questions.question: First drug to be given in acute angle-closure glaucoma is _________.
questions.explanation:
The first drug to be given in acute angle-closure glaucoma is oral acetazolamide or intravenous mannitol.

Acetazolamide reduces IOP by decreasing the production of aqueous.

The definitive drug is pilocarpine as it constricts the pupil and breaks the attack.

Finally, when the corneal edema resolves, the patient has to undergo laser iridotomy to prevent such attacks in the future. So, laser iridotomy is the definitive management for acute angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.question: The normal extent of the visual field superiorly is ________.
questions.explanation:
The extent of visual field superiorly is 50°

Normal extent of the visual field:

• Temporal: 90°/100°

• Inferiorly: 70°

• Nasal: 60°

• Superiorly: 50°

Note: According to Parson's 22nd Ed., Page no. 101, the visual field extends 60o superiorly. However, most journals and other standard textbooks consider the answer to be 50o. Hence, we choose 50o as the most appropriate answer.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are false about the ciliary body?
options: It consists of the pars plana and pars plicata.
Contraction of the ciliary body helps in accommodation.
It derives its blood supply from short posterior ciliary arteries.
questions.answer: D. It derives its blood supply from short posterior ciliary arteries.
questions.explanation:
The ciliary body derives its blood supply from the long posterior ciliary artery and anterior ciliary arteries, which form the major arterial circle at the root of the iris.

The ciliary body is a triangular structure that begins at the base of the iris and becomes continuous with the choroid at the ora serrata. It is approximately 6–6.5 mm in an anteroposterior dimension.

It consists of an anterior portion called the pars plicata and a posterior portion called the pars plana (option A). The pars plicata contains approximately 70 finger-like projections called ciliary processes, which are covered by the ciliary body epithelium. These processes secrete aqueous humor (option C). The pars plana is the flat part of the ciliary body and ends at the ora serrata.

The smooth muscle of the ciliary body is divided into three groups of fibers:

• Outer longitudinal portion that attaches anteriorly to the scleral spur and trabecular meshwork fibers

• Middle oblique portion

• Inner circular portion (responsible for accommodation) (option B)

questions.question: A 3-year-old child with the following finding has high myopia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image shows corectopia, an abnormal eccentrically placed pupil.

It can be a congenital anomaly or an acquired defect with essential iris atrophy. It may be associated with high myopia or ectopia lentis, among other conditions.

questions.question: A patient presents to the casualty after ocular trauma with a D-shaped pupil. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A D-shaped pupil is seen in iridodialysis.

Iridodialysis is the dis-insertion of the iris root from the ciliary body attachment. It may occur following ocular trauma. A red reflex can be obtained from the peripheral gap in the iris.

The given image depicts iridodialysis and a D-shaped pupil.

questions.question: Which of the following is the pathognomonic sign of acute anterior uveitis?
questions.explanation:
The pathognomonic sign of acute anterior uveitis is keratic precipitates (KP).

Keratic precipitates are proteinaceous cellular deposits at the back of cornea. The composition of KPs varies with the type of uveitis.

Anterior uveitis is the inflammation of the uveal tissue from the iris to the pars plicata of the ciliary body. Slit-lamp examination shows the following signs in anterior uveitis:

1. Corneal signs

• Corneal edema

• Keratic precipitates (Pathognomonic)

• Posterior corneal opacity

2. Anterior chamber signs

• Aqueous cells

• Aqueous flare (earliest sign)

• Hypopyon

• Deep and irregular anterior chamber due to posterior synechiae

3. Iris signs

• Loss of normal pattern

• Change in color

• Iris nodules (Koeppe, Busacca)

• Posterior synechiae

• Neovascularization

4. Pupillary signs

• Constricted pupil

• Irregular pupil shape

• Ectropion of pupillary margin

• Occlusion pupillae

questions.question: What is the first sign a patient with anterior uveitis may show?
questions.explanation:
Aqueous flare is the earliest sign of acute anterior uveitis.

Aqueous flare is due to the leakage of protein particles into the aqueous humor from damaged blood vessels. It is demonstrated on the slit-lamp examination. It is based on the principle of Brownian movement or Tyndall phenomenon.

Aqueous flare is usually marked in non-granulomatous uveitis and minimal in granulomatous uveitis. The presence of cells in the anterior chamber denotes an active inflammatory process.

The image below is a high magnification slit-beam photograph 3×1 mm in size in a darkroom showing the presence of cells and flare.

questions.question: A 34-year-old lady presents with eye pain, photophobia, and red-eye. The slit-lamp examination finding is shown below. On which layer of the cornea are these present?
questions.explanation:
Eye pain, photophobia and red-eye along with the slit lamp finding of keratic precipitates suggests a diagnosis of acute anterior uveitis. Keratic precipitates are proteinaceous cellular deposits occurring at the back of the corneal endothelium.

Keratuc precipitates are arranged in a triangular fashion, occupying the center and inferior parts of the cornea (Arlt's triangle).

questions.question: You are evaluating a 45-year-old man admitted for acute anterior uveitis. What is the pupillary shape you expect to find in his eyes?
questions.explanation:
The pupil in acute anterior uveitis is constricted (pupillary sphincter spasm), irregular and sluggishly reactive to light

In an acute attack of uveitis, the pupil is irregular and narrow due to irritation of sphinchter pupillae. Pupillary signs in chronic anterior uveitis is as follows:

• Festooned pupil results from the application of mydriatics in segmental posterior synechiae.

• Occlusio pupillae results when the pupil is completely occluded due to the organization of the exudates across the pupillary area.

• Seclusio pupillae due to ring synechiae, that prevent the circulation of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber.

The image below shows a festooned pupil.

questions.question: A patient with sarcoidosis shows Koeppe's nodules on ophthalmologic examination. Where are these seen?
questions.explanation:
Koeppe's nodules and Bussaca's nodules develop on the iris in granulomatous uveitis.

Granulomatous uveitis is a chronic proliferative inflammation seen in reponse to tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis and sarcoidosis. Infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells, with proliferation of mononuclear cells leads to the formation of iris nodule. Koeppe's nodules are seen at the pupillary margin. Bussaca's nodules are seen on the peripheral part of the anterior surface of iris.

questions.question: What is the type of synechiae formed in iris bombe?
questions.explanation:
Iris bombe formation is due to the development of annular or ring synechiae.

Annular posterior/ring synechiae are 360° adhesions of the pupillary margin to the anterior capsule of the lens. They prevent the circulation of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber (seclusio pupillae). Thus, the aqueous collects behind the iris and pushes it anteriorly leading to iris bombe. This is usually followed by a rise in intraocular pressure. The anterior chamber is funnel-shaped when ring synechiae are present.

The image below shows iris bombe on slit lamp examination.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman has been having repeated episodes of red-eye, eye pain, and blurred vision. She is diagnosed with chronic granulomatous uveitis. Which of the following is not a cause?
questions.explanation:
Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a type of non-granulomatous uveitis.

Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is an insidious progressive anterior uveitis. It is mostly unilateral and associated with early cataract formation. Stellate keratic precipitates are seen and there is a notable absence of posterior synechiae.

Causes for chronic granulomatous uveitis include sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, herpes simplex, herpes zoster, syphilis, leprosy, brucellosis and phacoanaphylactic.

questions.question: Intermediate uveitis is also called as ________.
questions.explanation:
Intermediate uveitis refers to pars planitis. It involves inflammation of the pars plana.

The uvea consists of the iris, ciliary body and choroid. Inflammation of uveal tissue is called uveitis. It can be classified anatomically as follows:

• Anterior uveitis: Inflammation of iris and pars plicata, consisting of iritis, iridocyclitis and anterior cyclitis

• Intermediate uveitis: Inflammation of pars plana (pars planitis)

• Posterior uveitis: Inflammation of the retina with or without involvement of the retina. It includes choroiditis, chorioretinitis, retinochoroiditis and neuroretinitis.

• Panuveitis

Pathological classification divides uveitis into suppurative and nonsuppurative uveitis. Nonsuppurative uveitis is further classified into nongranulomatous and granulomatous uveitis.

The image is a schematic representation of the anatomical classification of uveitis.

questions.question: In a patient with intermediate uveitis, which of the following is a pathognomonic examination finding?
questions.explanation:
Snow banking is the hallmark of intermediate uveitis.

Snow banking refers to greyish white fibrovascular plaques over the pars plana, with or without peripheral retinal periphlebitis.

Intermediate uveitis is the inflammation of the pars plana and presents with retrolental flare, few keratic precipitates, vitreous cells and snow-ball opacities (Ant’s egg opacities). These are typical exudates present near the ora serrata in the inferior quadrant.

Treatment of intermediate uveitis is by the Kaplan 4-step protocol:

1. Periocular steroid: Sub tenon injection of triamcinolone acetate

2. Systemic steroid

3. Cryotherapy over snow banking

4. Pars plana vitrectomy

questions.question: While studying a cohort of patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, you are evaluating the risk of iridocyclitis among the different subtypes of JIA. Which subtype has the highest risk of iridocyclitis associated?
questions.explanation:
ANA-positive oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is associated with the highest risk for iridocyclitis (uveitis).

A positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test result confers increased risk for uveitis in children with JIA and requires periodic slit-lamp examination. Uveitis in JIA is characteristically chronic, non-granulomatous, and bilateral. It presents as a white eye without congestion- white uveitis. Complications include complicated cataracts, secondary glaucoma, and band-shaped keratopathy.

Note: Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation can be considered in most pediatric patients with well-controlled uveitis, but JIA-associated uveitis should be considered as a relative contraindication.

questions.question: Where is Amsler's sign seen?
questions.explanation:
Amsler sign is seen in Fuch's heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHI).

Amsler sign is the hemorrhage caused by cataract surgery in FHI. During cataract surgery, fine filiform hemorrhages from the opposite angle are seen to occur as soon as the anterior chamber is opened. This is due to neovascularization.

Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is an insidiously progressive, non- granulomatous anterior uveitis, that is usually unilateral. Stellate KPs are seen and tiny crystals (Russell bodies) may be present on the iris surface. There are no posterior synechiae. Rubeosis iridis may be present.

The 1st image shows Fuchs heterochromic uveitis. The right eye is normal. The left hypochromic eye is affected. The 2nd image shows stellate keratic precipiates.

questions.question: What is Posner-Schlossman syndrome?
options: Ipsilateral optic atrophy with contralateral papilloedemac
Unilateral glaucomatous changes with mild anterior uveitis
questions.answer: B. Unilateral glaucomatous changes with mild anterior uveitis
questions.explanation:
Posner–Schlossman syndrome is characterized by unilateral glaucomatous changes with mild anterior uveitis.

This syndrome, also known as glaucomatocyclitic crisis or hypertensive uveitis, presents with recurrent unilateral attachs of acute raised intraocular pressure (IOP) (>40 mmHg) changes, fine white central keratic precipitates (KPs) and mydriasis. Treatment includes topical corticosteroids, cycloplegics, and aqueous suppressants.

questions.question: A 44-year-old patient with AIDS and opportunistic infections was started on treatment. He develops a sterile hypopyon anterior uveitis that is suspected to be drug-induced. Which of the following drugs may be implicated here?
questions.explanation:
Rifabutin causes uveitis in AIDS patients.

Causes of drug-induced uveitis include:

• Cidofovir

• Rifabutin

• Bisphosphonates

• Oral moxifloxacin

questions.question: Which among the following is associated with transient hypopyon syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Behcet's disease presents with recurrent iridocyclitis associated with transient hypopyon.

Behcet's disease is a systemic vascular disease. It is associated with HLA B5 >> B51. Patients have obliterative vasculitis due to circulating immune complexes, leading to a recurrent, bilateral non-granulomatous uveitis. There is acute recurrent iridocyclitis, transient hypopyon, periphlebitis, retinitis, vitritis and cystoid macular edema (CME).

questions.question: A patient presents with photophobia and blurring of vision. On examination, the eye appears as shown below. What is the mainstay of treatment?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of photophobia and blurring of vision along with red-eye and irregularly shaped pupil suggests a diagnosis of anterior uveitis. Steroids and cycloplegics are the mainstay of the treatment of uveitis.

Steroids are the drug of choice in anterior uveitis. They reduce inflammation by their anti-inflammatory effect. Cycloplegics like 1% atropine relieve spasm of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscles. They prevent the formation of synechiae and reduce exudation. Systemic therapy includes steroids, NSAIDs, and immunosuppressants.

Immunosuppressants like voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) are used in severe cases. They are being studied under a program called LUMINATE.

questions.question: A patient describes the image below on the Amsler grid test. In which of the given conditions is this phenomenon noted?
questions.explanation:
The image shows metamorphopsia seen in posterior uveitis.

Metamorphopsia is a condition in which patients perceive distorted images of the object. It is measured using the Amsler grid, which tests the central 10 degrees of vision. In posterior uveitis, metamorphopsia occurs due to macular edema.

Posterior uveitis is a painless inflammation of the choroid. Patients present with various visual symptoms like defective vision, black spots floating in front of the eye, micropsia/macropsia and positive scotomas.

questions.question: Which of the following features is unlikely to be noted in a patient with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Iris heterochromia is not a feature of Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome.

Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome is an idiopathic, multi-system disorder characterised by autoimmunity against melanocytes. It is associated with HLA-DR1 and HLA-DR4 across different racial groups.

Patients may present with cutaneous, neurological and ocular features. Cutaneous features include alopecia, poliosis and vitiligo (option A). Neurological features include meningism, encephalopathy, tinnitus, deafness and vertigo (option B). Ocular features include bilateral chronic granulomatous panuveitis (option C), posterior uveitis, exudative retinal detachment, perilimbal vitiligo (Suguiura's sign) and sunset glow appearance of the fundus.

The modified diagnostic criteria for Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome are as follows:

• Absence of a history of penetrating ocular trauma

• Absence of other ocular disease entities

• Bilateral uveitis

• Neurological and auditory manifestations

• Integumentary findings, not preceding the onset of the central nervous system or ocular diseases, such as alopecia, poliosis, and vitiligo.

The treatment is high-dose (1–2 mg/kg/day) oral prednisolone, tapered over 3–6 months. This may be preceded by intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (500–1000 mg/day).

questions.question: A middle aged male presents with recurrent oral ulcers and ulcers over his scrotum. He also has pain and redness of both his eyes. A positive pathergy test is noted. What is the HLA association of the disease this patient is most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Recurrent oral ulcers, ulcers over his scrotum with binocular pain and redness and a positive pathergy test point to a diagnosis of Behcet's disease. HLA B5 (HLA B51) is associated with Behcet's disease.

Behcet's disease is a systemic vasculitis that can cause recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, skin lesions and ocular inflammation. Pathergy test is usually positive. Ocular inflammation occurs in about 70% of patients and tends to be more severe in men. A classical presentation is relapsing/remitting acute onset panuveitis with retinal vasculitis which resolves spontaneously even without treatment. It is usually bilateral and non-granulomatous. Patients present with a transient mobile hypopyon in a relatively white eye. They may develop visual impairment if retinal vascular disease (vasculitis and occlusion) occurs.

Other options:

Option A: HLA-B27 is associated with Reiter's syndrome.

Option B: HLA DR1 and HLA-DR4 are associated with Vogt–Koyanagi–Haradas disease.

Option D: HLA Bw54 is associated with Possner–Scholssman syndrome.

Note: The association between HLA-A29 and birdshot retinochoroidopathy is the most consistent of any medical disorder. Approximately 95% of patients with birdshot retinochoroidopathy are HLA-A29–positive.

questions.question: A 28 year old man presents to the medicine OPD with cough with hemoptysis of 1 month duration. A sputum culture done is shown below. What is the most common ocular manifestation associated with this infection?
questions.explanation:
The image shows the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) colonies on the Lowenstein-Jensen medium. In tuberculosis (TB), granulomatous panuveitis is the most common ocular feature.

Ocular TB commonly occurs due to hematogenous spread from pulmonary TB. It can have multiple presentations like lupus vulgaris of eyelid, tubercular conjunctivitis, interstitial keratitis, granulomatous uveitis and endophthalmitis. Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to the MTB antigen.

Treatment of granulomatous panuveitis is anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) plus steroids.

questions.question: In a patient showing salt and pepper appearance of the fundus, which of the following is not a differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Salt and pepper fundus is not seen in tuberculosis.

Salt and pepper fundus is seen when there are multiple small black and white spots present on the retina. It is also known as pseudo-retinitis pigmentosa. Its causes include congenital syphilis, rubella, Refsum’s disease, carriers of albinism, Leber’s congenital amaurosis and retinitis pigmentosa sine pigmentosa.

questions.question: A 32-year-old lady presented with dry, itchy eyes, blurred vision, and sensitivity to light. She says there are black dots floating around in her visual field. She denies wearing any spectacles or contact lenses. On fundoscopy, the following image is obtained. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Dry, itchy eyes, blurred vision, sensitivity to light with candle wax dripping on fundus examination points to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis is a chronic granulomatous multi-system disease. Ocular inflammation occurs in 25–70% of sarcoid patients, which includes uveitis, conjuctival and lacrimal gland involvement. Chronic granulomatous panuveitis may be seen. Anterior uveitis is the most common manifestation.
