In anterior uveitis due to sarcoidosis, "mutton fat" keratic precipitates (KPs) and/or small granulomatous KPs with iris nodules (Koeppe and/or Busacca) are seen. Trabecular meshwork (TM) nodules and/or tent-shaped peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) is also seen.

In intermediate uveitis, vitreous cells with snowbanking and snowball opacities/string of pearl appearance are seen. Posterior uveitis presents with candle-wax dripping (thick venous sheathing and periphlebitis), pre-retinal nodules (Lander’s sign), choroidal granulomata and sarcoid infiltration. Other ocular features seen are interstitial keratitis and band-shaped keratopathy. Steroids are the mainstay of treatment in sarcoidosis.

questions.question: What is the most common ocular manifestation in patients infected by the human immunodeficiency virus?
questions.explanation:
Microangiopathy is the most common ocular feature of HIV infection.

Microangiopathy of the retina in HIV consists of the hemorrhages, micro-aneurysms and cotton-wool spots or soft exudates (axonal debris). Cotton wool spots are the most common finding of HIV retinopathy.

HIV leads to multiple opportunistic infections of the eye like cytomegalovirus (CMV) - most common cause of posterior uveitis in HIV - toxoplasmosis, Pneumocystis carinii and herpes zoster. These infections present as keratitis, choroiditis, retinitis and endophthalmitis.

The most common ocular adverse effect in patients receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) is immune recovery uveitis (IRU). It is a non-granulomatous uveitis (usually anterior uveitis and vitritis) associated with a paradoxical or exaggerated reactivation of the immune system and an increase in intraocular inflammation. It occurs after receiving HAART for CMV chorioretinitis. Visual complications of IRU include cataract, cystoid macular edema (CME), glaucoma, and epiretinal membrane formation.

questions.question: An HIV positive patient presented to OPD with painless blurring of vision. On fundus examination, the following findings were seen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Painless blurring of vision in an HIV positive patient with "sauce and cheese" or "pizza pie" retinopathy (shown in the image) is characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis.

CMV retinitis is the most common ocular opportunistic infection in patients with HIV. It is often asymptomatic and can be classified as central or peripheral CMV retinitis. Central CMV retinitis is characterised by dense, white areas of retinal necrosis and retinal hemorrhage in the areas of necrosis - pizza pie or sauce and cheese appearance.

Peripheral CMV retinitis is less demarcated. The infection spreads along the vascular arcades in a brush fire-like fashion.

questions.question: A newly diagnosed HIV-positive lady with CD4+ count of 35/μL presented with decreased visual acuity and floaters. On fundus examination, there were dense, white areas of retinal necrosis with interspersed areas of retinal hemorrhage. What is the most rapid and accurate method to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Viral nucleic acid detection in intraocular fluid
Viral antibody detection in blood by ELISA
questions.answer: C. Viral nucleic acid detection in intraocular fluid
questions.explanation:
An HIV-positive patient with CD4+ count of 35/μL presenting with decreased visual acuity, floaters and pizza pie retinitis (dense, white areas of retinal necrosis with interspersed areas of retinal hemorrhage) likely has CMV retinitis. The most rapid and accurate method to diagnose cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is viral nucleic acid detection in the intraocular fluid.

CMV retinitis is an opportunistic infection seen in HIV patients with a CD4+ count less than 50/μL. Patients present with reduced vision due to macular involvement and floaters due to vitritis. One eye is usually affected initially. Retinitis is seen. Frosted branch angiitis (FBA), which is marked vascular sheathing that occurs in about 6% patients, may be seen. Cataract is common late-stage manifestation of CMV retinitis.

Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) is the mainstay of management, restoring the patient’s innate ability to suppress CMV activity. Valganciclovir is a prodrug of ganciclovir that is taken orally. Ganciclovir slow-release intravitreal implant can also be used.

Screening of patients with low CD4+ counts:

• 3-monthly, if <50/μl

• 6-monthly, if 50–100/μl

• Yearly, if >100/μl

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presented with blurring of vision in the right eye. Examination reveals mild iritis, severe vitritis, and a focal necrotic lesion on the macula. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Monocular iritis, severe vitritis with a focal necrotic lesion on the macula is a classical description of ocular toxoplasmosis.

Ocular toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan. It causes severe recurrent attacks of posterior uveitis in adults, due to reactivation at previously inactive cyst-containing scars. A single inflammatory focus of fluffy white retinitis or retinochoroiditis associated with a pigmented scar ("satellite lesion") is typical. "Headlight in the fog" is the classic description of a white retinal inflammatory nidus viewed through vitritis. "Spill-over" anterior uveitis is common.

Treatment:

• Prednisolone (1 mg/kg) is given initially and tapered according to clinical response.

• Pyrimethamine is administered as a loading dose of 75–100 mg for 1–2 days followed by 25–50 mg daily for 4 weeks in combination with oral folinic (not folic) acid 5 mg three times a week to retard thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and folate deficiency.

• Sulfadiazine 1 g four times daily for 3–4 weeks is usually given in combination with pyrimethamine.

• Intravitreal therapy with clindamycin (1 mg) and dexamethasone (400 μg) may be as effective as triple therapy in reactivated infection.

The image shows the characteristic "headlight in the fog" appearance:

questions.question: In which disease is the "headlight in fog" appearance seen?
questions.explanation:
The "headlight in fog" appearance is seen in toxoplasmosis.

Ocular toxoplasmosis presents with iridocyclitis, which can be granulomatous or non-granulomatous. There is focal superficial necrotizing retinochoroiditis along with vitritis, which gives the "headlight in fog" appearance (image). Fundoscopy shows deep retinitis and papillitis with granulomas. Old choroid lesions of toxoplasmosis are punched-out lesions with pigmented borders.

The treatment of choice for ocular toxoplasmosis is triple therapy with systemic steroids, pyrimethamine, and sulfadiazine. Clindamycin is also used.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presented with red-eye, ocular pain, and acute loss of vision to the casualty. On fundoscopy, areas of retinal ischemia and necrosis were seen, leading to a diagnosis of acute retinal necrosis. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?
options: It is seen in immunocompetent individuals.
Posterior pole is involved initially with centrifugal spread.
It may lead to retinal detachment.
questions.answer: C. Posterior pole is involved initially with centrifugal spread.
questions.explanation:
In acute retinal necrosis, the posterior pole is typically spared until late.

Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) occurs in immunocompetent individuals. It is a severe posterior uveitis causing retinal necrosis. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is the most common cause of acute retinal necrosis in adults. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus (HSV) are the commonest causes of acute retinal necrosis in children.

Patients present with confluent peripheral necrotizing retinitis, retinal arteritis with vaso-occlusion, and vitritis. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments are common due to retinal thinning from large areas of necrosis. The posterior pole is involved only in the later stages.

Aciclovir is administered intravenously (10 mg/kg, every 8 hours) for 10–14 days, and then orally (800 mg, five times daily) for 6–12 weeks. Oral valaciclovir or famciclovir may be substituted for oral aciclovir, with similar outcomes but better tolerability. Intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet may enhance the prognosis. Systemic steroids may be started 24 hours after the initiation of antiviral therapy, especially in severe cases. Laser retinopexy is performed around necrotic areas.

Progressive outer retinal necrosis is a manifestation of HSV or varicella zoster virus (VZV) that occurs in immunocompromised individuals. It may begin at the posterior pole or the periphery. It has a rapid course and is not generally associated with vasculitis.

questions.question: A 65-year-old male presents with a painful decrease in vision of his right eye for the past 3 days. He underwent right phacoemulsification with PC-IOL insertion 6 months ago. Examination revealed a mild granulomatous anterior uveitis with minimal hypopyon and mild vitritis. There is a white plaque seen on the posterior lens capsule. Which one of the following is the most appropriate therapy for this condition?
options: Vitrectomy and intravitreal injection of amphotericin B
Vitrectomy, removal of the IOL, and intravitreal injection of gentamicin
Vitrectomy, posterior capsulotomy, and intravitreal injection of vancomycin
questions.answer: D. Vitrectomy, posterior capsulotomy, and intravitreal injection of vancomycin
questions.explanation:
Painful decrease in vision following cataract surgery 6 months ago with granulomatous anterior uveitis, hypopyon, vitritis and a white plaque on the posterior lens capsule suggests a diagnosis of delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis caused by Propionibacterium acnes. The best management for the above clinical scenario would be vitrectomy and posterior capsulotomy, followed by intravitreal injection of vancomycin.

Delayed-onset endophthalmitis, a complication of cataract surgery, has a slow course and panuveitis like picture. There is low grade anterior chamber inflammation and vitritis. When caused by P. acnes, it typically presents from 3 months to 2 years after surgery with a characteristic white retro-lenticular plaque on the posterior capsule of lens. Endophthalmitis caused by Candida occurs within 3 months of surgery.

Management includes anterior vitrectomy, IOL explantation, posterior capsulectomy, intravitreal vancomycin, and a scleral-fixated intraocular lens (IOL) implantation.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of endophthalmitis in a patient following eye trauma?
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common cause of post-traumatic endophthalmitis, followed by Bacillus cereus.

However, if the trauma involves soil contamination, Bacillus cereus is the most common cause of post-traumatic endophthalmitis.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs should not be used in a patient with uveitis and raised IOP?
questions.explanation:
Pilocarpine should not be used in cases of uveitis with raised intraocular pressure.

Hypertensive uveitis or inflammatory glaucoma occurs when uveitis is associated with raised IOP. It is treated with topical cycloplegics (atropine), topical steroids and IOP-lowering drugs like topical timolol or systemic acetazolamide. Pilocarpine is contraindicated since it causes miosis and ciliary spasm. It also increases intraocular inflammation.

chapters.chapter: Retinal Vascular Disorders And Retinal Detachment

questions.question: The distance of the fovea from the temporal margin of the optic disc is _______.
questions.explanation:
The distance of the fovea from the temporal margin of the optic disc is 2 disc diameters.

The fovea is an excavation in the retinal surface at the center of the macula, with a diameter of 1.5 mm, which is about the same as that of the optic disc. The foveola forms the bottom of the fovea and has a diameter of 0.35 mm. It is devoid of ganglion cells. The umbo is the central floor the foveola, which corresponds to the foveolar light reflex. The foveal avascular zone (FAZ) is a central area (including foveola and surrounding areas) which contains no blood vessels but is surrounded by a continuous network of capillaries.

The macula is a round area at the posterior pole, lying inside the temporal vascular arcades. It measures 5.5 mm in diameter. The inner layers of the macula contain the yellow xanthophyll carotenoid pigments lutein and zeaxanthin in far higher concentrations than the peripheral retina (hence, the full name "macula lutea", which means yellow plaque).

questions.question: Which statement regarding Müller cells is false?
options: Their nuclei lie in the outer nuclear layer
Their foot processes form the inner & outer limiting membranes
They contribute to inner blood retinal barrier
questions.answer: B. Their nuclei lie in the outer nuclear layer
questions.explanation:
The nuclei of Müller cells lie in the inner nuclear layer.

Müller cells are a type of macroglial cells of the retina. The human retina contains 8–10 million Müller cells. Their nuclei lie in the inner nuclear layer and their processes extend across the retinal layers to form the inner and outer limiting membranes. Their functions include:

1. Providing structural stability to the retina
2. Interacting with other neurons and their functional and metabolic support
3. Providing neurons with trophic substances and removing metabolic waste
4. Playing a critical role in regulating the extracellular space volume as well as ion and water homeostasis and in maintaining the inner blood-retinal barrier

Astrocytes are another type of macroglial cells of the retina. They play a crucial role in retinal vascularization. In the mature retina, they are restricted to the nerve fiber and ganglion cell layers.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the development of retinal vasculature?
options: Grow to temporal ora by 34 weeks of gestation
Grow to nasal ora by 36 weeks of gestation
Originate from mesenchymal tissue during week 16 of gestation
questions.answer: A. Grow to temporal ora by 34 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation:
Retinal vessels reach temporal ora at approximately 40 weeks of gestation.

Retinal vessels develop de novo from mesenchymal tissue, beginning during the 4th month of gestation. They radiate outward (centrifugally) from the optic nerve, reaching the nasal ora by 36 weeks.

questions.question: A preterm baby treated for respiratory distress syndrome is found to have white pupillary reflex on opthalmologic examination. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A preterm baby, treated for respiratory distress syndrome, with leucocoria (white pupillary reflex) most likely has retrolental fibroplasia.

Retrolental fibroplasia, also known as retinopathy of prematurity, is a proliferative retinopathy. Risk factors include prematurity, very low birth weight and supplemental oxygen therapy (given for respiratory distress syndrome). ROP can be mild and may resolve spontaneously, but may lead to blindness in serious cases.

questions.question: Which of the following is included under threshold disease when screening neonates for retinopathy of prematurity?
options: ROP stage 1 extending from 6'o clock to 11'0 clock in zone 1 with plus disease
ROP stage 3 extending from 2'o clock to 7'o clock in zone 2 with plus disease
ROP stage 3 extending from 1'o clock to 4'o clock in zone 1 without plus disease
ROP stage 2 extending from 3'o clock to 6'o clock in zone 2 with plus disease
questions.answer: B. ROP stage 3 extending from 2'o clock to 7'o clock in zone 2 with plus disease
questions.explanation:
ROP stage 3 extending from 2'0 clock to 7'o clock (6 clock hours) in zone 2 with plus disease fits into the definition of threshold disease.

Threshold disease of retinopathy of prematurity is defined by the CRYO-ROP study as:

• Stage 3 disease: Ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation into the vitreous

• Involvement of zones 1 or 2

• Involvement of either at least 5 contiguous (continuous) clock hours or 8 non-contiguous clock hours

• Associated with "plus disease": Dilatation and tortuosity of posterior pole vessels in at least two quadrants at the posterior pole.

 Treatment of threshold disease is laser photocoagulation of the involved part within 72 hours of diagnosis.

Treatment of the various stages of ROP includes:

• Pre-threshold type 1 disease - Treatment is now recommended within 48 hours and is done by laser photocoagulation of avascular retina.

• Pre-threshold type 2 disease (Any ROP not following under type 1)- Observation for progression

• Threshold disease - Laser photocoagulation of avascular retina

• Aggresive posterior-ROP- Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents, eg., bevacizumab

• Tractional retinal detachment (stage 4A) - Pars plana vitrectomy

questions.question:
All of the following are true statements regarding retinopathy of prematurity except:

(PNA - Post natal age, PMA - Post menstrual age, AP-ROP - Aggressive posterior retinopathy of prematurity)
options: First screening should be done 32 weeks PMA or 4 weeks PNA, whichever is later
For infants less than 28 week, screen at 3 week of postnatal age to detect APROP
Neonates are best examined at ophthalmology OPD and hence should be transported
Screening is done using indirect ophthalmoscopy by an expert ophthalmologist
questions.answer: C. Neonates are best examined at ophthalmology OPD and hence should be transported
questions.explanation:
Neonates are best examined in the neonatal unit itself under the supervision of the attending neonatologist. It is not recommended to transport infants to the ophthalmic outpatient department for examination.

The first screening examination should be carried out by indirect ophthalmoscopy at 32 weeks PMA or 4 weeks PNA, whichever is later. For infants born at less than 28 weeks, screening is done at 3 weeks PNA to detect APROP. Aggressive posterior ROP ("rush" disease, AP-ROP), if untreated, usually progresses to total retinal detachment (stage 5) within a few days. It is characterized by its posterior location, prominence of plus disease and ill-defined nature of the retinopathy.

questions.question: A preterm neonate admitted to NICU who received supplemental oxygen is being screened for retinopathy of prematurity. Fundus examination reveals a subtotal retinal detachment. How will you stage the disease?
questions.explanation:
Subtotal retinal detachment is considered to be stage 4 of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).

The clinical staging of ROP is as follows:

• Stage 1 - Formation of a demarcation line at the edge of vessels, dividing the vascular from the avascular retina.

• Stage 2- Formation of an intraretinal ridge

• Stage 3- Ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation into the vitreous

• Stage 4- Subtotal retinal detachment

• Stage 5- Total retinal detachment

questions.question: A 14-day-old neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation had developed respiratory distress syndrome at birth. You want to screen for retinopathy of prematurity. How many weeks from now would you schedule the screening?
questions.explanation:
In the scenario above, the postnatal age of the premature infant is 2 weeks, and therefore, the infant must be screened in 2 weeks i.e., 4 weeks of postnatal age, as per the guidelines for the management of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).

ROP guidelines state that the first examination should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of postnatal age (after birth) or between 31–33 weeks of post-conceptional age (calculated as gestational age + postnatal age), whichever is later. Ideally, 2 examinations must be performed; however, 1 may suffice if it shows complete retinal vascularisation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most important factor for the development of diabetic retinopathy?
questions.explanation:
The most important factor for the development of diabetic retinopathy is the duration of diabetes.

Diabetic retinopathy constitutes the retinal changes seen in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. The most important factor for its development is duration of diabetes after the onset of puberty, followed by glycemic control. It is more common in type 1 diabetes mellitus. The presence of hypertension increases the risk of diabetic retinopathy.

First fundus examination for type 1 diabetes is done after 5 years after diagnosis and for type 2 is done at the time of diagnosis. The frequency of follow-up for types 1 and 2 diabetes mellitus is every year. Diabetes in pregnancy is followed up every 3 months.

The earliest feature of diabetic retinopathy is microaneurysms, which are present in the inner nuclear layer of the retina.

questions.question: Which of the following findings on a fundus examination would suggest severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
options: Significant venous beading in any of the 4 quadrants
questions.answer: C. Severe hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants
questions.explanation:
Severe hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants is a feature of severe NPDR.

Note: Macular star is a feature of malignant hypertensive retinopathy.

questions.question: A 69-year-old patient with hypertension has silver wiring, papilledema, and arteriovenous nipping visible on fundoscopy, but no other changes. How would you grade his disease?
questions.explanation: A patient with hypertension having "silver wiring," papilledema, and arteriovenous nipping visible on fundoscopy has Grade IV retinopathy.

questions.question: A 40-year-old male, newly diagnosed with systolic hypertension, presents with a three-week history of bilateral blurry vision. His visual acuity is 20/30 and 20/120 in the right and left eye, respectively. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. Which of the following findings is least likely to be seen on his fundoscopy?
questions.explanation:
Systolic hypertension (systolic blood pressure over 200 mm Hg) with bilateral blurry vision and unremarkable examination findings point to a diagnosis of hypertensive retinopathy. Intra-retinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) are not seen in hypertensive retinopathy. IRMA is a feature of diabetic retinopathy.

Arteriolar narrowing occurs due to vasoconstriction and sclerosis of retinal vessels due to hypertension. Cotton wool spots are areas of nerve fibre layer infarcts. They occur due to capillary obliteration in hypertension.

questions.question: The following image shows the picture of the fundus in a patient taken 48 hours after sustaining severe head trauma. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image shows multiple cotton wool spots around the disc. This is Purtschers' retinopathy, which is classically associated with severe head injury.

It is also seen in pancreatitis and chest trauma due to fat/air embolism. Ophthalmoscopy reveals multiple, variably sized cotton-wool spots and intraretinal hemorrhages around the optic nerve. There is no effective treatment.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true regarding sickle cell retinopathy?
options: Sea-fan appearance is seen in supero-temporal quadrant.
HbSS has more severe ocular manifestations than HbSC.
Central retinal vein occlusion may be seen.
questions.answer: B. HbSS has more severe ocular manifestations than HbSC.
questions.explanation:
Hemoglobin SC and S-Thal disease have the most severe ocular manifestations, although sickle SS disease has the most severe systemic manifestations.

The incidence of proliferative retinopathy in SC disease (Hb SC) is 33%, sickle cell thalassemia (Hb S-Thal) is 14%, SS disease (Hb SS) is 3%. In sickle cell retinopathy, elevated blood viscosity may occlude venules and arterioles, as well as capillaries. The following fundus findings can be noted as a result:

• Retinal vascular peripheral non-perfusion

• Retinal hemorrhages: "salmon patches," "iridescent spots," and "black sunbursts" are hallmarks of nonproliferative sickle cell retinopathy.

• Peripheral retinal neovascularization in a "sea fan" configuration is the hallmark of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy. They are also described as "parachute" lesions. They are most commonly found in the supero-temporal vascular arcades.

• Angioid streaks (Rupture of Bruch’s membrane)

Conjunctival "comma-shaped" capillaries and iris atrophy are other ocular findings seen. Complications of sickle cell retinopathy include central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) (occurs due to retinal hypoxia), vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment.

The image below shows 'sea fans' as seen on fluorescein angiography.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with 6/6 vision in the right eye and vision for only hand movements in the left eye. On fundoscopy, the right eye appears normal. The left eye shows retinal detachment, subretinal yellowish exudates, and telangiectatic vessels. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Unilateral decreased vision with retinal detachment, subretinal yellowish exudates and telangiectatic vessels in a young boy points to the diagnosis of Coats' disease.

Coats’ disease, described by Coats in 1908, affects boys three times more often than girls, has no reported racial or ethnic predilection, and is usually unilateral. The average age at diagnosis is 8–16 years. The clinical course is generally progressive.

It is characterized by discrete zones of retinal vascular abnormalities like aneurysmal dilatation and leakage. It is associated with localized lipid deposition (hard exudates) and varying degrees of subretinal exudates. Vessels may appear telangiectatic, and they may have aneurysms that are grape-like, clustered, or light bulb-shaped.

The image below depicts the typical vascular abnormalities with aneurysmal dilatation, telangiectasia, exudation, and severe lipid deposition in the macula which are seen in Coat's disease.

questions.question: A 64-year-old female presented with complaints of blurring of vision and pain in her left eye. She also gave a history of redness in her left eye about 3 months back, which she passed off as normal conjunctivitis. On tonometry, the IOP is 55 mm Hg. The slit-lamp revealed rubeosis iridis in all four quadrants. The fundus picture of the patient is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Monocular blurring of vision and pain with "splashed sauce" appearance on fundoscopy points towards a diagnosis of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO).

Ischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) is characterised by sudden visual loss. There is splashed sauce appearance on fundoscopy due to retinal hemorrhages. Risk factors include high intraocular pressure (IOP), hypertension and blood viscosity syndromes.

Its complications include neovascularisation of the iris (rubeosis iridis) and neovascular glaucoma (NVG). NVG typically occurs 3 months after the occlusive event. Up to 50% of eyes develop NVG following ischaemic CRVO. Pan-retinal photocoagulation is the treatment of choice.

CRVO is classified into two types:

• Ischemic CRVO: Characterized by relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), markedly reduced visual acuity, and many cotton-wool spots

• Non-ischemic CRVO: Characterized by normal pupillary reaction, reduced visual acuity, and few cotton-wool spots
Treatment usually involves treating the underlying cause and complications.

questions.question: A man with history of hypertension and loss of vision in the left eye has the following fundoscopy findings. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image above demonstrates characteristic flame-shaped hemorrhages, localized to the superotemporal sector of the retina. The image, along with loss of vision and history of hypertension, points to a diagnosis of branched retinal vein occlusion (BRVO), specifically affecting the superotemporal branch of the retinal vein.

Occlusion of a single branch of the retinal vein leads to branched retinal vein occlusion. This occlusion leads to impaired venous drainage, resulting in the accumulation of blood within the retina. The visual defect in BRVO tends to be partial.

Note: The different types of retinal vascular obstructions are branched retinal vein obstruction (BRVO), central retinal vein obstruction (CRVO), branched retinal artery obstruction (BRAO) and central retinal artery obstruction (CRAO). Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) is the second most common retinal vascular disorder after diabetic retinopathy.

In CRVO, tortuosity and engorgement of all branches of the central retinal vein are seen, affecting all quadrants of the retina.

questions.question: A 67-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden painless vision loss in his left eye. He has had a similar episode before but his vision was quickly restored. On physical exam, a carotid bruit is heard and a relative afferent pupillary defect is noted on ocular examination. His fundus appears as shown below. Which of the following is the best immediate step in the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Sudden painless unilateral vision loss with carotid bruit (carotid artery disease) and the fundus picture showing a cherry-red spot is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The best immediate step in management is ocular massage among the given options.

Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) occurs due to obstruction of the retinal artery at the level of lamina cribrosa. Risk factors include heart disease, carotid artery disease, mucormycosis, varicella infection, radiation exposure and trauma. It may be caused by the following:

• Emboli of carotid artery or cardiac origin are the most common cause of CRAO. Other emboli are cholesterol emboli, calcium emboli, and platelet fibrin emboli

• Atherosclerosis-related thrombosis

• Retinal arteritis with obliteration

• Angiospasm

• Raised intraocular pressure

• Thrombophilic disorders

Patients often present with sudden painless monocular loss of vision with history of a similar episode that resolved spontaneously (amaurosis fugax). On examination, direct pupillary reflex is absent and relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is positive. Fundus examination shows marked attenuation of arteries (thread like arteries), interrupted blood flow in vein (cattle track appearance), cherry red spot, severe edema and retinal pallor.

A cherry-red spot of the macula is typical and arises in this area because of the absence of ganglion cells at the foveola resulting in the transmission of the normal choroidal color. This in contrast to the surrounding area where intense retinal whitening blocks the transmission of the normal choroidal color.

Treatment is to dislodge the emboli by suddenly decreasing the IOP by IV acetazolamide or ocular massage. Ocular massage is considered the most effective method. Other treatment options include IV mannitol, vasodilators (nitrates), fibrinolytic therapy, or laser photodisruption in some cases. In cases of giant cell arteritis, steroids are beneficial.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman presents with complaints of sudden painless loss of vision in the left eye since yesterday. She also gives a history of temporal headaches, myalgias, and pain in the jaw while chewing. Examination of the left eye reveals a visual acuity of HM+ and an RAPD. Fundus examination of the left eye shows cattle trucking of blood within the retinal veins on applying gentle pressure. Which of the following is the likely cause of fundal findings?
options: Non- ischemic central retinal venous occlusion
questions.explanation:
A 52-year-old woman temporal headaches, myalgias and pain in the jaw while chewing likely has giant cell arteritis (GCA). Given that she has sudden painless monocular loss of vision with RAPD and points to a diagnosis of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

GCA is the most common primary vasculitis in adults. It is a risk factor for the development of CRAO. CRAO occurs due to obstruction of the retinal artery at the level of lamina cribrosa. When obstruction to the blood flow is not complete, the flow may be partially restored. Thus, gentle pressure upon the globe may break the column of venous blood into red beads separated by clear interspaces. This gives the characteristic 'cattle truck' appearance.

Option A: Ischemic CRVO shows a characteristic "splashed tomato sauce" appearance on fundoscopy.

Option C: Non-Ischemic CRVO does not present with such a severe loss of visual acuity.

Option D: Branched retinal artery occlusion presents with hemifield visual defects.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden painless loss of vision. Fundoscopy findings are shown below. Which of the following findings do you expect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Sudden painless monocular loss of vision with fundoscopy showing Hollehorst plaque is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). Relative afferent pupillary defect is seen in these cases.

Hollenhorst plaques are cholesterol emboli that are seen in retinal arterioles. On fundus examination, it gives an appearance of a refractile yellow-white color substance in the retinal vessels.

Note: Although elevated intraocular pressure has been implicated as a cause of central retinal artery obstruction, it is unlikely that intraocular pressure can be raised high enough to block arterial inflow to the eye

questions.question:
A 61-year-old university professor presents with a loss of vision in his left eye. He describes the sensation that a curtain was coming up over his affected eye. In addition, 7 days ago the patient noticed what he described as flashing lights and floaters. He gives a history of having cataract surgery in the same eye 3 weeks ago. A B-scan image of his left eye is shown below. Which of the following statements best describes the pathology?

(NSR- Neurosensory retina , RPE- Retinal pigment epithelium)
options: Fibrovascular membranes in the vitreous causing traction
Fluid accumulation between NSR and RPE due to retinal tear
Fluid accumulation between NSR and RPE due to choroidal exudation
questions.answer: C. Fluid accumulation between NSR and RPE due to retinal tear
questions.explanation:
The prodromal symptoms of flashing lights, floaters followed by loss of monocular vision (curtain over the eye) and the B-scan suggest a diagnosis of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the result of the accumulation of fluid between NSR and RPE due to a retinal tear.

Retinal detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common type of retinal detachment. It occurs due to fluid accumulation after a retinal break (tear). High myopia, trauma, pseudophakia, aphakia are predisposing factors. Patients present with photopsia (flashes of light due to vitreoretinal traction at the site of the break), floaters and visual field defect (black curtain/veil in front of the eye).

Signs include hypotony, as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE and Shafers sign or tobacco dusting (pigments in the anterior vitreous). The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations. The most dangerous type of retinal break is horseshoe tear and the most dangerous location of retinal break is the supero-temporal retina.

Treatment is by prophylactic laser barrage, scleral buckling, pneumatic retinopexy and pars plana vitrectomy.

Other types of retinal detachment are tractional and exudative type:

Tractional retinal detachment occurs when fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularization exert traction on the retina. It is seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, central retinal venous occlusion, Eales disease and ROP. The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen. Treatment is with pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation.

Exudative retinal detachment is seen when exudative fluid from the choroid collects in the subretinal space. Patients present with visual field defects, floaters due to vitritis but no photopsia. The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen. Shifting fluid is seen.

The image below shows a fundus which reveals retinal detachment inferiorly from 3-9 o'clock with tear at 3:30.

questions.question: Pneumatic retinopexy is an outpatient procedure where retinal detachment is sealed with air insufflation. Which of the following gases would you use while performing the said procedure?
questions.explanation:
Sulphur hexafluoride is the gas used in pneumatic retinopexy for the treatment of retinal detachments

Pneumatic retinopexy is used for the treatment of fresh retinal detachments with a single retinal break in the superior two-thirds of the fundus. In this procedure, a bubble is injected intravitreally through the conjunctiva and postoperatively the patient is positioned so that the bubble tamponades the retinal break against the retinal pigment epithelium.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman who is 8 months pregnant, myopic, and diabetic presents to you with sudden painless loss of vision in her right eye. She is a known case of Eales' disease. Her blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg. Which of her conditions is responsible for a fundus finding of retinal detachment with a positive shifting fluid sign?
questions.explanation:
Exudative retinal detachment is characterized by positive shifting fluid sign. Among her conditions, toxemia of pregnancy is one of the causes of exudative retinal detachment.

Exudative retinal detachment occurs due to the presence of subretinal fluid in the absence of tear or traction. It is caused by:

• Malignant melanoma of the choroid

• Retinoblastoma

• Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) syndrome

• Uveal effusion syndrome

• Posterior scleritis

• Coat’s disease

• Malignant hypertension

• Pregnancy-induced hypertensive retinopathy

• Sympathetic ophthalmitis

Patients present with sudden and painless diminution of vision, visual field defects and grey reflex (detached retina looks grey). Indirect ophthalmoscopy is the investigation of choice.

The image depicts retinal detachment showing a smooth, detached convex retina with subretinal fluid.

questions.question: Hollenhorst plaques are seen in _______.
questions.answer: A. Central retinal arterial occlusion ( CRAO)
questions.explanation:
Hollenhorst plaques are seen in central retinal arterial occlusion (CRAO).

They are cholesterol emboli seen in retinal arterioles. They originate from atherosclerotis plaques in larger arteries. The image below shows Hollenhorst plaques (arrow).

questions.question: Identify the condition.
questions.explanation:
The above image shows a loss of foveal reflex and central serous retinopathy, therefore showing focal foveal detachment.

There is oedema at the fovea signifying foveal detachment from underlying retinal pigment epithelium. Macular oedema is also present (grey dull retina with a ring reflex around the site of oedema). Thus, the most appropriate choice would be foveal detachment.

Central serous retinopathy is the spontaneous serous detachment of neurosensory retina in the macular region. It occurs due to increased permeability of choriocapillaris, leading to fluid accumulation in the subretinal space. Therefore, it is now known as central serous choriopathy (CSC).

If there is serous retinal detachment at macula, there is sudden painless loss of vision. Patients also have relative positive scotoma, micropsia and metamorphopsia. On ophthalmoscopy, a circular ring reflex present. The foveal reflex is absent. On fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), an enlarging ink-blot pattern or smoke-stack pattern is seen.

Treatment is generally not required. It is usually self-limiting, but often recurrent. Steroids are contraindicated.

questions.question: In which of the following conditions is the given sign seen?
questions.explanation:
The image depicts fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showing an enlarging ink-blot pattern/enlarging dot sign, which is seen in central serous retinopathy (CSR). Smokestack appearance is another pattern of fundus seen in CSR and is a characteristic sign of this condition.

Amsler grid is used for:

• Assess macular function and detecting maculopathy.

• Evaluate the visual field of 10°

• Good for follow-up in CSR

questions.question: The ETDRS chart is used for visual evaluation in diabetic patients. What does ETDRS stand for?
options: Extended treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
Early treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
Emergency treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
Emerging treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
questions.answer: B. Early treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
questions.explanation:
ETDRS stands for Early Treatment for Diabetic Retinopathy Study.

ETDRS was a clinical trial designed to evaluate if argon laser photocoagulation or aspirin treatment can reduce the risk of visual loss or slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy in patients with mild-to-severe nonproliferative or early proliferative diabetic retinopathy. During the study, three new visual acuity charts were created in place of Snellen's visual chart.

chapters.chapter: Macular Disorders, Retinal Dystrophies, And Vitreal Disorders

questions.question: A 25-year-old artist visits an art gallery. A painting of checkered squares appears distorted only to him, as shown below. He decides to go see an ophthalmologist who after initial evaluation, suggests an FFA. The FFA shows a characteristic smoke stack appearance. Breakdown of which of the following barriers is responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with a characteristic smoke stack pattern on FFA is suggestive of a diagnosis of central serous retinopathy. In CSR, the outer blood-retinal barrier is disrupted.

CSR is the serous detachment of the neurosensory retina with focal and multifocal areas of leakage at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), mainly affecting the macular area. That is why the patient who is usually a young male presents with macular symptoms such as blurring of central vision, metamorphopsia.

The blood-retina barrier (BRB) is composed of inner and outer barriers. The outer BRB refers to the barrier formed at the retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell layer and regulates the movement of solutes and nutrients from the choroid to the sub-retinal space. By contrast, the inner BRB, similar to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is located in the inner retinal microvasculature and comprises the microvascular endothelium, which lines these vessels.

The image given below shows the smoke-stack pattern seen in CSR.

Amsler grid is used in detecting maculopathy.

Uses:

• Assess macular function

• Evaluate the visual field of 10°

• Good for follow-up in CSR

The image below shows Amsler's grid.

questions.question: Where does fluid accumulate in central serous retinopathy?
options: Between the Bruch membrane and retinal pigment epithelium
Between the outer plexiform layer and inner nuclear layer
questions.explanation:
Fluid accumulation in central serous retinopathy (CSR) is in the subretinal space due to abnormal permeability of the choriocapillaris.

The image depicts optical coherence tomography showing fluid accumulation in the subretinal space, with shallow retinal detachment.

questions.question: A 60-year-old female presented with acute loss of vision and metamorphopsia. There is a history of the positive scotoma. Fundal changes are given below. What will be the fundus fluorescein angiography finding?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario and the fundal image depicting focal fundal detachment are suggestive of central serous retinopathy. An enlarging inkblot pattern or smoke stack pattern is seen in FFA.

Central serous retinopathy refers to the spontaneous serous detachment of the neurosensory retina in the macular region. Recent studies implicate an abnormal choroidal circulation as the cause of CSR.

Clinical features:

• Retinal detachment - Sudden painless loss of vision

• Relative positive scotoma

• Micropsia

• Metamorphopsia

Investigations:

• Ophthalmoscopy - circular ring reflex present and foveal reflex absent

• FFA - enlarging inkblot pattern or smoke stack pattern

Spontaneous resolution is seen in most cases and hence observation is enough. Steroids are contraindicated. The disease is usually self-limiting but may recur.

The image depicts fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), showing an enlarging ink-blot pattern/enlarging dot sign, which is seen in central serous retinopathy (CSR).

Other options:

Option B- Petaloid appearance is seen in cystoid macular edema

Option C- Stars in the sky appearance is suggestive of drusen

Option D- Dual circulation is a pathognomonic feature of choroidal melanoma

questions.question: A 69-year-old man who is a chronic smoker, hypertensive, and has a BMI of 35 kg/m2 complains of diminished vision in the right eye. His visual acuity is 6/36 BE and the anterior segment appears normal. His fundus is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.answer: B. Age related dry macular degeneration
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario along with the image which shows drusen (druplets) are a feature of dry or non-exudative age-related macular degeneration (ARMD).

Drusen are the earliest visible clinical signs of ARMD. They are composed of lipid, amyloid, complement factors, and associated cellular components.

There are two types of ARMD:

• Dry (non-exudative, non-neovascular) ARMD is the most common form, comprising around 90% of the diagnosed cases. Initially characterized by macular Drusens, which later progress to geographical atrophy. Geographic atrophy (GA) is the advanced stage of dry ARMD. Antioxidants like the AREDS2 supplements have proven effective.

• Wet (exudative, neovascular) ARMD is much less common than the dry type, but it is associated with more rapid progression to advanced sight loss.

Clinical classification:

age-related changes

changes

questions.question:
Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is primarily indicated in which of the following conditions?

CNVM - choroidal neovascular membrane
questions.explanation:
Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is primarily indicated in an occult choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM).

ICGA is used to visualize the choroidal vasculature.

Its main use is to differentiate between classic and occult CNVM when the clinical picture is not clear.

questions.question:
Intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF is used in the treatment of which of the following conditions?

ARMD - age-related macular degeneration
questions.explanation:
Intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is used as the treatment of wet age-related macular degeneration (ARMD).

Wet ARMD is characterized by retinal pigment epithelial detachment and choroidal/subretinal neovascularization.

Treatment of ARMD depends on the location of the choroidal neovascularization membrane:

• For extrafoveal membrane - Laser photocoagulation

• For subfoveal and juxta foveal membranes, treatment options are as follows:

• Intravitreal injection of anti -VEGF agents

• Photodynamic therapy - the dye used is verteporfin followed by exposure to light from a diode

• Transpupillary thermotherapy

questions.question: An old cab driver whose livelihood depends on his driving is distressed. He complains that everything appears distorted and he perceives objects to smaller than their usual size. His anterior segment appears normal. Examination of the fundus reveals a honeycomb appearance of the macula. FFA is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image is that of fluorescein angiography showing the "flower petal pattern," which is seen in cystoid macular edema (CME). The characteristic flower-petal appearance is due to the accumulation of dye in the outer plexiform layer and inner nuclear layer at the macula

The accumulation of fluid in the outer plexiform layer and the inner nuclear layer leads to retinal thickening at macula and loss of foveal depression, formation of cystic spaces (honey-comb macula). Risk factors include retinitis pigmentosa, uveitis, niacin, PGE2 analogues, epinephrine in aphakia, diabetic retinopathy, retinal venous occlusion and Irvin-Gass syndrome (CME post-cataract surgery).

Symptoms may include blurring of vision, distortion, and micropsia.

Therapeutic approaches for treating CME depend on the underlying etiology. This includes steroids, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, anti-VEGF agents, PPV for associated vitreomacular traction.

questions.question: A 45-year old patient on systemic treatment for rheumatoid arthritis develops bilateral painless decrease in vision. What does the image show?
options: Fluorescein angiography showing bull’s eye maculopathy
Autofluorescence showing changes of bull’s eye maculopathy
questions.answer: B. Autofluorescence showing changes of bull’s eye maculopathy
questions.explanation:
The investigation shown in the image is an autofluorescence showing bull’s eye maculopathy.

Hydroxychloroquine, which is generally used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, toxicity causes bull’s eye maculopathy. Chloroquine binds to melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium, causing cytotoxic effects. RPE atrophy occurs in the macula, resulting in dark areas on the autofluorescence image.

Other causes of Bull’s eye maculopathy include chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, congenital cone dystrophy, juvenile X-linked retinoschisis, and juvenile Batten's disease.

Fundus autofluorescence is a non-invasive imaging modality. It reflects the morphological changes associated with the metabolism of lipofuscin and does not require the injection of any fluorescent dye.

A fundus image of bull’s eye maculopathy is shown below:

The following image shows the difference between fundus autofluorescence and fluorescence angiography

Other ocular effects of chloroquine include:

• Chloroquine keratopathy—vortex keratopathy

• Ocular palsy, ptosis

• Electroretinographic depression

• Optic neuritis

• Posterior subcapsular cataract

questions.question: A study used electroretinography(ERG) in military conscripts whose visual abnormalities could not be explained by the findings of ophthalmologic, neurological, and psychiatric examinations. The ERG of pure malingerers was found to be, as shown below. The activity of which cells of the retina is depicted by the a-wave?
questions.explanation:
"a" wave in an electroretinogram (ERG) represents rods and cones.

Electroretinography is used to evaluate retinal functions by examining the electrical response to a light stimulus.

Electroretinograms (ERGs) show the amplitudes of currents that flow within the eye following exposure to a point of light. The amplitudes are analyzed into waves, which are composed of the responses of neuronal, glial, and retinal pigment epithelial cells.

ERG:

• The a-wave originates from photoreceptors (rods and cones)

• The b-wave originates from Muller and bipolar cells, but is directly dependant on photoreceptors

• The c-wave originates from retinal pigment epithelial cells and retinal glial cells

• Oscillatory potentials (OPs) originate in the inner retina

Scotopic ERGs are used to evaluate responses starting from rod photoreceptors exposed to flash-light in darkness, and photopic ERGs are used to evaluate responses starting from cone photoreceptors exposed to flash-light under constant light exposure.

questions.question: Which area of the retina has the highest concentration of rods?
questions.explanation:
Mid-periphery of the retina has the highest concentration of rods.

The following table lists the differences between rods and cones
