questions.question: A researcher is studying mutations in the rhodopsin gene which are responsible for some forms of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. On which chromosome is this gene located?
questions.explanation:
The gene for rhodopsin is located at 3q22.1

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a dystrophy of rods and cones, with rods being primarily affected. It is a genetic disease. The non-hereditary/sporadic type is most common. Among the hereditary types, it can occur in an autosomal dominant (AD), autosomal recessive (AR), or X-linked recessive (XLR) pattern. AD disease generally has the best prognosis.

The presenting feature is night blindness.

Investigations:

• Perimetry - the initial stage will have ring scotoma, which further develops into tunnel vision.

• Electroretinography - reveals a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves.

Retinitis pigmentosa is a condition with no cure. There are drugs used to slow down the progression such as acetazolamide for concomitant cystoid macular edema. Recently, vitamin A has been recommended, although the efficacy has not been established.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?
options: RPE forms the inner blood retinal barrier
Electroculogram is an assessment of RPE health
Bruch’s membrane is the basement membrane of RPE
questions.answer: A. RPE forms the inner blood retinal barrier
questions.explanation:
Tight junctions between retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) form the outer blood-retinal barrier. The inner blood-retinal barrier is formed by the tight junctions between the endothelial cells of retinal capillaries.

RPE serves many functions, like

• Development of photoreceptors during embryogenesis

• Tight junctions between RPE form the outer blood-retinal barrier

• Absorption of fluid from the subretinal space and adhesion of the underlying neurosensory retina

• Selective transport of metabolites to and from the retina

• Uptake, transport, storage, metabolism, and isomerization of vitamin A

• Regeneration of the visual pigment rhodopsin

• Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segment tips

• Absorption of stray light by melanin

If the RPE is damaged, this is seen as a loss of autofluorescence (RPE-deficient areas appear darker on autofluorescence images).

Bruch's membrane is the basement membrane of RPE.

questions.question: Which of the following disorders is not associated with retinitis pigmentosa?
questions.explanation:
Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is associated with abetalipoprotenemia (Bassen–Kornzweig syndrome) and not with abetaglobulinemia.

Syndromes associated with RP (Atypical RP)

Usher syndrome
Sensory neural deafness + RP

Bardet–Biedl syndrome

(Previously called Lawrence–Moon–Biedl–Bartum Syndrome)

Polydactyly, obesity, mental handicap, and kidney disease + RP

Kearn–Sayre syndrome
Ocular myopathy and heart disease + RP

Refsum Syndrome

Varied skin as well as neurological and visceral features + RP

Bassen–Kornzweig syndrome

Abetalipoprotenemia and acanthocytosis + RP

Neuropathy, ataxia, and retinitis pigmentosa (NARP)
Neuropathy and Ataxia + RP

questions.question: What is the diagnosis from the image given below?
questions.explanation:
The fundus shows a pale waxy disc, attenuated arteries, and bony spicules, which implies retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a dystrophy of rods and cones, with rods being primarily affected. It is a genetic disease. The non-hereditary/sporadic type is most common. Among the hereditary type, it can occur in an autosomal dominant (AD), autosomal recessive (AR), or X-linked recessive (XLR) pattern. AD disease generally has the best prognosis.

The presenting feature is night blindness.

Investigations:

• Perimetry - the initial stage will have ring scotoma, which further develops into tunnel vision.

• Electroretinography - reveals a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves.

Atypical types of RP are as follows:

• Sectoral RP

• Pericentric/Inverse RP

• RP sine pigmento

• RP punctata albescens

There is no effective treatment for RP.

questions.question: In which of the following conditions is the Mizuo phenomenon seen?
questions.explanation:
Mizuo phenomenon is seen in Oguchi's disease.

Oguchi's disease is a type of congenital stationary night blindness with abnormal fundus. Congenital stationary night blindness refers to a group of disorders characterized by infantile-onset nyctalopia but non-progressive retinal dysfunction. The fundus has an unusual golden yellow color in the light-adapted state, which becomes normal after prolonged dark adaptation (Mizuo or Mizuo–Nakamura phenomenon).

The following image shows a comparison in the fundus appearances ("A" shows the golden yellow color of the fundus in a light-adapted state; "B" shows normal-appearing funds after prolonged dark adaptation of 3 to 4 hours)

Rod function is absent even after 30 minutes of dark adaptation (normal dark adaptation time is 20–30 mins) but recovers to a near-normal level after a long period of dark adaptation (4 hours).

questions.question: Flat electrooculogram (EOG) is an Arden ratio of _______.
questions.explanation:
A flat electrooculogram (EOG) is an Arden ratio of less than 1.25.

An EOG measures the standing potential of the eye. It reflects the activity of the RPE and the photoreceptors. This means that an eye blinded by disease proximal to the photoreceptors will have a normal EOG. Arden ratio is the ratio between the light peak and the dark trough in an EOG.

The normal Arden ratio is 1.85 and above. A flat EOG occurs when the Arden ratio is less than 1.25.

Best disease is an autosomal-dominant childhood disease characterized by the dystrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium. In Best disease, the Arden ratio is less than 1.50.

questions.question: A young patient presents with loss of central vision. ERG is normal, but EOG is abnormal. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis based on the above scenario is Best's disease.

Best's disease/Vitelliform macular dystrophy is an inherited macular dystrophy in which lipofuscin accumulates in the central macula causing progressive central vision loss. It is autosomal-dominant and linked to the mutation in the bestrophin (VMD2) gene.

It is characterized by bilateral yellow, yolk-like (vitelliform) macular lesions.

The stages of evolution of the macular lesions are described as progressing from:

• Pre-vitelliform stage

• Vitelliform stage - scrambled egg stage with or without hypopyon

• Vitelliruptive - the lesion breaks and visual acuity drops

• The atrophic stage

Patients with Best’s disease usually have good visual acuity when the "yolk" remains intact.

Diagnosis: This is the only disease with relatively normal ERG results associated with an abnormal EOG. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) reveals that the vitelliform material appears as a dome-shaped, hyperreflective, and homogenous lesion, located below the hyperreflective photoreceptor layer.

The image below shows Best’s disease - the typical vitelliform lesion in an 11-year-old girl.

questions.question: A young patient presents with loss of central vision. There is a family history of a similar condition. Both EOG and ERG are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis based on the given scenario is Stargardt's disease.

Stargardt's disease also known as Stargardt macular dystrophy or fundus flavimaculatus is the most common macular dystrophy. It most commonly is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner caused by a mutation on an adenosine triphosphate-binding cassette (ABCA4) gene.

Characterized by macular "pisciform" flecks that accumulate at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), sometimes resulting in central macular atrophy early in life. Patients develop a macula with a “beaten bronze” appearance caused by atrophic changes in the RPE. In addition, a "dark" or "silent" choroid is seen on the fluorescein angiography that appears as a prominent retinal circulation against hypofluorescent choroid.

The electroretinogram (ERG) and electro-oculography (EOG) are normal early in the disease but may be reduced in more advanced cases. Of note, the ERG findings do not directly correlate with clinical findings.

There is no known proven treatment for this disease. Because ABCA4 plays a role in vitamin A processing in the visual cycle, additional vitamin A is suspected to make the disease worse.

The image below shows macular pisciform flecks.

Other options:

Option A: Retinitis pigmentosa: abnormal electroretinogram (ERG).

Option B: Rod–cone dystrophy: abnormal ERG.

Option D: Best's disease: Normal ERG with abnormal electrooculogram (EOG).

questions.question: A neonate with leukocoria and strabismus is diagnosed to have persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV). Which of the following congenital disorders is it associated with?
questions.explanation:
Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) is associated with Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13).

PHPV is a developmental disorder of the vitreous humor. In this condition, there is persistence of the embryonic hyaloid vessel.

• Anterior PHPV - Here, the remnant vessel is attached to the back of the lens but does not reach the optic nerve.

• Posterior PHPV- In this form of the disease, the vessel arises from the optic nerve.

Clinically, PHPV presents with leucocoria and microphthalmia, and there can be complications such as tractional retinal detachments.

This condition has a poor prognosis regardless of the time of intervention.

questions.question: When compared to blood, vitreous humor has a high concentration of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
When compared to blood, vitreous humor has a high concentration of ascorbate. The vitreous: plasma ratio of ascorbic acid concentration is 9:1.

This high concentration of ascorbic acid is maintained by the active transport by the ciliary body epithelium, and it is attributed to the ability of the ascorbate to absorb ultraviolet rays and act as a free radical scavenger.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman complains of discomfort in her left eye. There is a past history of blunt trauma in her childhood which made her left eye blind. Slit-lamp examination of her left eye is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
These are synchysis scintillans, which are floaters composed of cholesterol bodies, found in the vitreous (extending into the anterior chamber in this picture).

Synchysis scintillans are vitreous opacities that occur as a consequence of chronic vitreous haemorrhage, often in a blind eye. This condition is usually discovered, when frank haemorrhage is no longer present. They are composed of cholesterol derived from plasma cells or degraded products of erythrocytes.

Vitreous opacities can be caused by a variety of pathological processes and the following are few examples of vitreous opacities:

• Vitreous haemorrhage

• Asteroid hyalosis

• Synchysis scintillans

• Amyloidosis

• Vitreous cyst

• Persistent fetal vasculature.

questions.question: A slit-lamp examination reveals the following finding. It is also noted that these yellow-white vitreous opacities do not settle down when the eye is immobile. All of the following statements about this condition are true except:
questions.explanation:
The examination findings are suggestive of asteroid bodies/hyalosis. It is not common in myopes.

Asteroid hyalosis is a common degenerative process in which calcium pyrophosphate particles collect within the vitreous gel. It is seen clinically as numerous tiny round yellow-white opacities of varying size and density. These move with the vitreous during eye movements but do not sediment inferiorly when the eye is immobile.

Only one eye is affected in 75% of patients; it rarely causes visual problems and the majority of patients are asymptomatic. The cause of asteroid hyalosis is unknown, but it has been associated with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. The prevalence of asteroid hyalosis increases with age and affects 3% of those aged 75–86 years. It is more common in men than in women. While treatment of asteroid hyalosis is usually unnecessary, vitrectomy may occasionally be indicated.

questions.question: A young male presents with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
For a young male presenting with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage, the diagnosis is Eale's disease.

Eales disease is an idiopathic occlusive peripheral periphlebitis. It is characterized by three overlapping stages: inflammatory, occlusive, and retinal neovascular. Visual prognosis is good in the majority of cases. It is an important cause of visual morbidity in young males from the Indian subcontinent.

Diagnosis:

• Symptoms - Floaters or sudden visual reduction due to vitreous hemorrhage. There can be neurological deficits as well.

• Mild anterior uveitis

• Fundus - The condition is typically bilateral, although often asymmetrical.

• Peripheral periphlebitis

• Branch retinal vein occlusion

• Peripheral capillary non-perfusion; microaneurysms, tortuosity, vascular shunts, and neovascularization with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage

Treatment:

• Steroids: Periocular, systemic, topical, and intravitreal steroids seem to be helpful in the inflammatory stage.

• Antitubercular treatment

questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic of Eale’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Eale’s disease is an idiopathic inflammatory venous occlusion (phlebitis) that primarily affects the peripheral retina that is periphlebitis and is characterized by recurrent bilateral vitreous hemorrhage.

Superficial retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots can be sometimes seen, but they are not characteristic of Eales disease.

questions.question: What is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of a vitreous hemorrhage?
questions.explanation:
The investigation of choice for vitreous hemorrhage is ultrasonography (USG) B-scan. Mild hemorrhage causes sudden onset floaters and diffuse blurring of vision, but may not affect visual acuity, whilst a dense bleed may result in sudden painless loss of vision.

B-mode ultrasonography(B-scan) in unclotted vitreous hemorrhage generally shows a uniform appearance, and once cellular aggregates develop, small particulate echoes become visible.

Causes of vitreous hemorrhage:

• Acute posterior vitreous detachment associated either with a retinal tear or avulsion of a peripheral vessel

• Proliferative retinopathy

• Diabetic

• Retinal vein occlusion

• Sickle cell disease

• Eales disease

• Vasculitis

• Miscellaneous retinal disorders

• Macroaneurysm

• Telangiectasia

• Capillary hemangioma

• Trauma

• Systemic

• Bleeding disorders

• Terson syndrome- refers to the combination of intraocular and subarachnoid hemorrhage secondary to aneurysmal rupture, most commonly arising from the anterior communicating artery.

Treatment is dictated by severity and cause, but an increasingly low threshold is being adopted for early vitrectomy.

questions.question: Sub-hyaloid hemorrhage is _______.
questions.explanation:
Sub-hyaloid hemorrhage is dome-shaped or boat-shaped.

Subhyaloid hemorrhage is the collection of blood in the potential space between the posterior vitreous and internal limiting membrane of the retina.

The image depicts a sub-hyaloid hemorrhage which is boat-shaped.

questions.question: What is a reverse hypopyon?
options: Collection of pus in the vitreous
Collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber
questions.answer: B. Collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber
questions.explanation:
Reverse hypopyon is the collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber.

Silicone oil is the vitreous substitute that is injected into the vitreous cavity after vitrectomy. When it gets emulsified, it enters the anterior chamber and collects in the upper part.

Complications of silicone oil in the anterior chamber:

1. Glaucoma

2. Band-shaped keratopathy

The image below shows reverse hypopyon.

questions.question: Which anti-fungal can be administered intravitreally?
questions.explanation:
Voriconazole and amphotericin-B can be given intravitreally.

Vancomycin and ceftazidime is the preferred combination for endophthalmitis (intravitreous). Amikacin (0.4 mg in 0.1 ml) or gentamicin (0.4 mg in 0.1 ml) are used less frequently in endophthalmitis owing to the risk of macular infarction.

topics.topic: Eyelids, Lacrimal System, Orbit and Tumours

questions.question: Which of the following is defined as loss of eyelashes?
questions.explanation:
Madarosis is the loss of eyelashes or eyebrows.

• Loss of eyebrows is seen in leprosy and myxedema.

• Loss of eyelashes is seen in chronic blepharitis.

Other options:

Option A: Tylosis is a thickening of the tarsal border of the eyelid.

Option C: Trichiasis is an inward misdirection of cilia, with the normal position of the lid margin.

Option D: Distichiasis is the presence of a double row of eyelashes.

questions.question: A term neonate is referred to the district hospital for an ophthalmic exam. Partial fusion of her right upper and lower eyelids by a central narrow band of tissue is noted as shown below. The left eye examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows an adhesion between the margins of the upper and lower eyelids, which suggests ankyloblepharon.

It may occur as a congenital anomaly or as acquired adhesions after healing of chemical burns, ulcers, or traumatic wounds of the lid margins. Treatment is the excision of the adhesions between lid margins. In severe cases where the adhesions involve the angle of the eyes, epithelial grafts can be used.

Other options:

Option A: Symblepharon is the adhesion between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, whereby the eyelids become adherent to the eyeball.

Option C: Blepharophimosis is a congenital anomaly in which the extent of the palpebral fissure is decreased. It appears contracted at the outer canthus.

Option D: Lagophthalmos is characterized by the inability to close the eyelids voluntarily. It may be due to a malfunction of the facial nerve. The image below shows nocturnal lagophthalmos (inability to close eyelids during sleep).

questions.question: A male patient complains of a foreign body sensation, irritation, and lacrimation in the right eye. During the evaluation, you notice the following findings with normal lid margins. What is this condition known as?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the above image is suggestive of trichiasis.

Trichiasis refers to the inward misdirection of cilia, which usually rub against the eyeball with the normal position of the lid margin. These patients present with foreign body sensations and photophobia. They experience troublesome irritation, pain, and lacrimation. On examination, one or more misdirected cilia touching the cornea are seen. The conjunctiva may be congested.

Treatment includes:

• Epilation: Mechanical removal with forceps

• Electrolysis: Method of destroying the lash follicle by electric current.

• Cryoepilation

• Surgical correction.

questions.question: What defines telecanthus?
options: Widened root of the nose with normal inter-pupillary distance
questions.answer: D. Widened root of the nose with normal inter-pupillary distance
questions.explanation:
Telecanthus means an increased distance between medial canthi (widened root of the nose) with normal inter-pupillary distance.

In hypertelorism, there is a wide bony separation of the orbits.

In epicanthus, there are bilateral vertical folds of skin that extend from the upper or lower lids towards the medial canthi. They may give rise to pseudoesotropia.

questions.question: Weiss operation is done in which of the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Weiss operation is done in senile entropion. In this operation, the transverse lid split, and everything sutures are placed.

Entropion refers to the inward rolling and rotation of the lid margin towards the globe. It is more common in the lower lid.

Causes include:

• Horizontal lid laxity

• Vertical lid instability

• Over-riding of the pretarsal by the preseptal orbicularis during lid closure

• Orbital septum laxity

questions.question: For which of the following is medial conjunctivoplasty the surgical modality of treatment?
questions.explanation:
Medial conjunctivoplasty is done in involutional ectropion.

Ectropion is the eversion of the lid margin and eyelashes away from the globe.

Types:

• Involutional/senile - affects the lower lid of elderly patients.

• Cicatricial - caused by the scarring or contracture of the skin and underlying tissues

• Paralytic - caused by ipsilateral facial nerve palsy

• Mechanical - caused by tumors on or near the lid margin that mechanically evert the lid

• Congenital

questions.question: Which among the following is not a feature of blepharophimosis syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Entropion is not a feature of blepharophimosis syndrome.

Blepharophimosis, ptosis, and epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES) consists of the following:

• Narrow palpebral fissure

• Ptosis

• Congenital ectropion of the lower lid

• Telecanthus

• Epicanthus inversus: an extra fold of skin arising from the lower lid

The image below shows blepharophimosis.

questions.question: The physician noticed the following finding in a patient that came to the OPD for an eye exam. Which of the following pair of muscles are likely to be affected in this patient?
options: Levator palpebrae superioris and superior oblique
Levator palpebrae superioris and Muller's muscle
questions.answer: D. Levator palpebrae superioris and Muller's muscle
questions.explanation:
The patient has mild right eye ptosis. Injury or weakness of levator palpebrae superioris and Muller's muscle leads to ptosis.

Levator palpebrae superioris is the important upper eyelid retractor. Frontalis and Muller’s muscle assist in the elevation of the upper eyelid.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is a cause of pseudoptosis?
questions.explanation:
Brow ptosis is a type of pseudoptosis, not ptosis.

Ptosis is abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid to a level that covers more than 2mm of the superior cornea.

Types of ptosis:

• Mechanical ptosis - Can be due to lid tumors, multiple/big chalazions, and conjunctival scarring

• Aponeurotic ptosis - Due to dehiscence of the aponeurosis and in postoperative patients

• Involutional ptosis seen in old age

• Neurogenic ptosis due to a 3rd nerve palsy, Horner syndrome and synkinetic ptosis/Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking ptosis

• Myogenic ptosis

• Congenital: most common myogenic ptosis

• Simple

• Blepharophimosis syndrome

• Congenital synkinetic ptosis

• Acquired

• Myasthenia gravis

• Lambert–Eaton syndrome

• Ocular myopathy

Causes of pseudoptosis (apparent ptosis):

• Lack of support of the lids by the globe e.g. artificial eye, microphthalmos, phthisis bulbi, or enophthalmos.

• Contralateral lid retraction

• Ipsilateral hypotropia

• Brow ptosis occurs due to excessive skin on the brow, or seventh nerve palsy, which is diagnosed by manually elevating the
eyebrow

• Dermatochalasis

questions.question: Which of the following conditions will not have a finding of bilateral ptosis?
questions.explanation:
Bilateral ptosis is not seen in Marfan's syndrome.

Causes of unilateral ptosis:

1. Horner's syndrome

2. Oculomotor nerve palsy

Causes of bilateral ptosis:

1. Congenital

2. Senile/involutional/aponeurotic

3. Blepharophimosis syndrome

4. Myasthenia gravis

5. Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) - seen in Kearns-Sayre syndrome

6. Myotonic dystrophy

7. Ocular myopathies

The image below shows a case of botulinum toxicity with bilateral ptosis.

questions.question: During OPD hours, a patient came with the finding shown below. On examination, the upper 4 mm of the cornea is covered by the upper eyelid. What is the grade of ptosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
In this question, 4 mm of the cornea is covered by the upper eyelid. Subtracting 2 mm from this implies that there is 2 mm of ptosis, which is classified as mild grade.

In bilateral cases, the grade of ptosis can be determined by measuring the amount of cornea covered by the upper lid and then subtracting 2 mm. Depending upon this value, the ptosis is graded as follows:

• Mild: 2 mm

• Moderate: 3 mm

• Severe: 4 mm

questions.question: A child with a high risk of amblyopia is planned for surgical correction of unilateral simple congenital ptosis. He has poor levator function. What is the treatment of choice in this case?
questions.explanation: Frontalis sling procedure is the treatment of choice for congenital ptosis with poor levator function.

questions.question: A patient presents to you with anhidrosis and enophthalmos. Examination reveals miosis along with mild ptosis. You decide to correct the ptosis by performing a Fasanella-Servat operation, by resecting which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Horner's syndrome and the associated mild ptosis in this condition can be corrected by resecting Muller's muscle.

Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is due to the paralysis of Muller's muscle.

Fasanella-Servat operation is indicated in cases having mild ptosis(< 2 mm) and good levator function. In this surgery, the upper tarsal border along with its attached Muller’s muscle and conjunctiva are resected.

questions.question: A couple brought their 11-month-old child for an eye exam when they noticed that his left upper eyelid was in a lower position than his right one. The mother also noticed that his left upper eyelid goes "up and down” when she breastfeeds him. His delivery was unremarkable. When the baby opens his mouth or sucks his thumb, the left eyelid ptosis disappears. What is the pathology behind this condition?
options: Superior division of the third cranial nerve is misdirected
Sympathetic nerves to Muller's muscles are misdirected
Ophthalmic division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected
Mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected
questions.answer: D. Mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon. In this condition, the mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected to the levator muscle.

Some cases of congenital ptosis are associated with the Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon. The vast majority are unilateral. Signs include retraction of the ptotic lid in conjunction with stimulation of the ipsilateral pterygoid muscles by chewing, sucking, opening the mouth, or contralateral jaw movement. Less common stimuli to winking include jaw protrusion, smiling, swallowing, and clenching of teeth. Jaw-winking does not improve with age although patients may learn to mask it.

The following image shows a woman with Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon. See how her right eyelid ptosis retracts with the opening of the mouth.

questions.question: Which of the following is the causative agent for blepharitis acarica?
questions.explanation:
Blepharitis acarica is caused by Demodex folliculorum.

Blepharitis is a chronic inflammation of the margins of the lids.

The two types are

• Anterior

• Seborrheic and ulcerative types

• Caused by staphylococci, mainly

• Posterior – Mebomianitis

Occasionally caused by

• Demodex folliculorum – Blepharitis acarica

• Crab louse – Phthiriasis palpebrarum

The following image shows swollen and inflamed eyelid suggestive of blepharitis.

questions.question: What is the most common malignant tumor of the eyelid?
questions.explanation:
Basal cell carcinoma constitutes 85–90% of all malignant epithelial eyelid tumors. It is locally malignant and most commonly involves the lower lid, followed by the medial canthus, upper lid, and outer canthus.

Type
Common location
Clinical features

Basal cell carcinoma

• Nodule

• Central ulceration with pearly surface, telangiectasia

Lower lid, from previous actinic keratosis

• Ulcer with thickened margins, keratosis

• papillomatous

• Vascularization

Local, vascular lymph nodes

questions.question: Which of the following systemic drugs is used specifically in the management of periocular basal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Vismodegib is the systemic drug used for the management of periocular basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

Vismodegib is an eye-sparing adjuvant therapy of periocular and orbital BCC for patients:

• Who cannot tolerate surgery or radiotherapy, or

• With relapsed locally advanced disease after surgery or

• With metastatic disease.

Vismodegib is a Hedgehog pathway inhibitor, given 150 mg orally twice a day.

Treatment options for BCC consist of surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. Surgical excision using Mohs micrographic surgery or wide surgical excision with frozen section margin control is the first-line treatment of periocular BCC.

Other options:

Option A: Imiquimod 5% topical cream can also be used in patients with BCC. But, it is not a systemic drug.

Option C: Siponimod is the drug approved for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis.

Option D: Interferons are generally not used in periocular BCC.

questions.question: A 6-month-old girl was brought by her worried parents due to a swelling on the eyelid as shown below. They were told by a local village doctor that the swelling will disappear on its own but recently it has been increasing rapidly. What would be the most likely management of this baby's condition?
options: Treatment with intralesional steroids at 2 years of age
questions.answer: D. Immediate treatment with oral propranolol
questions.explanation:
The history and image are suggestive of capillary hemangioma involving the left upper lid and periocular region causing severe mechanical ptosis. Immediate management with oral propranolol is the treatment of choice in this case.

The ptosis is so severe that it obstructs the pupillary area (visual axis) with the risk of sensory deprivation amblyopia. This warrants immediate treatment to reduce the bulk of the tumor.

Capillary hemangioma regresses spontaneously very often. It may be managed by oral propranolol, oral prednisolone, or intralesional steroid.

Indications for treatment of patients with capillary hemangioma with pharmacologic therapy are:

• Visual symptoms (amblyopia, astigmatism, occlusion, strabismus)

• Cosmesis

• Optic nerve compression

• Exposure keratopathy

questions.question: Identify the clinical condition.
questions.explanation:
The image shows plexiform neurofibroma of the upper lid causing an S-shaped deformity of the upper lid and mechanical ptosis. This is seen particularly in neurofibromatosis type 1.

NF1 is caused by the autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. It is a tumor suppressor gene that encodes neurofibromin, a negative RAS regulator. The disease is clinically diagnosed when any two of the following seven features are present:

• Six or more café-au-lait macules (CALMs) - They are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis and are present in almost 100% of patients. They are present at birth but increase in size, number, and pigmentation, especially during the first few years of life, and are scattered over the entire body.

• Axillary or inguinal freckling

• Two or more iris Lisch nodules - They are iris hamartomas that are best identified by a slit-lamp examination. They are present in the majority of patients with NF1.

• Two or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma

• A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or cortical thinning of long bones such as the tibia

• Optic gliomas (most frequently observed CNS tumor in NF1)

• A first-degree relative with NF-1

questions.question: Which of the following sign is used to describe the fullness of eyelids seen in Grave's ophthalmopathy?
questions.explanation: The fullness of the eyelids is described as the Enroth's sign in Graves ophthalmopathy.

chapters.chapter: Disorders Of Lacrimal Apparatus And Glands Of The Eye

questions.question: Moll glands are examples of _______
questions.explanation:
Moll glands are examples of apocrine sweat gland.

Moll glands are present in the eyelid. They are a type of modified apocrine sweat glands opening either into a lash follicle or directly onto the anterior lid margin between the lashes.

Zeis glands are a type of modified sebaceous glands associated with lash follicles. Meibomian glands are modified sebaceous glands found in the tarsal plates.

questions.question: A patient presented with a painless swelling and watering in his left eye. Examination revealed the following finding. Which of the following statements is false regarding his diagnosis?
options: It needs to be surgically treated.
It does not have malignant potential.
It is a chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation.
questions.answer: C. It does not have malignant potential.
questions.explanation:
A painless swelling on the lower lid is suggestive of a chalazion (tarsal cyst/meibomian cyst). It has the malignant potential to become an adenocarcinoma of the meibomian gland.

Chalazion is the chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation (option D) of the meibomian gland (option B). It presents as painless swelling of the eyelid. It is more common in adults than children. Treatment includes incision and curettage (option B) and intralesional injection of triamcinolone acetate.

questions.question: A recurrent chalazion should be subjected to histopathological evaluation to exclude the possibility of _____.
questions.explanation:
A recurrent chalazion should be subjected to histopathological evaluation to exclude the possibility of sebaceous gland carcinoma.

Note: A chalazion can undergo malignant change into sebaceous gland carcinoma (adenocarcinoma of meibomian gland).

Recurrences of chalazia are not uncommon. However, the physician should entertain the possibility of malignancy in such cases and should biopsy a lesion that recurs or appears atypical. The pathologist should be alerted to the suspicion of sebaceous gland carcinoma and frozen sections and lipid stains should be requested.

questions.question: A patient presented to the clinic with severe left eye pain, watering, and swelling of the lid for 2 days. He says it's difficult to see the laptop screen while working and he is unable to complete his daily targets. On examination, tender swelling is noted as shown below. What is the cause of this finding?
questions.answer: C. Acute infection of meibomian gland
questions.explanation:
The patient has acute presentation and painful swelling in the palpebral conjunctiva as shown in the image, suggestive of internal hordeolum. It is an acute suppurative inflammation of the meibomian gland associated with blockage of the duct.

Other options:

Options A and B: Hordeolum externum or stye is the acute staphylococcal infection of the hair follicle/Zeis gland/Moll gland.

Option D: Chalazion is a chronic non-suppurative lipogranulomatous inflammation of the Meibomian gland.

questions.question: What is the length of the nasolacrimal duct?
questions.explanation:
The nasolacrimal duct is 12–18 mm long.

The lacrimal drainage system consists of the lacrimal sac, which is 10–12 mm long. It lies in the lacrimal fossa, between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests. The lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla separate the lacrimal sac from the middle meatus of the nasal cavity.

The nasolacrimal duct is the inferior continuation of the lacrimal sac. It is 12–18 mm long and is directed downwards, backward, and laterally. The opening of the duct into the inferior meatus is partially covered by a mucosal fold (valve of Hasner).

The puncta are openings on the lid margin. There are two canaliculi from the puncta. Each canaliculus (superior and inferior) has two parts: Vertical (2 mm) and horizontal (8 mm). The superior and inferior canaliculi usually unite to form the common canaliculus, which opens into the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac. A small flap of mucosa (Rosenmüller valve) overhangs the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac and prevents the reflux of tears into the canaliculi.

The image below shows structures of the lacrimal apparatus.

questions.question: Where does the nasolacrimal duct open?
questions.explanation:
The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.

The nasolacrimal duct is the inferior continuation of the lacrimal sac. It is 12–18 mm long and is directed downwards, backward, and laterally. The opening of the duct into the inferior meatus is partially covered by a mucosal fold, called the valve of Hasner. The valve of Hasner prevents reflux from the nose.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman came for an eye exam due to a gritty sensation that has been causing her a lot of discomfort. On examination, Rose Bengal staining is positive. She is diagnosed with keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Which of the following layer of the tear film is deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is due to the deficiency of the aqueous layer of the tear film.

In keratoconjunctivitis sicca, patients present with irritation and foreign body sensation. Marginal tear strip is reduced. The conjunctiva become dry and lustreless with positive Rose Bengal staining. Causes of keratoconjunctivitis sicca:

• Sjogren's syndrome (primary keratoconjunctivitis sicca)

• Non-Sjogren's keratoconjunctivitis sicca

• Primary age-related hyposecretion (most common)

• Lacrimal gland deficiencies - congenital, infiltration by tumors or sarcoidosis, surgical removal

• Lacrimal gland duct obstruction - old trachoma, burns, SJS

• Reflex hyposecretion (neurogenic causes) - Parkinson disease, 7th nerve palsy, reflex sensory block

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the phenol red test for dry eye?
options: It measures tear production based on the length of colour change in the thread
If color changes to blue, it depicts mucin deficiency.
questions.answer: B. It measures tear production based on the length of colour change in the thread
questions.explanation:
Phenol red test measures the tear production according to the length of colour change in the thread.

In phenol red test, the alkalinity of tears changes its colour to bright orange on contact. It doesn't require anaesthesia (unlike Schirmer's test). Three millimetres of a fine dye-impregnated 75-mm cotton thread is placed under the lateral one-fifth of the inferior palpebral lid margin for 15 seconds.

Based on length of colour change,

• >20 mm - normal tear production

• 10 to 19 mm - borderline dry eye

• <10 mm - severe dry eye

questions.question: Identify the test shown below.
questions.explanation:
The image shows a tear strip placed in the lower lid of the eye. This is the Schirmer test which is used to check for dry eye.

Dry eye is a multifactorial disease of the eye characterised by loss of homeostasis of the tear film. Patients present with irritation, foreign body sensation and dryness. Treatment of dry eye includes medical treatment (lubricating eyedrops, most commonly methylcellulose derivatives) or surgical treatment (lacrimal punctum occlusion using silicone plugs).

Other tests for dry eye include:

1. Tear film break-up test is used to determine the interval between a complete blink and appearance of first randomly distributed dry spot on the cornea. A drop of fluorescein is instilled in the eye, following by examination in the cobalt-blue light of a slit-lamp.

2. Rose Bengal staining is used for the detection of dry, dead epithelium in dry eye.

3. Tear osmolarity test is performed with an osmometer.

Other options:

Option B: Ishihara plates are used to test colour vision. They help detect red-green colour blindness.

Option C: Jones test is used in watering eye. It uses fluorescein dye.

Option D: Goldmann's tonometry is used to measure intra-ocular pressure. It consists of a double prism mounted on a slit-lamp.

questions.question: You are conducting retrospective research on factors responsible for dry eye disorder. As a part of your study, you are looking through the files in the clinic of dry eye patients. Which among the following patients would not be included in your study?
options: A 26 year old patient showing decreased levels of lactoferrin in tear samples
A 20 year old patient showing tear film break up at 18-20 seconds
A 24 year old patient showing A pattern stain in Rose bengal staining
A 22 year old patient showing Schirmer test tear strip wet upto 9 mm
questions.answer: B. A 20 year old patient showing tear film break up at 18-20 seconds
questions.explanation:
A patient with tear film break up at 18-20 seconds is considered to be normal. All the other patients have dry eye.

Tear film break-up (BUT) time is the interval between a complete blink and the appearance of a first randomly distributed dry spot on the cornea. It is an indicator of the adequacy of the mucin component of tears.

Inference:

• 15-35 seconds - normal

• < 10 seconds- unstable tear film

Other options:

Option A: Tear samples can be assayed for the presence of markers known to be decreased (e.g. lactoferrin) or elevated (e.g. matrix metalloproteinase-9) in dry eye. This is known as tear constituent measurement.

Option C: A patient with A pattern on Rose Bengal staining has severe dry eye.

Option D: A patient with 9mm wet Schirmer strip has moderate dry eye.

questions.question: The findings of a test done in a patient under evaluation for dry eye are shown below. Identify the test.
questions.explanation:
The image above depicts lacrimal scintigraphy.

Lacrimal scintigraphy (dacryoscintigraphy) is used to assess the lacrimal drainage function. A radioactive tracer (technetium-99m) is instilled into the conjunctival sac. Its path is then visualised with an Anger gamma camera. It is useful for the evaulation of watering eye.

Other tests for evaluation of watering eye include regurgitation test, syringing, fluorescein dye disappearance test (FDDT), Jones dye test and dacryocystography.

Other options:

Option A: In regurgitation test, steady pressure with the index finger is applied above the medial palpebral ligament.

Option B: In dacryocystography, a radioopaque material is inserted into the lacrimal sac, following which X-rays are taken.

Option C: The image shows the Jones dye test.

questions.question: What is the site of blockage in congenital dacryocystitis?
questions.explanation:
The site of blockage in congenital dacryocystitis is the nasolacrimal duct.

Congenital dacryocystitis occurs due to the stasis of secretions in the lacrimal sac due to congenital blockage in the nasolacrimal duct. Membranous occlusion at its lower end near the valve of Hasner is the commonest cause.

The image below shows a neonate with congenital dacryocystitis.

questions.question: A mother noticed the following finding in her 3-month-old child. There is a history of watering and discharge from his right eye since birth. Which of the following is the best next step in the treatment?
questions.answer: C. Sac massage with topical antibiotics
questions.explanation:
The image showing right-sided swelling in the lacrimal sac area along with watering of the eye is suggestive of congenital dacryocystitis. Treatment for a 3-month-old child includes sac massage with topical antibiotics.

Congenital dacryocystitis is chronic inflammation of the lacrimal sac in newborn infants. It occurs due to congenital blockage of the nasolacrimal duct. More than 90% of patients with undergo spontaneous resolution by 1 year of age.

Treatment of congenital dacryocystitis depends on the age of the child:

• Less than 9 months: Massaging (Crigler’s massage which increases the hydrostatic pressure within the sac) and antibiotic eye drops

• 9 months to 4 years: Probing

• Older children (> 4 years): Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) gives the best result. In DCR, an opening is made into the nasal cavity from the lacrimal sac.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with watering from the right eye for 1 year. Syringing revealed a patent drainage system. Rest of the ocular examination was normal. A provisional diagnosis of lacrimal pump failure was made. Which of the following test will help in the confirmation of the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Lacrimal pump failure can be confirmed with dacryoscintigraphy.

Lacrimal pump failure means an inability of the lid muscles to push tears towards the punctum for drainage. It is also called functional obstruction and may be secondary to lower lid laxity or orbicularis muscle weakness (eg. facial nerve palsy. It is confirmed by dacryoscintigraphy, in which a radioactive tracer (technetium-99m) is instilled into the conjunctival sac and its path visualised with an Anger gamma camera. An atonic lacrimal sac is seen.

Note: In cases of partial obstruction of the lacrimal apparatus, forced injection of fluid into the canalicular system (dacryocystography) can overcome the obstruction sites and point to a diagnosis of lacrimal pump failure. Thus, dacryoscintigraphy is better for the confirmation of lacrimal pump failure.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman is being counseled for surgery for her long-standing dacryocystitis. Which of the following is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation:
The treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)

DCR involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. It re-establishes the lacrimal drainage and is hence the preferred surgery for chronic darcyocystectomy.

Chronic dacryocystitis is a long-standing inflammation of the lacrimal sac. Streptococcus hemolyticus and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common etiological agents. Initial treatment is with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents. Sequelae include lacrimal fistula formation and mucocele formation, which when infected, leads to pyocele formation and finally lacrimal fibrosis. Treatment of lacrimal sac fibrosis is dacryocystectomy. Treatment of lacrimal fistula is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).

questions.question: A patient with chronic dacryocystitis, refractory to the medical treatment, has been scheduled for dacryocystorhinostomy. Following the surgery, the sac would be draining into the _______.
questions.explanation:
After dacryocystorhinostomy, the lacrimal sac drains into the middle meatus.

Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. This allows tears to drain directly from the sac via a new low-resistance pathway into the middle meatus.

questions.question: What is the most common ocular manifestation in mumps?
questions.explanation:
The most common ocular manifestation in mumps is dacryocystadenitis.

Dacryocystadenitis, or inflammation of the lacrimal gland, is seen in mumps. It presents as a painful swelling in the lateral part of the upper lid.

questions.question: Which of the following structures does not pass through the superior orbital fissure?
questions.explanation:
The optic nerve (2nd cranial nerve) passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.

Anatomy of the orbit

Orbit is a pear-shaped cavity, the stalk of which is the optic canal. The volume of the orbit is 30 cc.

Walls of the orbit
Bones forming them

Roof

Lesser wing of the sphenoid

The orbital plate of the frontal bone

Lateral wall (strongest wall)

Greater wing of the sphenoid

Zygomatic bone

Floor (most frequently fractured wall)

Zygomatic bone

Maxillary bone

Palatine bone

Medial wall (thinnest wall)

Maxillary bone

Lacrimal bone

Ethmoid bone

Sphenoid bone

The image below shows the bones forming the orbit.

The inferior orbital fissure lies between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the maxilla, connecting the orbit to the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae. Through it run the maxillary nerve, the zygomatic nerve, and branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion, as well as the inferior ophthalmic vein.

questions.question: You are volunteering in a medical camp held in an orphanage. You see a kid with hypoplasia of the zygoma and mandible along with antimongoloid slant of palpebral fissures as shown below. These findings correspond to which of the following syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The given findings correspond to Treacher–Collins syndrome.

Treacher–Collins syndrome/Mandibulofacial dysostosis refers to a condition resulting from the hypoplasia of the zygoma and mandible.

Ocular features:

• Indistinct inferior orbital margin

• Coloboma of the lower eyelid

• Anti-mongoloid slant of palpebral fissures

Systemic features

• Macrostomia with a high-arched palate

• External ear deformity

• Bird-like face

The image below shows features of Treacher–Collins syndrome.

Craniofacial dysostosis/Crouzon syndrome refers to the premature closure of the coronal and sagittal sutures (brachycephaly—clover-leaf skull) associated with maxillary hypoplasia. Ocular associations include the following:

• Blue sclera

• Megalocornea

• Aniridia

• Glaucoma

• Cataract

• Ectopia lentis

• Optic nerve hypoplasia

The image below shows a baby with Crouzon syndrome.

Apert syndrome is the most severe form of craniosynostosis, involving premature closure of multiple cranial sutures (acrocephaly), along with syndactyly of the fingers and toes.

The image below shows the hands of a patient with Apert syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the clinical sequelae expected in a patient with orbital blowout fracture is false?
options: Anesthesia of the cheek is very common.
Emphysema of eyelids is more common with medial wall fracture.
Enophthalmos develops about 10 days after the injury.
Severe ocular damage is seen in most cases.
questions.answer: D. Severe ocular damage is seen in most cases.
questions.explanation:
Severe ocular damage associated with a "blowout" fracture is rare.

This is because a "blowout fracture" is nature’s way of protecting the globe from injury.

Clinical features of blow out fracture are as follows:

• Periorbital edema

• Paresthesia and anesthesia in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve (lower lid, cheek, side of the nose, upper lip, and upper teeth)

• Emphysema of the eyelids-more frequent with medial wall fractures

• Proptosis-seen initially due to orbital edema and hemorrhage.

• After about 10 days, as the edema decreases, the eyeball sinks backward and somewhat inferiorly, resulting in enophthalmos and mechanical ptosis.

• Double diplopia- diplopia in upward as well as downward gaze

questions.question: Two people who got in a brawl are brought to the emergency department because of severe facial injuries. In one of those patients, there is periorbital ecchymosis and anesthesia over the cheek. Orbital blowout fracture is suspected. What X-ray finding will confirm this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The X-ray finding seen in an orbital blowout fracture is hanging drop/tear-drop sign.

Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum. The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is Water’s view.

The optimal time for surgery following a blowout fracture is 10–14 days.

Indications for surgery in a blowout fracture are as follows:

• Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma

• A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum

• Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze

• Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

questions.question: All of the following are characteristic clinical findings that are associated with a history of blunt trauma to the eye, except:
questions.explanation:
Vossius ring, not Soemmering’s, is seen after blunt trauma to the eye

Soemmering’s ring refers to a thick ring of after cataract, also known as "secondary cataract." It is the opacity that persists or develops after extracapsular lens extraction.

Blunt trauma to the eye produces:

• Vossius ring - It is a circular ring of brown pigment seen on the anterior capsule. It occurs due to the striking of the contracted pupillary margin against the crystalline lens.

• Rosette cataract - It is the most typical form of concussion cataract.

• Commotio retinae (Berlin’s edema) - It manifests as milky white cloudiness involving a considerable area of the posterior pole with a "cherry-red spot" at foveola.

questions.question: What is the most common site of globe rupture following trauma?
questions.explanation:
The superonasal limbus is the most common site of globe rupture.

This occurs due to the contrecoup effect—the lower temporal quadrant is the most exposed to trauma; hence, the effect is seen in the superonasal limbus, which lies on the opposite side.

questions.question: In which of the following conditions is the following clinical finding seen?
questions.answer: B. Bilateral anterior cranial fossa fracture
questions.explanation:
The image shows bilateral periorbital ecchymoses, which is called the panda sign, and it is seen in bilateral anterior cranial fossa fracture. It is also known as panda eyes/raccoon eyes.

The pooling of blood surrounding the eyes is most commonly associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. This finding is typically not present during the initial evaluation and is delayed by 1 to 3 days. If bilateral, this finding is highly predictive of a basilar skull fracture.

questions.question: Clinical examination patients with which of the following conditions would show Dalen Fuchs Nodules?
questions.explanation:
Dalen Fuchs nodules are seen in sympathetic ophthalmitis and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease (VKH) syndrome.

These are local granulomas due to the proliferation of lymphocytes and epithelioid cells and are located between RPE and Bruch's membrane.

The image below shows Dalen Fuchs nodules.

questions.question: Which of the following views would you advise, so as to visualize the optic foramina?
questions.explanation:
The Rhese view in an X-ray scan helps in the visualization of the optic foramina.

The optic foramen/optic canal transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery.

Rhese view: for optic foramen

Other X-ray views of the orbit:

1. Caldwell's view: Occipitofrontal

Structures seen:

• Superior orbital fissure

• Greater and lesser wing of the sphenoid

• Ethmoid and frontal sinus

• Floor of the sella

2. Water's view:

• Occipitomeatal: floor of the orbit is seen (important in "blow-out" fractures)

• Occipitomental: maxillary sinus and floor of the orbit

3. Towne’ s view:

Structures seen

• Dorsum sellae of the sphenoid bone

• Inferior orbital fissure

questions.question: Heterochromia iridis may be caused by which of the following intraocular foreign bodies?
questions.explanation:
Heterochromia iridis may be caused by iron deposition.

Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. In siderosis bulbi, the iris is first stained greenish and later turns reddish brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

Chalcosis refers to the specific changes produced by the alloy of copper in the eye. Clinical features include the following:

• Kayser–Fleischer ring- a golden brown ring that occurs due to the deposition of copper in the Descemet’s membrane of the cornea.

• Sunflower cataract- produced by the deposition of copper under the anterior capsule of the lens. It is brilliant golden green in color and arranged like the petals of a sunflower.

The image below shows siderosis bulbi.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is most likely to produce this finding on CT?
questions.explanation:
The CT image shows hyperostosis of the lateral wall of the left orbit.

Hyperostosis causing lesions are:

1. Sphenoid wing meningioma

2. Fibrous dysplasia

3. Metastasis from cancer prostate

questions.question: A 30-year-old construction worker presented to the emergency department with complaints of pain and decreased vision over his right eye. He gives a history of accidental exposure with a cleaning agent that contains ammonia. Ocular examination finding is given below. According to the Roper-Hall system, what is the grade of chemical injury?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a grade II chemical injury. There is limbal ischaemia in the lower left quadrant involving <1/3 of the limbus and a hazy cornea with visible iris details.

The Roper–Hall system is used for the classification of chemical injuries to the eye.

Chemical injuries to the eye:

• Alkali burns are twice as common as acid burns.

• Alkalis tend to penetrate more deeply than acids, as the latter coagulate surface proteins, forming a protective barrier.

• Most commonly involved alkalis are ammonia, sodium hydroxide, and lime.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of bilateral proptosis in children?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of bilateral proptosis in children is neuroblastoma.

Most common cause:

Unilateral proptosis
Bilateral proptosis

In children: Orbital cellulitis
In children: Neuroblastoma and leukemia (chloroma)

In adults: Thyroid ophthalmopathy
In adults: Thyroid ophthalmopathy

The image below shows the bilateral proptosis.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions does not presents as pulsatile proptosis?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, hemangioma will not present with pulsatile proptosis.

Causes of pulsatile proptosis:

• Pulsating vascular lesions:

• Caroticocavernous fistula- most common

• Saccular aneurysm of ophthalmic artery

• Transmitted cerebral pulsations in conditions with a deficient orbital roof:

• Congenital meningocele/meningoencephalocele

• Neurofibromatosis

• Traumatic or operative hiatus

Causes of intermittent proptosis:

• Orbital varix- most common

• Periodic orbital edema

Causes of reducible proptosis:

• Orbital varix

• Hemangioma

• Caroticocavernous fistula

questions.question: A patient presents with unilateral non-pulsatile proptosis, which is compressible and increases on bending forward. No thrill or bruit is present. MRI shows a retrobulbar mass with enhancement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The likely diagnosis from the above clinical scenario is orbital varix.

The type of proptosis seen in orbital varix is non-pulsatile, intermittent, and reducible proptosis. On activities such as forward bending or lowering of the head, turning the head forcefully, hyperextension of the neck, and coughing, the varices fill up, causing proptosis, and then, they regress on shifting to a non-dependent position.

All the other conditions listed, namely, carotid cavernous fistula, orbital encephalocele, and neurofibromatosis, present with pulsatile proptosis.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man with a history of blunt trauma to the head 2 months earlier presented with rapidly progressive swelling, pain, and diminishing vision in the left eye. The physical examination of the left eye revealed chemosis and pulsating proptosis. A bruit could be heard with a stethoscope placed on the left temple. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of carotid–cavernous fistula.

All the given options are causes of proptosis following trauma, but among these, only a carotid-cavernous fistula presents with the classic triad:

1. Pulsatile proptosis

2. Chemosis

3. Bruit

Selective carotid angiography is the investigation of choice.

A carotid-cavernous fistula requires a definitive treatment, which currently involves the endovascular technique. The fistula can usually be occluded with a balloon or coil, without the sacrifice of the carotid artery.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions will present with pseudoproptosis?
questions.explanation:
Buphthalmos causes pseudoproptosis.

The other listed conditions, namely, pseudotumors, orbital hemorrhage, and cavernous sinus thrombosis, produce actual proptosis.

Pseudoproptosis is a condition in which the eyeball appears to be proptosed, but there is no actual forward displacement.

Causes of pseudoproptosis:

• Buphthalmos is the term used when the eyeball enlarges in children who develop congenital glaucoma before the age of 3 years.

• Axial high myopia- increase in the size of the eyeball in myopia causes pseudoproptosis

• Retraction of the upper lid

• Enophthalmos of the opposite eye

questions.question: A 48-year-old lady presents with unilateral mild axial proptosis. On examination, the following nail and skin changes were seen as shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step of investigation?
options: CT scan to rule out meningioma
USG to rule out orbital pseudotumor
T3 and T4 measurement to check for thyrotoxicosis
questions.answer: C. T3 and T4 measurement to check for thyrotoxicosis
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario along with the image showing thyroid acropachy and dermopathy is suggestive of Graves' disease. The most appropriate next step of the investigation is T3 and T4 measurement to check for thyrotoxicosis.

Thyroid ophthalmopathy is the most common cause of proptosis in adults, which may present as unilateral or bilateral, axial or non-axial, painful or painless proptosis.

The image given below shows unilateral proptosis in the right eye.

questions.question: What is the most common clinical feature of Graves’ ophthalmopathy?
questions.explanation:
Dalrymple’s sign (retraction of the upper lids) is the most common clinical feature of Graves’ ophthalmopathy. It is caused by the overaction of Muller’s muscle. Levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) recession surgery may be done to correct upper lid retraction.

The image given below shows Dalrymple’s sign (retraction of the upper lids) in the right eye:

NOSPECS classification by Werner reflecting the severity of thyroid ophthalmopathy.

Class

1
Only signs, no symptoms (signs limited to upper lid retraction, stare, lid lag, and proptosis of up to 22 mm)

2
Soft tissue involvement (symptom and signs)

3

4

5

6

NOSPECS: No signs or symptoms; Only signs; Soft tissue; Proptosis; Extraocular muscle; Cornea; Sight loss

questions.question: A 40-year-old male presents with heat intolerance and weight loss for the past few weeks. He has lost 10 kgs despite having an increased appetite. On examination, he has a fine tremor of the hands, and his thyroid is enlarged. Lab investigations reveal low TSH and elevated T3 and T4. What is the most common ocular motility defect seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Grave's disease. The most common ocular motility defect seen in Grave's disease is elevator restriction.

It occurs due to the fibrotic contracture of the inferior rectus muscle. The inferior rectus muscle has to relax during the elevation of the eye. The fibrosis of the muscle restricts its relaxation and thus elevation of the eye is restricted.

There is an inability to look up (in both adducted and abducted positions) along with esotropia (fibrosis of the medial rectus).

Only the belly of the muscle is involved in thyroid myopathy; the tendon is characteristically spared.

Ocular motility restriction in order of frequency is as follows:

• Elevation defect

• Abduction defect, due to fibrosis of the medial rectus

• Depression defect, due to fibrosis of the superior rectus

• Adduction defect, due to fibrosis of the lateral rectus

questions.question: What is known as the infrequent blinking seen in Graves’ ophthalmopathy?
questions.explanation: Infrequent blinking is known as Stellwag’s sign.

questions.question: A lady is referred from the medicine department for an eye exam due to gritty sensation in her eyes. She is a known case of hyperthyroidism. Her ophthalmic examination shows the following finding along with the inability to look up. Which of the following is not a treatment modality for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of grittiness in the eyes (due to ocular dryness), hyperthyroidism and the image showing exophthalmos are suggestive of Graves ophthalmopathy.

Beta-blockers are not indicated in the treatment of graves ophthalmopathy, however, they are used in the symptomatic management of hyperthyroidism.

Treatment of thyroid ophthalmopathy:

(A) Non-surgical management

• Systemic steroids- These form the mainstay of the treatment. Oral, intravenous or orbital steroid injections can be used depending upon patient indications. (Option B)

• Radiotherapy- Orbital radiation given in a dose of 2000 rads over 10-14 days can be considered in cases where steroids are ineffective/ contraindicated. It is contraindicated in cases of extensive thyroid eye disease as it can worsen it. (Option A)

• Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor)- is used for persistent, corticosteroid-resistant disease or non-response to first-line treatment. It is effective in reducing proptosis and clinical activity in patients.

(B) Surgical management:

• Orbital decompression- It may be required for an acutely progressive optic neuropathy and/or exposure keratitis, in patients not responding to aggressive steroid therapy. (Option D)

• Extraocular muscle surgery- Inferior rectus recession is the most commonly performed surgery. These should be performed after the orbital decompression since decompression may alter extraocular motility. Extraocular muscle surgery helps in achieving a binocular single vision in the primary gaze and reading position.

• Eyelid surgery- This is done to correct eyelid retraction. Various surgeries that can be performed are mullerectomy, levator recession/ disinsertion, scleral grafts with LPS recession, recession of lower eyelid retractors, and blepharoplasty.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man with a history of repeated pain over the medial canthus and chronic use of nasal decongestants presents to the OPD with high-grade fever and chills, headache, and bilateral proptosis. On further history, it is noted that the proptosis began in the right eye, and a few days later, the left eye was also affected. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Pain over the medial canthus and use of nasal decongestants indicate that the patient was suffering from sinusitis, which can spread to cause orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, or panopthalmitis.

The differentiating feature here is the presentation pattern and bilaterality of the proptosis.

In cavernous sinus thrombosis, proptosis is initially unilateral but soon becomes bilateral due to the spread of infection to the contralateral sinus through intercavernous communication. Also, cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with high-grade fever with chills, rigor, and headache.

On the other hand, orbital cellulitis and panophthalmitis are unilateral conditions.

questions.question: Among the following, which muscle is affected first in cavernous sinus thrombosis?
questions.explanation:
The first muscle to be affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis is the lateral rectus.

Ophthalmoplegia in cavernous sinus thrombosis occurs in the following sequence:

• 6th nerve palsy (lateral rectus palsy) occurring first of all as it passes through the cavernous sinus.

• 3rd and 4th nerves are involved later as they are related to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.

questions.question: MRI of a patient revealed features of right cavernous sinus thrombosis. Which of the following would not be seen in this patient?
options: Constricted right pupil in response to light
questions.answer: A. Constricted right pupil in response to light
questions.explanation: Dilation of the pupil will be seen in cavernous sinus thrombosis due to the involvement of the 3rd cranial nerve.

questions.question: A 40-year-old male presented with a 1-day history of fever, headache, and bilateral periorbital and mid-facial swelling. He had attempted to burst a furuncle in the inner margin of his right nostril 2 days back. On examination, marked facial and periorbital swelling with chemosis and proptosis are noted. MRI is suggestive of bilateral cavernous sinus thrombosis. Which of the following veins is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Infection from the dangerous area of the face (the area from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose, including the nose and maxilla) spreads to the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic veins.

questions.question: A child is brought to the OPD with fever, severe pain, and swelling of the left eye. He was bitten by a dog over the eye a few days back. On examination, there is mild proptosis with restriction of ocular movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of orbital cellulitis.

It is the acute inflammation of the soft tissues of the orbit behind the orbital septum. It can occur due to exogenous infection (penetrating injuries) or extension of an endogenous infection (dental infection).

It presents with fever, severe pain, and eye swelling which increases with movement, chemosis, axial proptosis, and restriction of ocular movements. Complications include subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and general septicemia.

The image shows orbital cellulitis in the left eye.

Option B: Endophthalmitis is defined as the inflammation of the inner structures of the eyeball, i.e., uveal tissue and retina, associated with the pouring of exudates into the vitreous cavity, anterior chamber, and posterior chamber.

Option C: Panophthalmitis is an intense purulent inflammation of the whole eyeball, including Tenon’s capsule.

Option D: Preseptal cellulitis refers to infection of the subcutaneous tissues anterior to the orbital septum. In this condition, proptosis is absent and ocular movements are normal.

questions.question: An 8-year-old child presents with fever and painful swelling of the left eye. He is being treated for acute ethmoiditis for 5 days. On examination, the visual acuity in the left eye is 6/12, there is chemosis, axial proptosis, limitation of ocular motility in all directions, and RAPD. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis of this patient is orbital cellulitis.

Orbital cellulitis is the most common cause of unilateral proptosis in children. Ethmoidal sinusitis is the most common cause of orbital cellulitis in children.

Orbital cellulitis presents with pain, lid edema, erythema, chemosis, and axial proptosis. Decreased ocular motility and elevated intraocular pressure can be seen. Systemic symptoms include malaise and fever. A rapid loss of vision is due to the involvement of the optic nerve. With posterior exenteration cavernous sinus thrombosis, subdural empyema, and intracranial abscess develop.

WARNING SIGNS: Dilated pupil, marked ophthalmoplegia, loss of vision, afferent pupillary defect, papilledema, and violaceous lids.

questions.question: What is the surgery of choice for panophthalmitis?
questions.explanation:
The surgery of choice for panophthalmitis is an evisceration. Evisceration gives a better cosmetic outlook after the surgery and is hence preferred. Enucleation is contraindicated in panophthalmitis due to the risk of meningitis through the exposed meningeal sheath of the optic nerve stump.

Some definitions:

• Evisceration- removal of the contents of the eyeball, leaving behind the sclera. It is done in panophthalmitis.

• Enucleation- removal of the eyeball, with the maximum part of the optic nerve. Extraocular muscles are left behind. The length of the optic nerve removed is 10 to 15 mm. Absolute indications for enucleation are retinoblastoma and malignant melanoma.

• Exenteration- mutilating surgery in which all the contents of the orbits along with the periorbita are removed. It is indicated for malignant tumors arising from the orbital structures or spreading from the eyeball.

• Debulking- reduction of as much of the bulk (volume) of a tumor as possible. Nowadays, debulking of the orbit is preferred over exenteration.

questions.question: A 72-year-old female presents with normal visual acuity, diminished corneal sensation, and global impairment of ocular motility of the right eye. The patient also has a severe boring headache. The MRI shows an enhancing mass within the right cavernous sinus. The pain and ophthalmoplegia respond dramatically to corticosteroid therapy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The patient presents with acute ophthalmoplegia with the involvement of ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve that responds promptly to steroid therapy. The most likely diagnosis is Tolosa-Hunt syndrome.

It is an idiopathic, sterile inflammation that primarily affects the cavernous sinus. It is characterized by painful acute ophthalmoplegia with or without the involvement of the optic nerve and the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

The pain is described as gnawing or boring and may precede ophthalmoplegia.

The inflammation and pain in patients typically responds rapidly and dramatically to corticosteroid therapy. However, it is a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.question: The clinical distinction between a cavernous sinus syndrome and an orbital apex syndrome is best made by the dysfunction of which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation:
The clinical distinction between a cavernous sinus syndrome and an orbital apex syndrome is made by the dysfunction of the optic nerve (CN II).

The optic nerve passes through the optic canal and does not enter the cavernous sinus. Patients with orbital apex syndrome manifest complete ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, decreased corneal sensation, and vision loss. They usually develop optic nerve signs such as relative afferent pupillary defect. Proptosis is often present, but patients do not always complain of pain.

questions.question: A patient was being evaluated for retro-orbital pain in the ward. After multiple investigations, he was diagnosed with Tolosa-Hunt syndrome. Which of the following findings will not be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy due to 6th cranial nerve involvement is seen in Tolosa–Hunt syndrome, not contralateral.

Tolosa–Hunt syndrome refers to idiopathic, nonspecific, granulomatous inflammation, involving the superior orbital fissure and/or orbital apex and/or cavernous sinus. It is a unilateral eye condition.

Clinically, it manifests as painful ophthalmoplegia and depending on the extent of involvement, it may present as superior orbital fissure syndrome or orbital apex syndrome.

Superior orbital fissure syndrome is characterized by the following:

• Pain, typically labeled as retro-orbital ache

• Sensory loss/disturbances in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the 5th cranial nerve

• Ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia due to the involvement of the 3rd, 4th, and 6th cranial nerve involvement

• Ptosis, due to 3rd nerve paralysis

Orbital apex syndrome includes the following:

• Features of superior orbital fissure syndrome described above

• Features of optic nerve involvement, i.e., early visual loss and afferent pupillary defect.

questions.question: Which among the following is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults?
questions.explanation:
Malignant melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults.

Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children.

questions.question: Which is the most common primary malignant tumor of the lid?
questions.explanation:
The most common primary malignant tumor of the lid is basal cell carcinoma.

The second most common tumor of the lid is squamous cell carcinoma

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common lid malignancy in HIV patients?
questions.explanation:
Kaposi sarcoma is the commonest malignancy of the lid and conjunctiva in HIV patients.

It appears as a violaceous non-tender nodule on the eyelid or conjunctiva. It is a rapidly growing acquired neoplasm composed of malignant stromal cells densely vascularized by blood vessels of capillary size.

The typical lesion appears as an expanding, bright red subepithelial mass that projects through and replaces the overlying conjunctival epithelium. Spontaneous bleeding leading to bloody tears or a subconjunctival hematoma is relatively common.

Conjunctival Kaposi’s sarcoma can be treated by excision, cryotherapy, radiation therapy (external beam or contact therapy), chemotherapy, or topical or intralesional interferon-α.

questions.question: Which of the following cannot be used in the management of the clinical condition shown below?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a capillary hemangioma involving the left upper lid and periocular area. Interferon beta is not used in the management of capillary hemangioma. However, note that interferon alfa-2a is used in resistant cases.

A capillary haemangioma is the most common tumor of the orbit and periorbital area in childhood.

It may present as small isolated lesions or large masses that can cause visual impairment (due to mechanical ptosis and the resulting sensory deprivation amblyopia), systemic effects (severe thrombocytopenia), or exist as part of PHACE syndrome (Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangioma, Arterial lesions, Cardiac abnormalities, Eye or Endocrine abnormalities)

30% of lesions resolve by the age of 3 years and about 75% by the age of 7.

Indications for treatment are:

1. Visual (amblyopia, astigmatism, occlusion, strabismus)

2. Cosmesis

3. Optic nerve compression

4. Exposure keratopathy

Treatment options include:

• Beta blockers- oral propranolol, topical timolol.

• Steroids- intralesional triamcinolone or betamethasone, topical clobetasol, systemic steroids.

• Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine- for steroid-resistant sight-threatening lesions

• Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser.

questions.question: An 8-year old child presented with right-sided proptosis. Biopsy of the orbital mass was done and histopathological examination revealed this picture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS). Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood.

40% of rhabdomyosarcomas develop in the head and neck, and they are the most common primary orbital malignancy in children but are still a rare condition. The older age of the child presenting with proptosis suggests rhabdomyosarcoma (average age 7 to 8 years) than retinoblastoma (average age at presentation is 18 months).

The histopathology shows elongated to round spindle cells with features of skeletal muscle at different stages of maturation with highly eosinophilic cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei – the embryonal type of rhabdomyosarcoma

Immunohistochemistry is useful in identifying skeletal muscle proteins, such as alpha-actin, myosin, desmin, and myoglobin
