Rhabdomyosarcoma shows a strong tendency for local invasion, local recurrence, and hematogenous and lymphatic metastases.

Decision-making for management is based on histopathologic confirmation as well as the staging of orbital RMS, which includes imaging (MRI of primary tumor, chest-CT, Tc bone scan), pathology, and work-up for metastases(bone marrow biopsy).

Treatment options include chemotherapy (vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and actinomycin D) and radiotherapy.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presents with jaundice. He was recently diagnosed with malignant melanoma of the uvea but did not receive proper treatment due to the prevalent pandemic situation. Investigations reveal liver secondaries. What would be the ideal line of management?
questions.explanation:
The spread of malignant melanoma of the uvea outside the orbit is treated with enucleation + chemotherapy + immunotherapy.

Orbital spread of the malignant melanoma necessitates exenteration but metastasis elsewhere can be treated by enucleation, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy.

questions.question: A father has noticed that his child's left pupil appears white as shown below. Worried about this, the father consults an ophthalmologist. All of the following should be included in the differential diagnosis except:
questions.explanation:
The child has leukocoria and congenital glaucoma is not to be included in the differential diagnosis.

Various conditions, other than retinoblastoma, which present as leukocoria are collectively called pseudoglioma.

Differential diagnosis of leukocoria:

1. Retinoblastoma

2. Congenital cataract

3. Coloboma of the choroid

4. Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous

5. Toxocara infestation

6. Norrie disease

7. Coat's exudative retinopathy

Intraocular pressure (IOP) is usually raised in retinoblastoma and lowered in pseudoglioma.

questions.question: Retinoblastoma arises from which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Retinoblastoma (also called glioma retinae) arises from the neurosensory retina. It is a proliferation of neural cells that have failed to evolve normally.

Tumours are composed of small basophilic cells (retinoblasts), with large hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm.

It is of 4 types:

1. Endophytic (into the vitreous) with seeding of tumor cells throughout the eye

2. Exophytic (into the subretinal space) leading to retinal detachment

3. Mixed type

4. Retinocytoma: retina may be diffusely infiltrated

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common clinical presentation of retinoblastoma?
questions.explanation:
The most common clinical presentation of retinoblastoma is leukocoria plus strabismus.

Clinical features of retinoblastoma:

• Present within the first two years of life

• Leukocoria

• Strabismus

• Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma

• Orbital inflammation mimicking orbital or pre-septal cellulitis.

• Orbital invasion or visible extraocular growth may occur in neglected cases.

• Metastatic disease involving regional lymph nodes and the brain before the detection of ocular involvement is rare.

Signs:

• An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

• An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

• An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

• Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

• Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

• MRI of the orbit + brain

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy was brought by his parents with concern about being increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On examination, there is leukocoria with an absence of the red reflex in the left eye. As further workup reveals a tumor, the eye is enucleated and the microscopic appearance is as shown in the image. Molecular analysis of the tumor indicates loss of cell cycle control in the tumor cells. Where is the responsible gene located?
questions.explanation:
The histology showing Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes and clinical history of white reflex point towards a diagnosis of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is due to mutation in Rb gene located on chromosome 13q14.

Retinoblastoma was first cancer known to be directly associated with a genetic abnormality.

 The HPE image below shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, the clustering of small blue cuboidal or short columnar cells around a central lumen.

questions.question: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis describes the occurrence of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Knudson's two-hit hypothesis describes the occurrence of retinoblastoma.

Knudson's hypothesis can be stated as follows:

• Two mutations (hits), involving both alleles of RB are required to produce retinoblastoma.

• In familial retinoblastoma, one of the pair of alleles of RB1 is mutated in all the cells of the body. When a further mutagenic event ("second hit" according to the "two-hit" hypothesis proposed by Knudson) affects the second allele, the cell may then undergo malignant transformation. A large majority of these children develop bilateral and multifocal tumors.

• In sporadic cases, both RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast (two hits).

Familial retinoblastoma patients also have a predisposition to non-ocular cancers because of the presence of the mutation in all cells, such as pinealoblastoma (usually before the age of 5 years), osteosarcomas, soft tissue sarcomas, and melanomas.

Note:

Trilateral retinoblastoma = Pinealoblastoma + Bilateral retinoblastoma

questions.question: Why would an ophthalmologist use the Reese-Ellsworth classification for retinoblastoma?
options: For the management of the tumor
For the staging of the tumor
For the assessment of the survival of the eye after local therapy
For the assessment of the survival of the patient after surgery
questions.answer: C. For the assessment of the survival of the eye after local therapy
questions.explanation:
Reese–Ellsworth classification is used in predicting which eye would survive the local therapy (cryotherapy, photocoagulation, plaque radiation therapy) and retain useful vision.

Cryotherapy is used for retinoblastoma lesions anterior to the equator and photocoagulation for lesions posterior to the equator.

Group
Prognosis for maintenance of sight
Features

1
Very favorable

• Solitary tumor, <4DD, at or behind the equator

• Multiple tumors, all <4DD, all at or behind the equator

2
Favorable

• Solitary tumor, 4–10 DD, at or behind the equator

• Multiple tumors, all 4–10DD all behind the equator

3
Possible

• Any lesion anterior to the equator

• Solitary tumor, >10DD behind the equator

4
Unfavorable

• Multiple tumors, some >10 DD

• Any lesion extending anteriorly to ora serrata

5
Highly unfavorable

• Massive tumors involving more than one half of the retina

• Vitreous seeding

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy who presented with strabismus and leukocoria is suspected to have retinoblastoma. A B-scan detects multiple endophytic masses with calcifications, the largest measuring 6DD, and the smallest measuring 4 DD. CT scan reveals intraocular foci of calcifications and no other anomaly. The ophthalmologist decides to use chemo-reduction and local therapy to treat this child. According to Reese-Ellsworth classification, this belongs to which group?
questions.explanation:
Multiple tumors of 4-10 DD in size behind the equator belong to group 2.

Group
Prognosis for maintenance of sight
Features

1
Very favorable

• Solitary tumor, <4DD, at or behind the equator

• Multiple tumors, all <4DD, all at or behind the equator

2
Favorable

• Solitary tumor, 4–10 DD, at or behind the equator

• Multiple tumors, all 4–10DD all behind the equator

3
Possible

• Any lesion anterior to equator

• Solitary tumor, >10DD behind equator

4
Unfavorable

• Multiple tumors, some >10 DD

• Any lesion extending anteriorly to ora serrata

5
Highly unfavorable

• Massive tumors involving more than one half of the retina

• Vitreous seeding

questions.question: What is the treatment of choice when retinoblastoma involves the optic nerve?
questions.explanation:
Optic nerve involvement is treated by enucleation + adjuvant chemotherapy + radiotherapy

Indications for enucleation [Group E tumor - according to the International Classification of Retinoblastoma (ICRB)]:

• Tumor involves more than half of the retina

• Optic nerve involved

• Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

Chemotherapy commonly used is a three-drug regimen containing vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide.

questions.question: What is the treatment of choice for anterior lesions of retinoblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Cryotherapy is used for anterior lesions of retinoblastoma.

Photocoagulation for posterior lesions of retinoblastoma.

questions.question: The most common secondaries in choroid are from _____.
questions.explanation:
The most common secondaries in choroid originate from the breast (overall and in females), and lungs (in males).

Examination shows the elevation of the retina, usually at the posterior pole. It is usually bilateral.

Metastases are usually treated with systemic chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Radiotherapy may also be given.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the actions of the muscle marked in the figure?
questions.explanation:
The muscle marked in the above image is the superior oblique.

Actions of the superior oblique:

• Intorsion

• Depression

• Abduction

Longest extraocular muscle: Superior oblique

Shortest extraocular muscle: Inferior oblique

The primary action of a muscle is its major effect when the eye is in the primary position.

Subsidiary actions are the additional effects; these depend on the position of the eye.

The spiral of Tillaux is an imaginary line joining the insertions of the four recti and is an important anatomical landmark when performing surgery.

questions.question: Which of the following pair of muscles are responsible for the intorsion of the eyeball?
questions.answer: A. Superior rectus and superior oblique
questions.explanation:
The muscles producing intorsion of the eyeball are the superior rectus and superior oblique.

Extorsion of the eyeball is due to the action of the inferior oblique (major) and the inferior rectus muscle.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs constitute yoke muscles?
options: Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR)
Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior oblique (IO)
Right medial rectus (MR) and left medial rectus (MR)
Right medial rectus (MR) and right lateral rectus (LR)
questions.answer: A. Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR)
questions.explanation:
Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR) are the yoke muscle pair for levodepression.

The term "yoke muscles" refers to contralateral synergists. Includes a pair of muscles, one from each eye, which contract simultaneously during version movements.

Examples are:

• Right MR and Left LR for levoversion

• Right LR and Left MR for dextroversion

An easy method to determine other yoke muscle pairs:

Just take the opposite of each word-

Left → Right

Superior → Inferior

Oblique → Rectus

“Left SO and Right IR” are a yoke muscle pair.

Similarly, the following are yoke muscle pairs:

• Right IO and Left SR - Levoelevation

• Right SR and Left IO - Dextroelevation

• Right IR and Left SO - Dextrodepression

questions.question: During ocular motility, increased flow of innervation to the contracting muscle is accompanied by a decreased flow of innervation to the relaxing antagonist muscle. This statement describes which law?
questions.explanation: The above statement elucidates Sherrington's Law of reciprocal innervation.

questions.question: You are an intern posted in the ophthalmology department. You are asked to check the cardinal fields of gaze to check the range of extraocular movements. How many cardinal fields are there?
questions.explanation:
There are six cardinal positions (fields) of gaze. These are the positions that allow examination of each of the twelve extraocular muscles.

They are as follows:

• Dextroversion (right lateral rectus and left medial rectus)

• Laevoversion (left lateral rectus and right medial rectus)

• Dextroelevation (right superior rectus and left inferior oblique)

• Laevoelevation (left superior rectus and right inferior oblique)

• Dextrodepression (right inferior rectus and left superior oblique)

• Laevodepression (left inferior rectus and right superior oblique)

Note: There are 3 other positions, namely, normal primary position, supraversion, and infraversion. These are, however, not cardinal positions as the action of the muscles causing these positions can be elicited by the 6 cardinal positions themselves.

The image below illustrates the 6 cardinal positions of gaze.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines saccades?
questions.answer: A. Sudden jerky conjugate eye movements
questions.explanation:
Saccades are sudden, jerky eye movements that occur as the gaze shifts from one object to another.

They are performed to bring the image of an object quickly on the fovea.

The image below shows saccadic movement of the eyeball

Eye movements that have a supranuclear control:

1. Saccades

2. Pursuits- smooth eye movements

3. Vergence movement system- slow, disconjugate movements

4. Vestibular eye movement- compensate for the effects of head movements

5. Optokinetic system- during sustained head rotation

6. Position maintenance system- consist of rapid micromovements such as flicks and drifts

questions.question: An ophthalmologist tests a particular phenomenon using the instrument shown below. Which of the following statements is false regarding the same?
options: The phenomenon is a physiological one
Frontal lobe controls the slow pursuit movement
Reversal of optokinetic nystagmus, in congenital motor nystagmus
questions.answer: B. Frontal lobe controls the slow pursuit movement
questions.explanation:
The given image shows an optokinetic drum used to elicit optokinetic nystagmus (OKN). The parieto-occipital lobe controls the slow pursuit component, whereas the frontal lobes control the saccadic component.

OKN is normal physiological nystagmus in response to motion/continuously moving objects. It occurs in response to a repetitive visual stimulus moved across the visual field. The slow phase occurs in the direction of the moving stimulus; the fast phase occurs as a saccadic refixation movement in the opposite direction. In patients with congenital motor nystagmus, a reversal of the OKN response may occur. An OKN response elicited in a person who feigns visual loss indicates that visual input is present and is a malingerer.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a nystagmoid movement?
questions.explanation:
All are nystagmoid movements except optokinetic.

 Optokinetic nystagmus is a physiological nystagmus.

Nystagmoid movements:

• Ocular flutter

• Ocular bobbing

• Opsoclonus

• Superior oblique myokymia

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presented with progressive diminution of vision, headache, and unsteadiness of gait. A comprehensive clinical evaluation revealed coarse, left-beating nystagmus with leftward gaze and a fine primary-position right-beating nystagmus which increased on rightward gaze, consistent with Brun's nystagmus. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Bruns nystagmus is an unusual type of bilateral nystagmus most commonly occurring in patients with cerebellopontine angle tumors.

It is caused by the combination of slow, large-amplitude nystagmus (gaze paretic nystagmus) when looking towards the side of the lesion, and rapid, small amplitude nystagmus (vestibular nystagmus) when looking away from the side of the lesion.

Option A- Cerebellar lesions and Arnold–Chiari malformation: downbeat nystagmus

Options C and D- Arnold–Chiari malformation and demyelination syndromes: periodic alternating nystagmus (left beating nystagmus->null phase->right beating nystagmus->null phase).

questions.question: Which of the following is a wrong statement regarding diplopia?
options: Anisometropia is a cause for binocular diplopia.
Crossed diplopia occurs in convergent squint.
Incipient cataract is a cause for uniocular diplopia.
Harmonious diplopia refers to uncrossed binocular diplopia.
questions.answer: B. Crossed diplopia occurs in convergent squint.
questions.explanation:
Crossed diplopia is seen in a divergent squint, as in medial rectus paralysis.

Binocular diplopia: Simultaneous perception of two images of a single object when seen by both eyes.

Causes:

• Anisometropia

• Paralysis of extraocular muscles; commonest

• Mechanical restriction of movements

Types:

 Uncrossed—Harmonious

• False image on the same side of the deviation

• Seen in convergent squint

Crossed—Unharmonious

• False image on the opposite side of the deviation

• Seen in divergent squint

Uniocular diplopia: Simultaneous perception of two images of a single object when seen by a single eye.

Causes:

• Subluxated clear lens

• Subluxated intraocular lens (IOL)

• Double pupil

• Incipient cataract

• Keratoconus

questions.question: Hirschberg test is used to detect which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The Hirschberg test is used to detect squint.

The Hirschberg test gives a rough objective estimate of the angle of manifest strabismus. A pen torch is shone into the eyes from arm’s length, and the patient is asked to fixate on the light. The corneal reflection of the light will be (more or less) centered in the pupil of the fixating eye but will be decentred in a squinting eye, in the direction opposite to that of the deviation. The distance of the corneal light reflection from the center of the pupil is noted; each millimeter of the deviation is approximately equal to 7°.

questions.question: As an intern posted in the ophthalmology department, you are performing Hirschberg's test on a patient who is being evaluated for strabismus. The finding observed is shown below. What is the angle of deviation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
From the given image of a Hirschberg test, it can be inferred that the patient has 90 prism dioptres (PD) of exotropia.

On the Hirschberg test, if the light reflection is on the nasal limbus, it means 45 degrees exotropia. One degree is equal to 2 PD (prism dioptre). Therefore, 45 degrees exotropia would mean 90 PD exotropia in the right eye.

questions.question: You are evaluating a case of strabismus in a 3-year-old child. Which of the following tests would you use to assess binocular single vision?
questions.explanation:
Binocular single vision is tested by a synoptophore.

Binocular single vision is the state of simultaneous vision, which is achieved by the coordinated use of both eyes so that separate and slightly dissimilar images arising in each eye are appreciated as a single image by the process of fusion.

The synoptophore compensates for the angle of squint and allows stimuli to be presented to both eyes simultaneously. It can thus be used to investigate the potential for binocular function in the presence of a manifest squint and is of particular value in assessing young children (from age 3 years), who generally find the test process enjoyable. It can also detect suppression.

questions.question: Which grade of binocular vision does the following image represent?
questions.explanation: The given image depicts Grade II of binocular vision, fusion.

questions.question: You are an intern posted in the ophthalmology department where you are observing a patient subjected to the Worth’s four-dot test. The patient is suffering from left suppression. Which of the following images would he most likely see?
questions.explanation:
The patient will see 2 red lights as shown in image C as he is suffering from left suppression.

Worth's four-dot test is a sensory function test. A box is viewed which has four lights: one red, two green, and one white. The patient has to wear red-green goggles.

Inference:

• A: Normal—All 4 lights seen

• B: Abnormal retinal correspondence—All 4 lights seen in the presence of manifest squint

• C: Left Suppression—2 red lights seen

• D: Right suppression—3 green lights seen

• E: Diplopia—5 lights seen (2 red, 3 green)

questions.question: While evaluating a case of squint, an ophthalmologist does a forced duction test. What is the use of this test?
questions.answer: A. To detect ocular muscle palsy
questions.explanation:
Forced duction test (FDT) is done to find out ocular muscle palsy.

It is performed to differentiate between the incomitant squint due to paralysis of the extraocular muscle and that due to the mechanical restriction of the ocular movements.

Forced duction test:

• Positive in cases of incomitant squint due to mechanical restriction

• Negative in cases of extraocular muscle palsy

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?
options: Direct cover test is helpful in detecting presence of heterophoria.
Alternate cover test helps to differentiate concomitant squint from paralytic squint.
Cover-uncover test confirms the presence of manifest squint.
In direct cover test, the squinted eye is covered and normal eye is uncovered.
questions.answer: B. Alternate cover test helps to differentiate concomitant squint from paralytic squint.
questions.explanation: Alternate cover test helps in differentiating concomitant squint from paralytic squint is a true statement. In a concomitant squint, the eye moves rapidly to fixate, whereas in a paralytic squint, the eye will not move to fixate.

questions.question: A patient presented to an ophthalmologist with complaints of crowding of words, while reading for long hours. The results of the test that was performed are shown below What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given test is a Maddox rod test, and the pattern of the appearance of white dot/light in relation to the red line denotes a case of left eye exophoria. In the given image, the above image refers to the examiner's view and the below image refers to the patient's view.

The Maddox rod can be used to test for horizontal and vertical deviations, and when used in conjunction with another Maddox rod, for cyclo-deviations.

Interpretation:

To test for horizontal deviations, the Maddox rod is placed in front of one eye (for this example, the left eye) with the cylinders in the horizontal direction. The patient fixates a point source of light and then sees a vertical red line with the left eye and white dot/light with the right eye:

• Orthophoria: if the light/dot superimposes the line.

• Exo-deviation/exophoria: In this example, light/dot is on the left side of the line (rod placed on left eye)

• Eso-deviation/esophoria: if the light was on the right side of the line (rod placed on left eye)

Maddox Rod Test involves the use of a Maddox rod and the Maddox tangent scale. It uses a specially constructed device, consisting of a series of parallel cylinders, that converts a point source of light into a line image. The optical properties of the cylinders cause the streak of light to be situated 90° to the orientation of the parallel cylinders.

In the image given below, the interpretation of the result is based on how the patient visualizes it. It would appear to be crossed to the patient. Pictorial representation of the eyes are as seen by the examiner. Imagine you are looking through a Maddox rod over your left eye while interpreting the images.

questions.question: A child is brought by her parents to the OPD with complaints of crossed eyes as shown below. By doing a simple torchlight test you conclude that the child has pseudostrabismus and the inter-pupillary distance is normal. Which of the following can be associated with the child's condition?
questions.explanation:
The child has pseudoesotropia (apparent convergent squint) which is associated with negative angle kappa and epicanthal folds.

Pseudostrabismus—apparent squint (visual axes are parallel, but eyes seem to have a squint)

Types:

• Pseudoesotropia

• Apparent convergent squint

• Prominent epicanthal fold

• Negative angle kappa

• Pseudoexotropia

• Apparent divergent squint

• Hypertelorism

• Positive angle kappa - due to retinopathy of prematurity, hypermetropia

Few definitions:

• Orthophoria- implies perfect ocular alignment in the absence of any stimulus for fusion

• Heterophoria ("phoria")- implies a tendency of the eyes to deviate when fusion is blocked (latent squint)

• Heterotropia ("tropia")- implies a manifest deviation in which the visual axes do not intersect at the point of fixation

• Hypertropia- upward displacement of one eye relative to the other is termed as hypertropia and a latent upward imbalance, a hyperphoria

• Hypotropia- downward displacement is termed a hypotropia and a latent imbalance, a hypophoria

questions.question: A child presents to the OPD with a mild squint. The rest of the history is quite insignificant. On examination, Hirschberg's corneal reflex test is found to be normal. All other eye parameters are also normal except for hypertelorism. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pseudoexotropia.

Features of Pseudoexotropia:

• Normal Hirschberg's corneal reflex test

• Apparent divergent squint

• Associated with hypertelorism/a positive angle kappa.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is least likely to present with diplopia?
questions.explanation:
Latent squint does not always present with diplopia.

Heterophoria (Latent squint) is a condition in which the tendency of the eyes to deviate is kept latent by fusion. When the influence of fusion is removed, the visual axis of one eye deviates away.

Types:

• Esophoria-convergent

• Exophoria-divergent

• Hyperphoria-deviation upwards

• Hypophoria-deviation downwards

• Cyclophoria-rotation around AP axis

Symptoms:

• Usually asymptomatic-compensated type.

• In cases where there are symptoms-decompensated type

• Headache

• Eye ache

• Photophobia

• Intermittent diplopia (only under fatigue – temporarily)

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common type of squint seen in children?
questions.explanation:
Accommodative esotropia is the most common type of squint seen in children.

Most common type of squint overall: accommodative esotropia

Second most common overall: congenital/Infantile esotropia

Most common type of exotropia: primary exotropia

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding comitant squint?
options: No co-relation between primary and secondary deviations
questions.explanation:
In comitant squint (concomitant), the primary deviation is equal to the secondary deviation.

Primary deviation = Deviation of the squinting eye

Secondary deviation = Deviation of the normal eye under cover when the patient fixes with the squinting eye.

In incomitant (paralytic and restrictive squint), secondary deviation > primary deviation due to Herring's Law of equal innervation.

questions.question: A mother noticed that her child has had malaligned eyes since birth but she couldn't afford treatment due to financial constraints. She now presents at 2-months of age and the child has the following finding on examination. An ophthalmoscopic examination under full cycloplegia reveals no abnormalities in refraction and media. Cranial nerves are intact. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
options: Angle of deviation is large and constant.
Amblyopia develops in 90 % of the cases.
It is associated with latent vertical nystagmus.
Correction by spectacles is the treatment of choice.
questions.answer: A. Angle of deviation is large and constant.
questions.explanation:
The age at presentation, esotropia, no refractory error, no media opacities, and no cranial nerve palsies suggest a diagnosis of essential infantile esotropia. The angle of deviation in infantile esotropia is fairly large (> 30°) and constant.

Infantile esotropia, also known as non-accommodative esotropia is the most common type of congenital esotropia.

Clinical features:

• Comitant convergent squint

• Age of onset- 1 to 2 months

• Angle of deviation- large and constant

• Amblyopia- develops in 25–40% of cases

• Associations include:

• Inferior oblique overaction

• Dissociated vertical deviation (70%)

• Latent horizontal nystagmus

Treatment:

• Surgery- treatment of choice

• Amblyopia correction measures: Patching of normal eye

• Recession of both medial recti

• Timing: Preferably before 1 year

questions.question: A surgeon decides to resect a part of a muscle while operating on a case of strabismus. This action would lead to which of the following?
options: No change in strength of the muscle
questions.explanation:
In squint surgery, muscle resection leads to the strengthening of the muscle.

The main types of procedure in squint surgery are as follows:

1. Weakening to decrease the effective strength of action of a muscle.

• Recession slackens a muscle by moving it away from its insertion. It can be performed on any muscle except the superior oblique.

• Disinsertion (or myectomy) involves detaching a muscle from its insertion without reattachment. It is most commonly used to weaken an overacting inferior oblique muscle.

• Posterior fixation suture: The principle of this (Faden) procedure is to suture the muscle belly to the sclera posteriorly so as to decrease the pull of the muscle in its field of action without affecting the eye in the primary position.

2. Strengthening, to enhance the pull of a muscle.

• Resection shortens a muscle to enhance its effective pull. It is suitable only for the rectus muscle.

• Tucking of a muscle or its tendon is usually confined to the enhancement of the action of the superior oblique muscle.

• Advancement of the muscle nearer to the limbus can be used to enhance the action of a previously recessed rectus muscle.

3. Vector adjustment procedures have the primary aim of altering the direction of muscle action.

4. Transposition refers to the relocation of one or more extraocular muscles to substitute for the action of an absent or severely deficient muscle. The most common indication is severe lateral rectus weakness due to acquired palsy of the 6th cranial nerve palsy.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best line of treatment in a 3-year-old child presenting with a recent onset of 15-degree accommodative esotropia?
questions.explanation:
The best line of treatment in accommodative esotropia is a refractive correction.

Esotropia for distance is corrected by the treatment of hypermetropia: convex glasses

Esotropia for near is corrected by +3DS lens.

Algorithm for the management of accommodative esotropia is as follows:

• R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics

• O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: for amblyopia

• O: Operative correction: for non-accommodative component

• P: Prism correction: for remaining error

questions.question: Charlie, a 5-year-old boy with crossed eyes received his first eye exam from a primary care ophthalmologist. Examination, including cycloplegic refraction and dilated fundus exam, resulted in diagnoses of constant right esotropia, and amblyopia in the right eye. By what age should his amblyopia be corrected?
questions.explanation:
Strabismic amblyopia should be corrected before 8 years of age.

The sensitive period during which acuity of an amblyopic eye can be improved is usually up to 7–8 years in strabismic amblyopia and maybe longer (into the teens) for anisometropic amblyopia when a good binocular function is present.

In the absence of an organic lesion, a difference in best-corrected visual acuity (VA) of two Snellen lines or more (or >1 log unit) is indicative of amblyopia.

Treatment of amblyopia:

1. Occlusion of the normal eye, to encourage the use of the amblyopic eye, is the most effective treatment.

2. Penalization, in which vision in the normal eye is blurred with atropine, is an alternative method.

questions.question: A 5-year-old female patient presented for her first complete eye examination after a school vision screening found unequal visual acuity. Her parents have not noted any eye problems. Visual acuity in the right eye was 20/20 and the left eye is 20/80. The rest of the examination was unremarkable and glasses were prescribed. She was diagnosed with anisometric hyperopia and amblyopia of the left eye when her visual acuity at a return appointment was found to be 20/20 RE and 20/60 LE at a distance while wearing her new glasses. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Occlusion of the normal eye is the treatment of choice for amblyopia.

Amblyopia is an uncorrectable decrease in vision in one or both eyes with no apparent structural abnormality seen to explain it. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. Generally, a difference of two lines or more on an eye chart test of visual acuity between the two eyes or a best-corrected vision of 20/30 or worse would be defined as amblyopia. For example, our patient has 20/20 vision with the right eye and only 20/80 with the left and the left eye even after best-corrected vision couldn't achieve <20/30 vision, the left eye is said to be amblyopic.

Clinical features:

• Decreased contrast sensitivity

• Diminution of vision

• Sunglass effect- brightness is less compared to the normal eye

• Crowding phenomenon- slipping of images

Treatment of choice:

• Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/day) using patches.

• Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine.

Prism correction is not the right treatment as the child doesn't have strabismus.

questions.question: A 3-year-old child presents with a right convergent squint of 6 months duration. Choose the most appropriate treatment strategy.
options: Immediate surgical correction followed by amblyopia therapy
Proper refractive correction, amblyopia therapy followed by surgical correction
Prescription of spectacles and defer surgery until 5 years
Botulinum toxin injection followed by occlusion therapy
questions.answer: B. Proper refractive correction, amblyopia therapy followed by surgical correction
questions.explanation:
The appropriate management in this case would be proper refractive correction, amblyopia therapy followed by surgical correction

The algorithm for management of accommodative squint is as follows:

• R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics

• O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: For amblyopia

• O: Operative correction: For non-accommodative component

• P: Prism correction: For remaining error

questions.question: In which of the following conditions should an ophthalmologist prescribe miotics?
questions.explanation:
Miotics are used in the management of accommodative esotropia.

The use of miotics in convergent strabismus is based on the peripheral spasm of accommodation caused by the drug. The accommodation triad involves convergence. An increased accommodative effort increases the amount of convergence. Pilocarpine would produce accommodation spasm and eliminate the accommodative convergence that would otherwise occur when the patient looks at a near object. It is useful in cases of an abnormal AC/A ratio as in, accommodative esotropia.

questions.question: Paralytic squint presents with all except
questions.explanation:
In squint, the deviation of the eye results in two vastly different images. The brain is unable to fuse them. Hence, there is no stereopsis.

Features of paralytic squint:

Symptoms:

• Diplopia

• Confusion

• Nausea, Vertigo

• Ocular deviation

Signs:

• Primary deviation < Secondary deviation

• Compensatory head posture–Ocular torticollis

• False projection or orientation

In adults- no amblyopia

In children <6 years- amblyopia can occur

questions.question: Identify the condition.
questions.explanation: The patient has left eye esotropia in primary gaze which is suggestive of left abducent (6th) nerve palsy which innervates the left lateral rectus muscle.

questions.question: A patient complains of difficulty in climbing down the stairs due to double vision. On examination, you notice his right eye has deviated upward and the deviation becomes more pronounced on the left gaze. The remaining extraocular movements are intact. Which nerve is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
The affected nerve in the given clinical scenario is the right trochlear nerve.

The right trochlear nucleus actually innervates the left superior oblique and vice versa. However, the nerve decussates at the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. So, lesions of the trochlear nucleus lead to contralateral palsy. While that of trochlear nerve peripherally lead to ipsilateral palsy.

In this patient, the right-sided symptoms could be due to a lesion in the right trochlear nerve (ipsilateral) or left trochlear nucleus (contralateral). He complains of diplopia while climbing down the stairs because the normal eye can look down but the paralytic eye has deviated. There is also a limitation of depression due to superior oblique palsy, and hence the eye is deviated upward due to overaction of the inferior oblique. The obliques exert maximum force in an adducted position and hence the deviation becomes more prominent on the left gaze when the right eye is adducted.

questions.question: A patient suffers head trauma following which he complains of diplopia. His extraocular motility testing in the 9 gazes is as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario suggests a left oculomotor nerve palsy.

It is evident by the upper lid ptosis and down and out deviation of the left eye, as seen in the primary position of gaze (central image).

questions.question: An 18-year-old destitute woman reports to a free eye camp with vision problems. Best-corrected visual acuity was 6/12 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Elevation in the right eye was absent. Her right eye showed 14–16 prism diopter (PD) hypotropia. Bell's phenomenon was absent in the right eye. Diagnosis of right eye double elevator palsy was made. Which of the following muscles are affected in her?
options: Levator palpebrae superioris and Muller muscle
Levator palpebrae superioris and superior rectus
questions.answer: D. Superior rectus and Inferior oblique
questions.explanation:
In double-elevator palsy, the muscles involved are superior rectus and inferior oblique.

It is commonly associated with ptosis or pseudoptosis.

questions.question: A patient reports to the OPD with complaints that he feels dizzy on lateral gaze. His range of movements is shown below. Jerky movements are also observed in the left eye on the left gaze however convergence is normal. Which of the following structures is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Lesion to the medial longitudinal fasciculus causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO).

The right gaze is normal but on the left gaze, there is an inability of right eye adduction and in the left abduction is possible but with nystagmus. This along with normal convergence are all in favor of diagnosis of a lesion in right medial longitudinal fasciculus(MLF) leading to internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

INO is seen in multiple sclerosis

The image below depicts internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to a lesion of the right MLF.

Total ophthalmoplegia

• All extraocular and intraocular muscles are paralyzed.

• Paralysis of 3rd, 4th, and 6th nerve

• Seen in orbital apex syndrome, cavernous sinus thrombosis

External ophthalmoplegia

• All extraocular muscles are paralyzed

• Lesions at the level of motor nuclei

• Sparing of Edinger Westphal nucleus

questions.question: Identify the condition
questions.explanation:
The image shows Duane’s retraction syndrome type 1.

Paradoxical innervation of LR where it gets innervated by some fibres of III nerve instead of VI nerve. On impulse for abduction via VI nerve there is no abduction limitation. On impulse for adduction via III nerve both LR and MR contract thus causing retraction of globe (as the antagonist LR instead of relaxation, starts to contract)

Duane’s retraction syndrome (DRS) is a cause of restrictive squint

There is a failure of innervation of the lateral rectus by a hypoplastic sixth nerve nucleus, with anomalous innervation of the lateral rectus by fibers from the third nerve. Retraction of the globe on attempted adduction. Widening of palpebral fissure on attempted abduction

Classification by Huber:

• Limitation of abduction- type 1

• Limitation of adduction- type 2

• Limitation of both- type 3

Note: DRS is an exception to Sherrington's law of reciprocal innervation.

questions.question: An eleven-year-old girl presented with a history of squint and poor vision. She had visual acuities of 6/24 and counting fingers in her right and left eyes respectively. There was a left hypotropia in the primary position of gaze with associated marked restriction of elevation in adduction and a positive forced duction test. A diagnosis of Brown syndrome was made. The pathology involves which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation:
Brown syndrome occurs due to mechanical restriction caused by a congenitally tight superior oblique sheath or by the impaired movement of the superior oblique tendon through the trochlea. It may be acquired in some cases.

Contracture of the superior oblique leads to restriction of its antagonistic muscle, the inferior oblique and that is why the patient presents with absence of elevation in adduction.

questions.question: Brown’s syndrome simulates which muscle palsy?
questions.explanation:
Brown’s superior oblique tendon sheath syndrome simulates palsy of inferior oblique muscle. In both of these cases, there is a limited elevation of the eye in adduction.

Brown’s superior oblique tendon sheath syndrome is a cause of restrictive squint.The forced duction test is positive.

Differential diagnoses of Brown's syndrome:

1. Inferior oblique palsy- differentiated by a positive head-tilt test (negative in Brown's syndrome) and a negative forced duction test (positive in Brown's syndrome)

2. Primary superior oblique overaction- differentiated by negative forced duction test (Positive in Brown's syndrome)

questions.question: Identify the condition.
questions.explanation:
The given image classically depicts an A pattern esotropia. Relative convergence on upgaze (esotropia increases on upgaze) is a feature of A-pattern esotropia.

A or V pattern heterotropia:

• "V" or "A" patterns occur when the relative contributions of the superior rectus and inferior oblique to elevation, or of the inferior rectus and superior oblique to depression, are abnormal, resulting in the derangement of the balance of their horizontal vectors in up and downgaze.

• Oblique muscle dysfunction is the commonest

• "V" pattern is said to be significant when the difference between upgaze and downgaze is ≥15 Δ.

• "A" pattern is considered significant if the difference between upgaze and downgaze is ≥10 Δ.

The image below shows A and V pattern heterotropia

chapters.chapter: Disorders Of Visual Pathway And Pupillary Reflexes

questions.question: Which of the following forms the third-order neurons in the visual pathway?
questions.explanation:
Third-order neurons in the visual pathway are the ganglion cells.

The afferent neuronal impulses are carried in the following manner:

Photoreceptors (I) ⇒ Bipolar cells (II) ⇒ Ganglion cells (III) ⇒ Lateral geniculate body (IV).

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman with a known pituitary microadenoma presented with sudden-onset visual disturbances, headache, and hypotension during the second trimester of pregnancy. What is the visual field defect this patient is most likely to experience?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pituitary apoplexy in pregnancy This acute onset event is almost always associated with compression at the level of optic chiasma causing heteronymous hemianopia (bitemporal hemianopia).

Pituitary apoplexy results from hemorrhagic infarction of a pre-existing pituitary adenoma or within a physiologically enlarged gland, which is well documented in pregnancy.

The nasal fibers of each retina cross through the chiasma. Slow-growing microadenomas compress lower nasal optic fibers causing superior temporal quadrantanopia initially, before progressing to bitemporal hemianopia. However, an abrupt infarction or hemorrhage of a pre-existing pituitary adenoma will lead to rapid progression of the visual defect.

Heteronymous hemianopia is the loss of half of the visual field on different sides in both eyes. It is separated into two categories:

• Binasal hemianopia – the loss of the fields surrounding the nose

• Bitemporal hemianopia – the loss of the fields closest to the temples.

Common causes of bitemporal hemianopia due to central chiasmal lesions are as follows:

• Suprasellar aneurysms

• Tumors of the pituitary gland

• Craniopharyngioma

• Suprasellar meningioma

• Glioma of the third ventricle

Other visual defects according to the site of the lesion are as follows:

questions.question: Which of the following cannot be tested with monocular visual field testing using a pin with a red pinhead?
questions.explanation:
Central scotoma, paracentral scotoma and temporal field defects can be tested by monocular visual field testing with a red-headed neurological pin.

A patient who has central scotoma will either not see the pinhead in the centre of the field or perceive it black. This can be defined by moving the pin outwards in four different directions until the patient sees the pinhead as being red.

Placing the pin in each of the quadrants close to the centre and checking if the patient sees the red pinhead can detect a paracentral scotoma. This can also detect temporal field defects.

questions.question: A lesion in which of the following structures is most likely to result in congruous homonymous hemianopia?
questions.explanation:
Congruous homonymous hemianopia is most suggestive of a lesion in the occipital cortex.

Homonymous hemianopia involves vision loss on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. This type of visual field loss is suggestive of a lesion posterior to the optic chiasma in the visual pathway.

Complete homonymous hemianopia involves the complete visual hemifields of both eyes and can occur with any large enough lesion posterior to the optic chiasma. Visual field examination alone cannot further localize the lesion in such cases.

Incomplete homonymous hemianopia is due to smaller lesions in the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasm. They are further divided into congruous and incongruous depending on the extent to which the defects in the two half fields match each other exactly.

Because of a relative disorder among axon bundles in the immediate post-chiasmal region, diseases in this location produce rather incongruent lesions.

More posteriorly, the axon bundles of the corresponding areas of the two hemifields are more closely aligned and hence, lesions of the occipital cortex produce congruous homonymous hemianopia while incongruous homonymous hemianopia is more likely seen with optic tract lesions.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a persistent headache for the past few months. On evaluation, her vision on Snellen's chart was 6/6 in both eyes. The fundus also appears to be normal. Visual field charting shows a bitemporal visual field defect. Site of the lesion is _________
questions.explanation:
The site of the lesion is optic chiasma. Lesions at the chiasma characteristically produce bitemporal field defects due to the decussation of nasal fibres.

In retrochiasmal lesions, homonymous hemianopia is seen. Further, in cortical lesions, macular (central) vision is spared.

questions.question: A young patient with visual disturbances was found to have a brain tumour. He was referred to ophthalmology for a complete visual field assessment before planning his resection. Humprey analyzer revealed the following plot. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
The visual field defect shown is the typical "pie in the sky" defect or superior quadrantic hemianopia. They are produced when the inferior fibers of the optic radiations in the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) are involved.

"Pie in the floor" defects refer to inferior quadrantic hemianopia. It is seen in the involvement of the superior fibers of optic radiations in the parietal lobe (Baum's loop).

questions.question: The primary visual cortex is located in the _______________.
questions.answer: C. Posterior part of calcarine sulcus
questions.explanation:
The primary visual cortex( Brodmann area 17) is located in the posterior part of the calcarine sulcus in the occiptal lobe.

Accessory visual areas are area 18 (secondary) and area 19 (tertiary).

Image: Brodman areas

questions.question: A 72-year-old lady was brought by her son with bilateral loss of vision for 3 days, associated with slurred speech. It was preceded by an occipital headache. Despite her obvious blindness, illustrated by her walking into objects, the patient denied visual loss. MRI revealed bilateral occipital infarcts. Which of the following statement is true regarding the given condition?
options: Direct and consensual reflexes are absent in both eyes.
Direct and consensual reflexes are present in both eyes.
Direct reflex is present but consensual reflex is absent.
Consensual reflex is present but direct reflex is absent.
questions.answer: B. Direct and consensual reflexes are present in both eyes.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cortical blindness with visual anosognosia (Anton syndrome). Since anterior visual pathways are not affected in cortical blindness, direct and consensual light reflexes are preserved.

Cortical blindness is usually associated with bilateral occipital infarcts where it is supplied by the posterior cerebral arteries and these infarcts usually involve both the primary visual cortex and visual association area. It is secondary to damage to the visual pathways posterior to the lateral geniculate nuclei; anterior visual pathways are intact. Visual field defects can vary depending on the extent and location of the infarct.

Direct and consensual reflexes are present in both eyes in cortical blindness as pupillary light reflex fibers exit the visual pathway at the level of the superior colliculus. They exit the optic tract before the lateral geniculate body (LGB) to reach the center for pupillary light reflex- pretectal nucleus at the midbrain.

Note: Anton syndrome is visual anosognosia (denial of loss of vision) associated with confabulation (defined as the emergence of memories of events and experiences which never took place) in the setting of obvious visual loss and cortical blindness.

questions.question: A neurology resident is demonstrating spinal reflexes in a comatose patient. When he pinches the skin over the side of the patient's neck, there is a rapid dilatation of the ipsilateral pupil. Which of the following forms the efferent limb of this reflex?
questions.answer: C. Sympathetic fibres of cervical ganglion
questions.explanation:
The given scenario describes cilio-spinal reflex. Sympathetic fibers of cervical ganglion form the efferent limb of this reflex.

Cilio-spinal reflex:

• Afferent inputs of this reflex are carried by the trigeminal nerve or cervical pain fibers (lateral spinothalamic tract).

• It synapses at the ciliospinal center of Budge, located at C8 to T2 in the intermediolateral (IML) horn of the gray matter of the spinal cord.

• The efferent branch of the reflex consists of:

• Preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the upper thoracic and lower cervical spinal cord which goes to the cervical sympathetic chain and its three ganglia.

• The postganglionic sympathetic fibers pass on the surface of the internal carotid artery and join the ophthalmic nerve at the cavernous sinus. Here, it passes through the nasociliary nerve to reach the ciliary body and innervates the dilator pupillae muscles, causing dilatation of the pupil.

This reflex is absent in Horner's syndrome and in lesions involving the cervical sympathetic fibers and it is enhanced in patients with cluster headache and barbiturate-induced coma.

questions.question: Which of the following is not part of the pupillary light reflex pathway?
questions.explanation:
The lateral geniculate body is not a part of the pupillary reflex pathway. It is part of the accommodation reflex and the visual pathway.

Pupillary light reflex pathway:

• First neurons (sensory) connects each retina with both pretectal nuclei in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculi.

• Second neurons (internuncial) connects each pretectal nucleus to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei.

• Third neurons (preganglionic motor) connects the Edinger–Westphal nucleus to the ciliary ganglion.

• Fourth neurons (postganglionic motor) leaves the ciliary ganglion and passes in the short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae.

Image: Pupillary reflex pathways

questions.question: A patient presented with diplopia to the casualty. On examination, the left pupil was dilated. Both direct and consensual light reflexes were lost in the affected eye. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical situation suggests that the patient has III nerve (oculomotor nerve) palsy.

Absence of contraction of the pupil in both direct and consensual reflex suggests a lesion in the efferent pathway of the affected eye. This is III nerve/oculomotor palsy.

Light reflex consists of direct and consensual reflexes.

When light is shone in an eye,

• Constriction of the pupil of the same eye is called direct reflex.

• Constriction of the contralateral pupil is called consensual reflex/indirect reflex

For the light reflex,

• Afferent nerve fiber is the II cranial nerve (optic nerve).

• Efferent nerve fiber is the III cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve)-Bilaterally

In II nerve palsy, there will be a loss of direct reflex in the affected eye and loss of consensual light reflex in the opposite eye.

questions.question: Which of the following would you suspect in a patient who presents with small pupils?
questions.explanation: Pontine hemorrhage is associated with small pupils. The remaining options, namely, carbon monoxide poisoning, ethylene glycol poisoning, and Holmes–Adie pupil, cause dilation of the pupils.

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman finally decides to get glasses, about thirty years after she actually needed them, and goes to an optometrist for an eyeglass prescription. Her eye examination reveals some unexpected findings. The pupils were small. When a pen-light is shone on to her eyes, neither pupil contracts. However, when the optometrist brings his fingers towards her face, both pupils constrict dramatically. What is the given condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical situation of bilateral small irregular pupils with light-near dissociation suggests a diagnosis of Argyll Robertson pupil.

Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP):

• Accommodation Reflex Present (ARP)

• Light Reflex absent

• Constricted pupil

• An example of light near dissocation.

• Seen in neurosyphilis

Option A: Anisocoria is when the pupils are not of the same size.

Option B: Adie's tonic pupil

• Light reflex absent or sluggish.

• Near reflex: Slow and tonic

• Pupil is larger

• Constricts with weak pilocarpine.

Option C: Ophthalmoplegia interna

• Dilated paralyzed pupil

• Does not respond to light or accommodation

questions.question: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is due to a lesion in the _______.
questions.explanation:
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is due to a lesion in the optic tract.

The optic tracts contain both visual and pupillomotor fibers.

The visual fibers terminate in the lateral geniculate body, but the pupillary fibers leave the optic tract anterior to the lateral geniculate body, projecting through the brachium of the superior colliculus to terminate in the pretectal nuclei.

An optic tract lesion may, therefore, give rise to an afferent pupillary conduction defect.

Characteristically, the pupillary light reflex will be normal when the unaffected hemiretina is stimulated and absent, when the involved hemiretina is stimulated (i.e., light is shone from the hemianopic side).

questions.question:
The casualty intern noticed that a patient had unequal pupils. The anisocoria was greater under light. Which of the following drugs would be helpful in quickly differentiating between the potential causes?

1. Phenylephrine

2. 1% Pilocarpine

3. 0.1% Pilocarpine

4. Cocaine 0.5%

5. Epinephrine
questions.explanation:
Anisocoria greater in the light indicates the large pupil to be abnormal due to poor pupillary contraction from a parasympathetic abnormality. Among the given options, 1% pilocarpine and 0.1% pilocarpine can be used to differentiate fixed dilated pupil.

Mydriasis due to neurologic origin (3rd nerve palsy) responds readily to 1% pilocarpine, whereas there will be no response if the dilation is due to anticholinergic causes. Pupillary constriction to 0.1% pilocarpine diagnoses Adie's pupil (due to denervation hypersensitivity). Application of 0.1% pilocarpine shows no response in other conditions or in the normal eye.

Example: A person presenting with dilated pupil following accidental application or inadvertent rubbing of atropine or antimuscarinic alkaloids from wild plants into the eye will not constrict in response to topical application of 1% Pilocarpine. But the patient showing dilation due to 3rd nerve palsy shows pupillary constriction in response to pupillary instillation of 1% pilocarpine.

Note: Cocaine and phenylephrine are used in anisocoria that is greater in the dark to diagnose Horner’s syndrome. In these patients, the small pupil fails to dilate even after the instillation of cocaine.

questions.question: A 55-year-old lady with advanced spondylosis underwent cervical vertebral fusion surgery. In the post-operative room, the resident noted that her pupils were unequal. Which of the following features would rule out the possibility of Horner's syndrome in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Horner's syndrome causes all the following except mydriasis. It causes miosis.

Horner's syndrome (oculosympathetic palsy)

The majority of the cases are unilateral.

Causes of bilateral involvement include cervical spine injuries and autonomic diabetic neuropathy.

Painful Horner syndrome, especially of acute onset, should raise the possibility of carotid dissection.

Clinical features

• Mild ptosis (usually 1–2 mm) as a result of weakness of Müller muscle

• Anisocoria is accentuated in dim light

• Pupillary constriction to light and near stimuli is normal.

• Hypochromic heterochromia (lighter color iris on affected side); in congenital cases.

• Mild ptosis (Mullers muscle is affected)

• Reduced ipsilateral sweating (only if the lesion is below the superior cervical ganglion)

Pharmacological tests

• Hydroxyamphetamine and adrenaline may be used to differentiate a preganglionic from a postganglionic lesion.

• Phenylepherine (1%)

• Result: In an established (10 days) postganglionic lesion, the Horner pupil will dilate and ptosis may be temporarily relieved. A central or preganglionic Horner pupil and a normal pupil will not dilate or will dilate minimally.

• Explanation: In postganglionic Horner's syndrome, the dilator pupillae muscle develops denervation hypersensitivity to adrenergic neurotransmitters due to its dysfunctional local motor nerve.

• Apraclonidine (0.5% or 1.0%)

• Result: A Horner pupil will dilate, but a normal pupil is essentially unaffected.

• Explanation: Alpha-1 receptors are upregulated in the denervated dilator pupillae.

• Cocaine (4%) is instilled into both eyes

• Result: The normal pupil will dilate, but the Horner pupil will not.

• Explanation: Cocaine blocks the re-uptake of noradrenaline secreted at the postganglionic nerve ending, which accumulates and causes dilatation of a normal pupil. In Horner's syndrome, there is no noradrenaline being secreted, so cocaine has no effect.

questions.question: Where is the cell body of the second-order neuron in the sympathetic pathway for the pupil?
questions.explanation:
The cell body of the second-order neuron in the sympathetic pathway for the pupil lies at the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8–T1).

The sympathetic pathway to the iris muscles consists of a chain of three neurons:

• The first neuron arises from the hypothalamus along the brain stem to synapse in the intermediolateral column of the spinal cord—the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T1).

• From here (C8-T1), the second-order neuron arises. This joins the cervical sympathetic chain and synapses at the superior cervical ganglion.

• The third-order neuron arises from the superior cervical ganglion and travels through the cavernous sinus along with the internal carotid artery.

• Sympathetic fibers join the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve and pass through the ciliary ganglion to the nasociliary and short ciliary nerves.

questions.question: A simultaneous lesion in both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply of the eye leads to which of the following?
options: Mydriatic pupil that reacts to light
Constricted pupil that reacts to light
Mid-sized pupil that doesn’t react to light
Mid-sized pupil that reacts to light
questions.answer: C. Mid-sized pupil that doesn’t react to light
questions.explanation:
Simultaneous lesion in both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply of the eye leads to mid-sized pupil that doesn’t react to light.

Pupillary dilation is achieved by sympathetic innervation of dilator pupillae. Therefore, any lesion of the sympathetic supply of the pupil leads to constricted pupil.

Pupillary constriction is a parasympathetic function. Lesions in this pathway leads to dilated pupil and failure to constrict.

A mid-sized unreactive pupil due to a lesion of both parasympathetic and sympathetic supplies is seen in aneurysms of the internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus.

questions.question: During the neurological examination of a patient, on shining light in his left eye, the left pupil does not constrict but the right pupil does. On shining light in his right eye, the right pupil constricts and left doesn’t. The defect is in:
questions.explanation:
The above scenario is suggestive of left eye efferent (oculomotor nerve) defect.

The loss of pupillary light reflex (both direct and consensual) in the left eye associated with a preserved direct pupillary response in the right eye is characteristic of an efferent pupillary defect.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man was brought to the OPD by his daughter with complaints of drooping of his left eyelid and double vision. The pupillary examination was normal. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Ptosis and double vision with no other features suggest an acquired, isolated 3rd nerve palsy with pupillary sparing. This is seen in ischemic conditions such as diabetes.

The vasoneurium supplies the nerve from outside to inside. As the somatic fibres are located in the inner part of the nerve, these fibres are affected more in the setting of ischemia. The parasympathetic pupillary fibres which run on the outside can remain unaffected (resulting in pupillary sparing). In compressive lesions, the parasympathetic fibres are affected before any disruption of the motor fibres. So pupillary sparing is not seen.

Isolated 3rd nerve palsy

Causes

• Microvascular disease associated with systemic risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes is the most common cause of third nerve palsy.

• Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery at its junction with the internal carotid, both direct and secondary to subdural hematoma with uncal herniation.

• Episodic- migraine, compression, ischemia, and alterations in intracranial pressure

• Miscellaneous- tumour and inflammatory diseases such as syphilis, Lyme disease, and sarcoidosis; giant cell arteritis; and vasculitis associated with collagen vascular disorders.

Signs

• Profound ptosis due to the weakness of the levator muscle

• Abduction and depression in the primary position ("down and out")

• Normal abduction as the lateral rectus is intact

• Limited adduction due to medial rectus weakness

• Limited elevation due to the weakness of the superior rectus and inferior oblique

questions.question: The patient presented with the following appearance when asked to look straight. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows adduction of the right eye due to paralysis of the right lateral rectus, indicating right abducens (6th) nerve palsy.

The nucleus of the sixth (abducens or abducent) nerve lies at the mid-level of the pons.

Nuclear lesion: A nuclear sixth nerve lesion also causes the failure of horizontal gaze towards the side of the damage due to the involvement of the adjacent horizontal gaze center (paramedian pontine reticular formation).

Foville (inferior medial pontine) syndrome is most frequently caused by vascular disease or tumors involving the dorsal pons. It is characterized by the following:

• Ipsilateral involvement of the fifth to eighth cranial nerves

• Central sympathetic fibers (Horner syndrome)

• Horizontal gaze palsy

Millard–Gubler (ventral pontine) syndrome involves the fasciculus as it passes through the pyramidal tract. As well as ipsilateral sixth nerve palsy, there is contralateral hemiplegia and often an ipsilateral lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy.

Clinical features:

• Esotropia in the primary position due to relatively unopposed action of the medial rectus

• Limitation of abduction on the side of the lesion

• Normal adduction of the affected eye

• A compensatory face turn is towards the side of the paralyzed muscle in unilateral palsy

chapters.chapter: Disorders Of Optic Nerve And Gaze Palsies

questions.question: The longest part of the optic nerve measures _____.
questions.explanation:
Intraorbital part is the longest part of the optic nerve.

It measures from 25 mm to 30 mm.

Length of the optic nerve ranges from 3.5 cm to 5.5 cm.

80% of the fibers originate from the macular region.

Parts of optic nerve:

Parts

Length

Intraocular part

1 mm

Intraorbital part

25–30 mm

Intracanalicular part

5–9mm

Intracranial part

10–16 mm

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of papilledema?
questions.explanation:
Disruption of neurofilaments is not a feature of papilledema.

Papilledema is the swelling of the optic nerve head secondary to raised intracranial pressure (ICP).

"Disc swelling" and "disc edema" are non-specific terms that include papilledema but also indicate a disc swollen from other causes.

All patients with papilledema should be suspected of harboring an intracranial mass.

Features of papilledema:

• Raised ICP

• Edema of the optic nerve head

• Blockage of axoplasmic flow

• Axonal swelling

• Collection of extracellular fluid

• Painless progressive loss of vision

• Enlargement of the blind spot

• Color vision, visual acuity, and pupillary reaction are normal, until optic atrophy sets in.

questions.question: A resident notes the following fundus picture in a patient referred to the ophthalmology OPD with visual complaints. What does it suggest?
questions.explanation:
The fundoscopic image shows dilated veins with a blurred disc margin which is suggestive of papilledema.

Ophthalmoscopic features of papilledema:

• Early-stage:

• Obscuration of the disc margins (nasal margins first)

• Absence of spontaneous venous pulsation at the disc

• Mild hyperemia of the disc

• The blurring of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer

• Established papilledema:

• The disc appears to be enlarged and elevated (mushroom or dome-shaped)

• Macular fan appears

• Paton’s lines- circumferential greyish white folds may develop due to the separation of nerve fibers

• Visual fields show enlargement of the blind spot

• Veins become tortuous and engorged

• Multiple cotton-wool spots and superficial hemorrhages

• Chronic or long-standing (vintage) papilledema:

• The optic disc gives the appearance of the dome of a champagne cork

• Small drusen-like crystalline deposits (corpora amylacea) may appear on the disc surface

• Atrophic stage:

• Secondary optic atrophy

questions.question: Which of the following conditions show ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema?
questions.explanation:
Ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema are seen in Foster–Kennedy syndrome.

Weber syndrome (superior alternating hemiplegia) is a form of stroke characterized by the presence of an ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral hemiparesis or hemiplegia.

Millard–Gubler syndrome is a lesion of the pons. It is also called ventral pontine syndrome.

Benedikt syndrome, also known as paramedian midbrain syndrome, involves the fasciculus of oculomotor nerve as it passes through the red nucleus and is characterized by ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral extrapyramidal signs such as hemitremor.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the casualty with a sudden loss of vision and painful ocular movements. On examination, the eye is white and there are no obvious signs on ophthalmoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a sudden painful loss of vision in the absence of fundoscopic changes is suggestive of retrobulbar neuritis.

There are 3 types of optic neuritis: papillitis, neuroretinitis, and retrobulbar neuritis. The common causes of retrobulbar neuritis include demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and neuromyelitis optica (NMO or Devic's disease).

Clinically, optic neuritis is characterized by sudden, progressive visual loss. Ocular movements are painful in retrobulbar neuritis and painless in papillitis and neuroretinitis. Glowing sensations known as phosphenes may be induced with sound or movement. Color vision may also be impaired.

On examination, Marcus Gunn pupil or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is usually noted due to asymmetric involvement. The most common visual field defect is a central or centrocecal scotoma.

Type
Retrobulbar neuritis
Papillitis
Neuroretinitis

Pathology
Inflammation of the optic nerve behind the disc
Inflammation of the optic nerve head
Inflammation of the optic nerve head and the macula

Fundus appearance
Optic disc appears normal

Hyperemia and oedema of the optic disc with or without peri-papillary flame-shaped hemorrhages

Macular star (due to exudates that form around macula)

Prevalence
Most common in adults

Most common in children

Least common type

Associated conditions
Strong association with demyelinating disorders like MS, NMO

Weak association with demyelinating disorders

Cat-scratch disease, Lyme disease, Syphilis etc.

The image below shows papillitis.

The image below shows macular star appearance in neuroretinitis.

questions.question: A 33-year-old patient has come to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints that her vision becomes temporarily blurry after a hot bath in the evening. This resolves by itself after a few hours. She has a past history of an episode of painful unilateral optic neuritis, 3 months back which resolved with steroids. What is being described here?
questions.explanation:
Episodic, transient obscuration of vision on exertion or on exposure to heat, which recovers on resting or moving away from the heat in an isolated optic neuritis patient is called Uhthoff phenomenon. It is commonly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS).

Option A: Pulfrich’s phenomenon is an illusion of depth perception. It is seen in MS.

Option C: Lhermitte’s sign refers to passive neck flexion causing an electric shock-like sensation radiating to the spine and shoulders. This is a result of the increased sensitivity of the myelin to stretch or traction; it is also seen in MS.

Option D: Riddoch phenomenon refers to ability to perceive kinetic but not static targets. It is seen in cortical blindness.

questions.question: In a patient with multiple sclerosis, which of the following visual field defects is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Central scotoma is more likely to occur with multiple sclerosis. It is also seen with retrobulbar neuritis and macular pathology.

Option A: Optic chiasma compression causes bitemporal hemianopia

Option C: Enlarged blind spot occurs with papilloedema

Option D: Tunnel vision occurs in glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa and Retinal pan photocoagulation

questions.question: Optic neuritis is a common presentation in which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
One of the common presentations of MS is optic neuritis. Multiple sclerosis (MS) results from demyelinating plaques in the central nervous system.

Option A: Myasthenia gravis is the autoimmune destruction of the acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

Option B: Guillain–Barré syndrome is the postinfectious autoimmune-induced destruction of peripheral nerves, resulting in an ascending paralysis.

Option D: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease of the motor nerve fibers of the lateral columns and anterior horns of the spinal cord that results in progressive muscular atrophy.

questions.question: A middle-aged man with suspected optic neuropathy is being evaluated for visual field defects. Goldman perimetry reveals bilateral centrocecal scotomas. Which of the following is most likely to be the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Centrocecal scotoma is most commonly seen in tobacco-induced amblyopia. It is also seen in vitamin B12 deficiency.

Tobacco amblyopia is caused by excessive smoking and chewing of tobacco. The toxic agent involved is cyanide found in tobacco. It is characterized by bilateral and gradually progressive impairment of central vision. The classic visual field defect is a centrocecal scotoma, often involving both the blind spot and the macula.

Option B: Ethanol amblyopia is similar to tobacco amblyopia but often presents with peripheral neuritis and a "central scotoma".

Option C: Methanol amblyopia often results in complete blindness.

Option D: Quinine amblyopia results in near-complete blindness with associated deafness and tinnitus.

questions.question: An anxious, young man came to the ER with complaints of having sudden trouble seeing with his left eye and a recent history of tripping over things. There was no associated pain or difficulty moving the eyes. An ophthalmology consultation was requested. On perimetry, the following visual field defect was picked up. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The perimetry result depicts altitudinal hemianopia, which is most commonly seen in anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION).

Altitudinal hemianopia can also be seen in suprasellar tumors and occipital lobe lesions, but the frequency is very low compared to that of AION. Hence, AION is the single best answer.

The two types of AION are as follows:

• Arteritic AION- caused by giant-cell arteritis

• Non-arteritic AION (NAAION)- more common

Clinical features:

Features
AAION

NAAION

Age
>70 years

<70 years

Sex
F > M

F = M

Headache

Jaw claudication

Present
Absent

Visual loss
Marked

Less marked

Optic disc
Pale disc edema

Hyperemic disc edema

C reactive protein
Raised

Normal

ESR
Highly raised

Raised

FFA

Disc delay and choroidal delay

Only disc delay

Treatment
Corticosteroids
Levodopa–carbidopa combination for 3 weeks and then double dose for 1 month

Note: Corticosteroids are not proven to be effective in NAAION.

The image given below shows pale disc edema of Arteritic AION.

questions.question: What does the given fundoscopic picture suggest?
questions.explanation: The given fundoscopic image clearly depicts cupping, thinning of the neuroretinal rim, and nasal shifting of vessels. This are characteristic of glaucomatous optic atrophy.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with optic atrophy?
questions.explanation:
Leprosy is not associated with optic atrophy.

All the other given conditions can cause optic atrophy.

Causes of optic atrophy:

• Primary optic atrophy

• Optic neuritis

• Compression by tumors and aneurysms

• Hereditary optic neuropathies

• Toxic and nutritional optic neuropathies

• Trauma

• Secondary optic atrophy

• Chronic papilledema

• Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

• Papillitis

• Consecutive optic atrophy

• Extensive retinal photocoagulation

• Retinitis pigmentosa

• Prior central retinal artery occlusion

• Glaucomatous optic atrophy

questions.question: A 24-year-old man with a history of pernicious anemia was referred to ophthalmology for complaints of gradually progressing visual disturbances. On perimetry, which of the following defects is most likely to be seen in him?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario of pernicious anemia with gradually progressive visual disturbances is suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency.

B12 deficiency is known to cause centrocecal scotoma and it is an important cause of nutritional optic atrophy.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy has bilateral optic atrophy with diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario suggests Wolfram syndrome. It is due to WFS1 gene mutation.

The presentation is usually between the ages of 5 and 21 years; diabetes mellitus is typically the first manifestation, followed by visual problems. It has a poor prognosis.

Clinical features are: (DIDMOAD)

• Diabetes insipidus

• Diabetes mellitus

• Optic atrophy

• Deafness (sensorineural type)

Option A: Kjer's optic neuropathy is an autosomal dominant condition. It presents with vision loss in early childhood and no significant systemic features.

Option B: Behr syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition. Clinical features include optic atrophy, pyramidal tract signs, ataxia, intellectual disability, urinary incontinence, and pes cavus

Option D: Leber's congenital amaurosis is an autosomal recessive condition. It usually presents with significant vision loss in infancy and nystagmus.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of amaurosis fugax ?
questions.explanation:
Amaurosis fugax is a sudden and transient monocular blindness, which is reversible.

It is a marker of advanced carotid artery atherosclerosis.

questions.question: Champagne cork disc is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Champagne cork disc is seen in chronic papilledema.

The optic disc gives the appearance of the dome of a champagne cork. Small drusen-like crystalline deposits (corpora amylacea) may appear on the disc surface.

The most reliable sign to differentiate between papillitis and papilledema is pupillary reaction. Pupillary light reflex is normal in papilledema whereas it is sluggish in papillitis.

questions.question: Which of the following defects is implicated in Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy?
questions.explanation:
