In Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), the defect is a mutation of maternal mitochondrial DNA. Therefore the condition has a maternal inheritance.

LHON causes bilateral, subacute painless loss of vision. The characteristic visual field defect is a centrocaecal scotoma. Pupillary light reflex is relatively preserved until the late stage of the disease. Optic neuritis and optic atrophy start in one eye and goes on to involve the other eye subsequently. It typically affects males between the ages of 15 and 35 years. The diagnosis of LHON should be considered in any patient with bilateral optic neuropathy, irrespective of age.

Prognosis is poor, although some visual recovery may occur in a minority of cases even years later.

Note: LHON plus refers to rare variants with additional manifestations such as neuromuscular dysfunction.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man developed a painless diminution of vision in his right eye 6 months ago but did not seek medical attention. Two weeks ago, he started to notice mild blurring in his left eye and has now come for evaluation. According to him, his elder brother and maternal uncle also had similar vision problems. Which fundus finding would point towards Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy in this patient?
options: Hyperemic optic disc with telangiectatic capillaries
questions.answer: C. Hyperemic optic disc with telangiectatic capillaries
questions.explanation:
Hyperemic optic disc with telangiectatic capillaries would be suggestive of LHON.

LHON is related to a mitochondrial DNA mutation. This results in impaired mitochondrial adenosine triphosphate production, which affects the highly energy-dependent optic nerve.

In the acute phase, the optic disc is hyperemic and swollen with telangiectatic capillaries. However, the optic disc does not leak on fluorescein angiography. Later stages may show primary optic atrophy.

questions.question: In order to diagnose a case as idiopathic intracranial hypertension, which of the following features is not necessary?
options: Elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture
questions.explanation:
Papilledema is not a mandatory criterion for the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH).

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is a diagnosis of exclusion. Obstructive, compressive, and infiltrative CNS lesions must be excluded by neuroimaging studies. Papilledema, although present in 90% of the patients, is not necessary for diagnosis. Elevated CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture is the hallmark of IIH.

Risk factors of IIH include:

• Female sex

• Obesity

• Nalidixic acid

• Tetracycline

• Vitamin A

• Oral contraceptives

• Use of or withdrawal from corticosteroids

questions.question: Which of the following is the most reliable sign to clinically differentiate between a case of papillitis and papilledema?
questions.explanation:
The most reliable sign to differentiate between papillitis and papilledema is pupillary reaction.

Pupillary light reflex is normal in papilledema whereas it is sluggish in papillitis. Visual acuity and colour vision are also relatively more preserved in papilledema compared to papillitis.

The other three disc signs seen on ophthalmoscopy are present in both papillitis and papilledema.

questions.question: A patient evaluated for dizziness and visual disturbances was found to have down-beating nystagmus. A brain lesion was suspected and the patient was referred for an MRI. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Pineal region and the dorsal midbrain
questions.explanation:
Down-beat nystagmus is usually due to a lesion at the cervico-medullary junction (e.g. Arnold-Chiari malformation, syringobulbia) or as a manifestation of cerebellar degeneration.

Other causes of down-beat nystagmus:

• Drugs (phenytoin, lithium, barbiturates, carbamazepine)

• Wernicke's encephalopathy

• Demyelinating disorders

Acquired nystagmus can be attributed to disturbances of the three mechanisms that normally ensure steady gaze—visual fixation, the vestibulo-ocular reflex, and the mechanism that makes it possible to hold the eyes at an eccentric eye position (e.g. far-right gaze).

Other types of nystagmus:

Type of Nystagmus
Etiology

Slow-horizontal
Large posterior cerebral lesions (e.g. stroke)

Mixed horizontal (Torsional)
Usually associated with vertigo and seen in vestibular system lesions

Up-beat
Medulla, the ventral tegmentum and the anterior vermis of the cerebellum

Periodic alternating
Cerebellar disease (In PAN, the horizontal jerk nystagmus spontaneously reverses the direction of the quick phase every few seconds)

See-saw
Lesion involving parasellar region and optic chiasm (e.g. pituitary tumours, third ventricle)

Gaze-evoked
Side-effect of drugs, including sedatives, anticonvulsants and alcohol, as well as cerebellar disease

questions.question: An RTA patient with severe head trauma is admitted to the surgical ICU for observation. On examination, nystagmus was noted. His CT scan reveals a transverse fracture of his left temporal bone. Which of the following statements is true regarding the nystagmus?
options: Slow phase is towards the left and fast phase towards the right
Slow phase is towards the right and fast phase towards the left
It is an up-beating type of nystagmus
It is a down-beating type of nystagmus
questions.answer: A. Slow phase is towards the left and fast phase towards the right
questions.explanation:
Fracture of the temporal bone causes vestibular injury resulting in a horizontal nystagmus with slow phase towards the affected side and fast phase towards the opposite side.

Peripheral vestibular nystagmus occurs in lesions of the labyrinth or vestibular nerve. Normally, there is tonic input to the brainstem vestibular nuclei from the periphery. Loss of the tonic input from the left vestibular nerve leads to deviation of the eyes towards the left side, which is the slow phase of the nystagmus. The cortical correction brings the eyes back to the centre in the primary gaze which is the fast-phase directed towards the right side.

questions.question: You are evaluating an elderly patient in the stroke ICU, who was admitted three days back with a history of sudden onset nausea, vomiting, and gait abnormalities. The visual examination showed conjugate horizontal left gaze palsy. He could maintain gaze near mid-position but could not cross the midline to the left side. His MRI is likely to show involvement of which of the following brain areas?
questions.explanation:
Horizontal gaze palsy can occur due to a lesion in parapontine reticular formation (PPRF).

Horizontal gaze:

• It involves 2 muscles- the ipsilateral lateral rectus and the contralateral medial rectus.

• Center for this pathway is parapontine reticular formation (PPRF).

• From here, they move to the ipsilateral 6th nerve nucleus.

• Next, they pass through the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus.

Lesions affecting the abducens nuclei will also cause ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy, because of damage to motor neurons and internuclear neurons originating from the nuclei. Lesions involving the PPRF will lead to horizontal gaze palsy, as PPRF acts as a relay centre that connects the frontal eye fields in the cerebral cortex to the abducens nuclei. Conjugate horizontal gaze palsy can also be caused by lesion(s) involving both the abducens motor fibres and the MLFs preceding the abducens nucleus. Bilateral horizontal gaze palsy will be caused if lesion(s) involve both abducens nuclei or bilateral PPRF.

Isolated damage to the MLFs will cause the classic INO where eye abduction is preserved, however, the ipsilateral eye will not be able to be adducted on conjugate horizontal gaze.

Conjugate eye movements

• Binocular movements in which the eyes move synchronously and symmetrically in the same direction.

• Main types

• Saccades: They are fast movements controlled by the contralateral frontal lobe.

• Pursuits: They are slow following movements controlled by the ipsilateral occipital lobe.

Image: The Horizontal gaze pathway

Lesions in this pathway

• Horizontal gaze palsy: Due to lesion in the PPRF of the same side

• Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO): Caused by lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)

• One and a half syndrome: Caused by lesions in both MLF and PPRF of the same side

Vertical gaze palsy

Center is located in the rostral interstitial nucleus of the dorsal midbrain (riMLF).

The important types of vertical gaze palsy are as follows:

• Parinaud's syndrome: Upgaze palsy

• Steel–Richardsons syndrome: Downgaze palsy

questions.question: A patient has normal vertical saccades. On attempted left gaze as shown in the image below, the patient develops left jerk nystagmus. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
The most likely location of the lesion according to the given clinical scenario and the image is the right medial longitudinal fasciculus.

The image depicts an attempted left gaze and concludes that there is an adduction deficit in the right eye. This causes jerk nystagmus in the abducting left eye.

This is most likely due to a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) ipsilateral to the side of the adduction deficit. Hence, this is a case of a right MLF lesion or Right Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO).

questions.question: Ophthalmoplegic migraine clinically presents as ___________.
options: Headache with irreversible loss of optic nerve function
Headache associated with recurrent third nerve palsy
Headache associated with third, fourth, and sixth nerve palsy
questions.answer: C. Headache associated with third, fourth, and sixth nerve palsy
questions.explanation:
Ophthalmoplegic migraine refers to headache associated with third, fourth, and sixth nerve palsy.

Ophthalmoplegic migraine almost always involves the third nerve. Rare cases of sixth nerve involvement, and even rarer cases that involve the fourth nerve, have also been reported.

Clinical criteria for the diagnosis of ophthalmoplegic migraine include:

• A prior history of typical common or classic migraine headaches

• Ophthalmoplegia that occurs during (or, rarely, just before) an established migraine attack

• Exclusion of other reasonable causes by clinical and radiological studies

questions.question: For a patient presenting with gradual, painless diminution of vision, the differential diagnosis would not include _________.
questions.explanation:
Methyl alcohol amblyopia causes sudden painless diminution of vision.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the procedure shown in the image?
options: The concept of the procedure was introduced by Goldmann.
It is used to treat after cataract

The instrument shown is an applanation tonometer, which is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP).

The concept behind the procedure was introduced by Goldmann. It is based on Imbert-Fick law, which states that the pressure inside a sphere(P) is equal to the force (W) required to flatten its surface divided by the area of flattening (A).

questions.question: Which among the following phases indicate complete filling of the retinal arterioles and capillaries on fundus fluorescein angiography?
questions.explanation:
Complete filling of retinal arterioles and capillaries is seen in the arterio-venous phase.

In FFA, sodium fluorescein dye is injected into the antecubital vein. A fundus camera is then used to take photographs:

• 1st picture- after 5 seconds, then every second for 20 seconds, every 3–5 seconds for the next 1 minute

• Last picture- after 10 minutes

• Pre-arterial phase- choroidal circulation is filling

• Arterial phase- start filling of retinal arteriole till its completely filled

• Arterio-venous phase- complete filling of retinal arterioles and capillaries followed by laminar filling of veins

• Venous filling- arterioles are emptying and veins are filling

questions.question: Which of the following deficiencies would you suspect in a patient with acute retrobulbar neuritis?
questions.explanation:
Vitamin B1 deficiency can cause acute retrobulbar neuritis.

Nutritional optic neuropathy is characterized by bilateral, symmetric, cecocentral scotomas and disturbance of color vision. Fundus morphology is usually normal.

Deficiencies in the following vitamins are primarily responsible for the damage caused to the optic nerve: B1 (thiamine), B6 (pyridoxine), B9 (folic acid), and B12 (cobalamin). These vitamins are cofactors for many metabolic reactions and their deficiency leads to toxic byproduct accumulation within cells, which inhibits the electron transport chain and depresses mitochondrial function. Depletion of ATP leads to nerve dysfunction and eventual nerve death.

Chronic alcohol abuse is a commonly associated risk factor and a cause of malnourishment.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presented to the emergency department with an extremely painful right foot. He stated that he had an alcohol binge the previous night. Ocular manifestations seen in acute gout are episcleritis, scleritis, and uveitis. Ocular structures have a relatively poor solvent ability, in addition to lower temperatures. Therefore, they are predisposed to tophi deposition. As a result of urate deposits, crystal-induced inflammation of the affected tissue is responsible for causing episcleritis, scleritis, and uveitis.

questions.question: A 10-year-old girl with neurological manifestations was referred from the pediatric OPD. Her ocular examination findings is as given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image shows the Kayser–Fleisher (KF) ring, which is a characteristic finding of Wilson’s disease.

KF ring consists of the deposition of copper in the Descemet membrane of the cornea. The rings are usually golden-brown and are visible only under the slit-lamp. They do not impair vision. They disappear on treatment with anti-copper drugs and reappear with disease progression. They are a characteristic sign of Wilson’s disease but are not pathognomonic. They can also be seen in:

• Primary biliary cholangitis

• Primary sclerosing cholangitis

• Cholestasis.

Sunflower cataract is a rare finding of Wilson's disease. It occurs due to the deposition of copper in the centre of the lens. It consists of a greenish central opacity with spoke-like radial opacities and is visible only under the slit-lamp. It is also seen in chalcosis (deposition of intraocular copper-containing foreign body).

questions.question:
Which of the following conditions can occur as an ocular manifestation in a patient with dengue?

1. Subconjunctival hemorrhage

2. Uveitis

3. Cataract

4. Retinal hemorrhage

5. Pappilitis
questions.explanation:
Cataract is not an ocular manifestation of dengue.

Dengue has varied manifestations, in different organ systems, mainly of inflammation and bleeding. Until recently, apart from retro-orbital pain, eye involvement was not recognized as a common feature of dengue infection. Potential pathogenic mechanisms include a direct viral effect on the eye, an immune-mediated vasculitis, and/or a variety of secondary effects related to dengue-induced vascular leakage and hemostatic derangements.

Ocular manifestations of dengue:

• Typically, patients complain of painless visual impairment within 1 week from illness onset, often around the time of the platelet nadir.

• Conjunctival injection and subconjunctival hemorrhage.

• Complications such as retinal hemorrhage, retinal edema, macular ischemia, macular edema, vitreous hemorrhage, vitritis, and optic neuritis or papillitis

• Depending on the severity of the ocular lesion, gradual improvement in vision occurs over several weeks, although in rare cases permanent visual impairment may result.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man presented with complaints of diminution of vision in both eyes for the last 6 - 8 months. On examination, bilateral cataracts were seen. Incidentally, you also note iris pearls. Which of the following conditions should you suspect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Iris pearls are pearly-white nodules seen on the iris in leprosy.

They are asymptomatic, 0.3 to 1.0 mm in diameter, dull yellowish-white in colour, and are seen at an early stage of the disease. It is not associated with any inflammatory changes in the anterior chamber. Histologically, it consists of lepromatous bacilli packed within mononuclear cells or acid-fast material with accompanying foreign body reaction. Inside the eye, leprosy bacilli preferentially lodge in the iris and ciliary body, due to the relatively cooler temperatures and high vascularity.

questions.question: An elderly patient admitted with multiple comorbidities in the ICU, developed exposure keratitis and ulceration. An ophthalmology opinion was sought. Incidentally, on fundoscopy, the resident found the following picture. What is this most likely due to?
questions.explanation:
The given image suggests a diagnosis of proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

The hallmark of Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is neovascularization. Abnormal new vessel formation, which occurs on the inner (vitreous) surface of the retina and may extend into the vitreous cavity, can cause vitreous haemorrhage. Neovascularization is often accompanied by pre-retinal fibrous tissue, which, along with the vitreous, can contract, resulting in traction retinal detachment. In addition, tiny microaneurysms can also be seen.

The treatment available for proliferative diabetic retinopathy is photocoagulation of the ischaemic areas to reduce the metabolic demand and decrease or prevent the release of vasoproliferative factors.

• Direct goniolens- provides a direct view of the angle

Application:

• To view the angle of the anterior chamber

• Localization of the foreign body, abnormal blood vessels, or tumors in the angle

• Demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae

• Direct goniolens can be used during goniotomy

questions.question: During a visit to the ophthalmology department, you see the following test being performed for visual field charting of a patient. Identify the instrument used from the options given below.
questions.explanation:
The image given above shows a Lister's perimeter. It is used in manual perimetry for visual field charting

Classification:

• Manual: Confrontation, Listers, Campimetry, Goldmann perimeter

• Automated: Octopus, Field Master, Humphrey Field Analyzer

• Static: Friedman, Automated

• Kinetic: Confrontation, Listers, Scotometry, Goldmann

The best type is automated perimetry.

questions.question: Which among the following would you use for the measurement of intraocular pressure in a patient with a scarred cornea?
questions.explanation:
Tonopen is used for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in a scarred cornea.

It is a hand-held electronic contact tonometer (a modified version of the older Mackay–Marg tonometer). Besides portability, its main advantage is the ability to measure IOP reasonably accurately in eyes with distorted or edematous corneas and through a soft contact lens.

Types of tonometry:

• Indentation tonometry- Reading depends on scleral rigidity, e.g., Schiotz tonometer

• Applanation tonometry- Based on the amount of force needed to flatten or applanate a known area of the cornea, Imbert–Fick principle. This is further divided into two types -

• Fixed force: IOP is proportional to the area, e.g., Maklakov, Barraquer

• Fixed area and variable force: IOP is proportional to force. The most reliable is Goldmann.

• Self-measurement: Rebound

• Non-contact type: Pulse Air, Air-Puff

• Irregular cornea: Tonopen, MacKay–Marg

Recent tonometers:

• Pascals tonometer (dynamic contour tonometry [DCT]): Contact; used for post-LASIK IOP measurement.

• Reichert Ocular Response Analyzer®: Non-contact

Note: Tonography is a non-invasive technique for determining the facility of aqueous outflow.

questions.question: A first-year ophthalmology resident is asked to counsel the parents of a 1-month-old infant diagnosed with a lamellar congenital cataract in both eyes. He discusses the treatment options and mentions that the following lens will be used in the surgery. This lens is a __________
options: Posterior chamber intra ocular lens (modified C-loop type)
Singh and Worst's iris claw lens
Posterior chamber intra ocular lens (four loop type)
questions.answer: B. Posterior chamber intra ocular lens (modified C-loop type)
questions.explanation:
Cataract surgery with an intraocular lens (IOL) implantation is the treatment of choice in congenital cataracts. The above image depicts a modified C-loop type of posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL) used in such cases.

This surgery involves an extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) with primary posterior capsulorhexis and anterior vitrectomy. After removal of the cataractous lens, a posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL) is implanted.

PCIOL rest entirely behind the iris. They may be supported and fixed as follows:

• Capsular bag fixation of PCIOL (most ideal method)

• Ciliary sulcus fixation

• Sclera fixation

Parts of the IOL:

• The central part overlying the optic axis is called the optic.

• The peripheral arms used for placement and stabilization are the haptics.

 The image given below shows different types of intraocular lens.

questions.question: As an intern posted in the department, you are assisting a senior surgical ophthalmologist for cataract surgery on a 72-year-old man. You notice the nursing head pass him the following lens for implantation. This is a ____________________
options: Posterior chamber intra ocular lens (modified C-loop type)
Singh and Worst's Iris claw lens
Posterior chamber intra ocular lens (four loop type)
questions.explanation:
The image depicts Kelman multiflex type of anterior chamber intraocular lens (ACIOL). It is the most commonly used ACIOL.

Anterior chamber IOLs lie entirely in front of the iris and are supported in the angle of the anterior chamber. IOL implantation is the method of choice for correcting aphakia.

These are associated with a higher incidence of bullous keratopathy.

questions.question: Identify the given instrument.
questions.explanation:
The given image depicts a Maddox wing. It is an instrument by which the amount of heterophoria for near vision can be measured.

Methods to examine heterophoria:

• Testing for refractive error

• Cover–uncover test

• Prism bar cover test (PBCT)

• Maddox rod test

• Maddox wing test

• Maddox tangent scale: heterophoria for distance

• Measurement of the near point of convergence: Using RAF rule (Normally, it is 70 mm)

• Measurement of fusional reserve- done with a synoptophore or prism bar

questions.question: You would identify the instrument shown in the image below as:
questions.explanation:
The image shows Jackson’s cross cylinder (flip-cross technique) which is used to refine the power and axis of the cylindrical lens.

Option A: Nagel’s anomaloscope is used to test color vision.

Option C: Maddox rod consists of parallel red or colorless cylinders stacked together. Maddox rod test is a macular function test used to measure the degree of heterotropia or heterophoria in cases of torsional diplopia.

Option D: Retinoscope

questions.question: What is the investigation shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
The given image depicts Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of a normal macula.

It is a non-invasive, noncontact imaging system providing high-resolution cross-sectional images of the posterior segment. It uses near-infrared light interferometry to do so.

questions.question: What is the principle of the test in which the patient is asked to read the chart shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
The given image depicts a duo-chrome test based on chromatic aberration. It is used to refine the final sphere in subjective refraction.

The patient is asked to compare the clarity of the letters on the green and the red side. If a myopic sees the letters of the green side clearer, he is overcorrected. So, +0.25 D sphere is added or -0.25D is removed. However, if a myopic sees the letters on the red side clearer, he is undercorrected and -0.25 D sphere is added. With optimal spherical correction, the letters on the red and green halves of the chart appear equally clear.

questions.question: Which optical instrument provides an inverted and reversed image of the retina?
options: Goldmann contact lens and slit lamp
questions.explanation:
An indirect ophthalmoscope produces a real, inverted and laterally reversed image of the fundus.

All the other instruments mentioned including direct ophthalmoscope, Hruby lens and Goldman contact lens produce a virtual and erect image of the fundus.

questions.question: You see the following examination being performed in the ophthal OPD. What is the instrument being used?
questions.explanation:
The image shows Hertel's exophthalmometer.

Exophthalmometry: measures protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin (with the eyes looking straight ahead).

An absolute protrusion of >20 mm or a difference of >2 mm between the two eyes is labeled as proptosis.

Instruments used to measure proptosis:

• Luedde exophthalmometer

• Hertel’s exophthalmometer- most common instrument used. Its advantage is that it measures both eyes simultaneously.

questions.question: Identify the instrument shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
The given instrument is a gonioscope.

It is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber (gonioscopy).

Types:

• Indirect gonioprism- provides a mirror image of the opposite angle

• Direct goniolens- provides a direct view of the angle

Application:

• To view the angle of the anterior chamber

• Localization of foreign body, abnormal blood vessels, or tumors in the angle

• Demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae

• Direct goniolens used during goniotomy

questions.question: While evaluating a child with suspected refractive error, you notice that the ophthalmology resident performs a retinoscopy. Which of the following is this test based on?
questions.explanation:
Retinoscopy is an objective method used to determine the error of refraction by applying the method of neutralization. It is also called skiascopy or shadow test.

Principle: When light is reflected from a mirror into the eye, the direction in which light will travel across the pupil will depend upon the eye's refractive state.

Distance: Usually, the doctor sits at a distance of 1 meter or an arm's length.

Types of retinoscopes:

• Priestley–Smith retinoscope

• Streak retinoscope
